title: Minimum Foreign Investment in Nepal: NPR 20 Million Rule
content:
Nepal's foreign investment rules are open in principle, but they are not open at any size. The law sets a minimum entry amount, and that figure shapes the structure, the approval route and the amount of capital that must be recorded at Nepal Rastra Bank. For most investors, the number to plan around is NPR 20 million.

This guide explains what the minimum means, what it covers, when it applies, and the mistakes that cause an otherwise viable project to fail at the approval stage.

Quick answer

The general minimum foreign investment in Nepal is NPR 20 million per foreign investor under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act, 2075 (FITTA) and the rules made under it. The threshold was reduced from NPR 50 million in October 2022. It is not a fee, and it is not the same as the company's paid-up capital. It is the minimum amount of foreign investment that must be approved and brought into Nepal through banking channels. Sector-specific exceptions and NRN concessions should be confirmed before you structure the investment.

ItemDetail
General minimumNPR 20 million per foreign investor
Legal basisFITTA 2075 and the rules made under it
ChangeReduced from NPR 50 million by gazette in October 2022
Who it applies toForeign investors, including foreign companies and eligible NRNs, subject to sector rules
What it is notA government fee, or the same thing as authorised or paid-up capital
Capital routeBanking channels, recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank
Approval authorityDepartment of Industry, or Investment Board Nepal above the statutory threshold
Typical timelineThree to five months end to end
If the minimum is not metApproval may be refused, or the structure must be revised

What the NPR 20 million minimum actually means

The minimum is an entry threshold for foreign investment. It is the amount the foreign investor must commit and bring into Nepal under an approved investment. It is not a fee paid to the government, and it does not disappear into a licence. It becomes capital in the Nepali company, or the approved investment vehicle, and it must be documented from the first remittance.

That documentation is what makes the investment usable later. Nepal Rastra Bank records the inflow, and that record is the evidence you rely on when you want to repatriate dividends, sale proceeds or capital on exit. An investment that is approved but not properly recorded can create a repatriation problem years later, even if the business itself is successful.

Is the minimum per investor or per company?

The general rule is expressed per foreign investor, not per company. That distinction matters in a joint venture. If two foreign investors each subscribe to shares, the DOI will look at the structure and the proposed shareholding when applying the threshold. Do not assume that a single NPR 20 million investment covers an unlimited number of foreign shareholders, and do not split an investment artificially to avoid the rule. Confirm the treatment with the DOI before you draft the shareholding.

What counts toward the minimum

Foreign investment can take several forms: equity in a Nepali company, a shareholder loan, reinvestment of profits, or a technology transfer arrangement. The minimum threshold is generally measured against the foreign equity investment. A shareholder loan or a technology transfer fee is a separate component and should not be assumed to satisfy the equity minimum on its own.

In-kind contributions, such as plant, machinery or equipment, can form part of the investment. They require valuation, customs clearance where applicable, and NRB approval. The value attributed to the goods must be documented and consistent with the approval. An inflated valuation creates problems at the banking and tax stages, and an undervaluation can leave the investor short of the threshold.

Sector exceptions and the negative list

The minimum applies alongside sector eligibility rules. Nepal maintains a negative list of activities that are restricted or closed to foreign investment. If your activity is on the list, the question is not how much you plan to invest; the activity cannot be approved in that form. Sector-specific rules can also impose different thresholds or conditions, so confirm the current position for your activity before you commit capital.

Some routes are treated differently. NRNs invest under FITTA and may have access to concessions, and certain sectors are subject to their own approval regimes. These are policy details that change, which is why the threshold should be checked at the time of investment rather than assumed from an older guide.

Information technology and digital services are the clearest exception. Following the October 2023 notice, foreign investment in the ICT sector is exempt from the minimum threshold. The approval and NRB recording requirements still apply, and the exemption should be confirmed for the specific activity.

The minimum is not the same as paid-up capital

Paid-up capital is the amount shareholders have actually subscribed and paid for their shares. The FDI minimum is the foreign investment threshold. For a foreign-owned company, the two should be aligned: the approved foreign investment, the issued share capital and the memorandum and articles of association should describe the same structure. A mismatch is one of the most common reasons a filing is returned or a bank delays the capital recording.

Authorised capital is a separate concept again. It is the maximum capital the company may issue, and it drives the OCR registration fee. Setting authorised capital higher than necessary increases the fee without helping the FDI approval. Set it to match the approved investment and the company's actual funding plan.

How the capital must enter Nepal

Capital must come in through formal banking channels and be recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank. The remittance should state the correct purpose, such as share investment or loan investment, and the amount should match the approval. The commercial bank handles the NRB reporting, and the investor should keep the remittance advice, the NRB record and the company's share register together.

Informal channels, offset arrangements and under-invoicing are not substitutes. They may move money, but they do not create a recognised investment. The consequence usually appears at the point of repatriation, when the bank and the regulator ask for evidence that the capital entered lawfully. By then, the problem is expensive to fix.

What happens if you invest less

If the proposed investment falls below the applicable minimum, the DOI may refuse the application or require the structure to be revised. In some cases, a different route or a different sector may have a lower threshold, but that is a legal question, not a workaround. Splitting an investment between related parties or using a nominee to stay under the threshold creates regulatory and repatriation risk.

A worked example

A Dubai-based investor wants to own 100% of an IT services company in Nepal. The general minimum is NPR 20 million, so the project is structured around that figure. The investor files for FDI approval, incorporates the private limited company at the OCR, opens a corporate bank account and remits the capital through banking channels. The bank reports the inflow to Nepal Rastra Bank, and the investor keeps the NRB record with the share register and the approval letter.

If the same investor had remitted only NPR 15 million, the approval and the capital record would not match. The company might still be incorporated and trading, but the shortfall would surface when the investor later applies to repatriate dividends or sale proceeds. Fixing it at that stage requires additional approvals, bank reconciliation and time.

Timeline and costs

A straightforward FDI approval usually takes two to six weeks after a complete filing, and the full sequence from approval to recorded capital commonly runs three to five months. Document legalisation, translation and banking delays are often the largest variables. Government fees depend on the company's authorised capital and the applicable schedules, while professional fees depend on the structure, the project report and the sector.

Common mistakes

  • Incorporating before FDI approval. The approval comes first, and the company documents should match it.
  • Sending capital before approval. Money that arrives early is difficult to recognise and can stall the file.
  • Under-invoicing or using informal channels. The capital may not be recognised for future repatriation.
  • Assuming the minimum is per company. The general rule is per foreign investor, so confirm the shareholding structure.
  • Ignoring sector rules. A negative-list activity cannot be fixed by increasing the investment.

Frequently asked questions

Is the minimum NPR 20 million per investor or per company?

The general rule is NPR 20 million per foreign investor, not per company. If more than one foreign investor subscribes, confirm how the DOI will apply the threshold to the proposed shareholding.

Can I invest less than NPR 20 million?

Generally no for a standard foreign investment. Some sectors and NRN routes may be treated differently, so confirm the current position with the DOI before structuring a smaller investment.

Does the minimum apply to loans and technology transfer?

The threshold is generally measured by foreign equity investment. A shareholder loan or technology transfer fee is a separate component and should not be assumed to satisfy the equity minimum.

Can I bring the capital in stages?

Often yes, if the approval and project plan allow it. The total approved investment must still meet the minimum, and every tranche must enter through banking channels and be recorded at NRB.

What if my investment is in machinery or equipment?

In-kind contributions can form part of the investment, but they require valuation, customs clearance and NRB approval. The value attributed must be documented and consistent with the approval.

Is the minimum the same as paid-up capital?

No. The minimum is the foreign investment threshold. Paid-up capital is the amount shareholders have actually subscribed. For a foreign-owned company, the two should be aligned in the approval and the charter.

Do NRNs have a lower minimum?

NRNs invest under FITTA and may have access to concessions or different treatment. The rules change, so confirm the current threshold for your route before relying on a lower amount.

Does the minimum apply to IT companies?

No. Following the October 2023 notice, foreign investment in information technology and digital services is exempt from the minimum threshold. The FDI approval and NRB recording requirements still apply.

What happens if I use informal channels or under-invoice?

Capital that is not brought in through banking channels and recorded at NRB may not be recognised for repatriation. That can block dividends, sale proceeds and exit payments later, and may create regulatory exposure.

title: Hotel Registration in Nepal Through Foreign Investment
content:
Opening a hotel in Nepal looks straightforward from the outside. The sector is open to foreign investment, tourism is a national priority, and the demand for well-run accommodation is steady. What first-time investors underestimate is the number of separate approvals a hotel needs, and the fact that they sit with different authorities. The result is that an investment can be approved and still not be ready to open.

This guide sets out the approvals a hotel needs, in the order they should be secured, so your opening date is a plan rather than a hope.

Quick answer

This guide covers the complete process of registering a hotel in Nepal through foreign investment, including the legal framework (Tourism Act 2035, Hotel Lodge Restaurant Bar Rules 2038, FITTA 2019, FITTR 2021, IEA 2020), why hotels are open to 100% foreign ownership (unlike travel agencies), the 8 hotel classification categories (General Tourist Standard through 5-Star Deluxe), minimum FDI threshold (NPR 20 million), the full 10-step process from DOI FDI approval through DoT hotel classification, the Standard Fixation Committee’s role, hotel construction standards, star classification criteria and fees (NPR 5,000 to NPR 60,000), the 5-year classification renewal requirement, NRB investment recording and profit repatriation rules, post-registration compliance obligations including semi-annual reporting, tax incentives for hotel investment, and 12 FAQs. Researched and verified against 2025 regulations by the Pluto Associates legal team, Kathmandu.

Introduction: Why Nepal’s Hotel Sector Is One of Its Best Foreign Investment Opportunities

Nepal’s tourism industry is one of the country’s most strategically important economic sectors. With over 1.2 million tourists visiting annually, a landscape that includes eight of the world’s ten highest mountains, world-heritage listed cities, ancient Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage sites, and national parks of extraordinary biodiversity, Nepal has the natural and cultural raw material to sustain a hospitality industry of far greater scale than currently exists.

The good news for foreign investors: Unlike travel agencies and trekking companies, which are on FITTA’s Negative List and closed to foreign ownership, hotels are explicitly open to foreign direct investment. A foreign national or foreign company can own 100% of a hotel in Nepal without requiring a Nepali joint venture partner. This is a significant distinction that makes the hospitality sector one of the most accessible for international capital in Nepal’s entire economy.

The process of establishing a foreign-invested hotel in Nepal is a multi-stage regulatory journey that spans the Department of Industry (for FDI approval), the Office of Company Registrar (for company incorporation), Nepal Rastra Bank (for capital recording and foreign exchange compliance), and the Department of Tourism (for hotel registration and star classification). Each stage has its own documents, timelines, and requirements. This guide walks through every step.

Legal Framework: Laws Governing Hotel Investment and Registration in Nepal

A foreign-invested hotel in Nepal sits at the intersection of investment law, tourism law, and company law. Understanding each layer is essential before committing capital or approaching any government office.

Law / Instrument

Year

Relevance to Hotel Registration

Tourism Act (Paryatan Ain)

2035 (1978)

Primary tourism legislation. Section 10 governs hotel registration. Section 11 establishes the Standard Fixation Committee for hotel classification. Section 47 requires semi-annual reporting by registered hotels. Defines the legal basis for all hotel licensing in Nepal.

Hotel, Lodge, Restaurant, Bar and Tourist Guide Rules (HLRB Rules)

2038 (1981)

Detailed operational rules implementing the Tourism Act for the hospitality sector. Rule 3 sets out the hotel registration application procedure. Rule 5 requires star hotels to adhere to standards fixed by the Standard Fixation Committee. Defines minimum facility requirements for each hotel category.

Hotel Standard (Hotelको Maan)

2077 (2020)

Updated classification criteria for all hotel categories. Specifies the exact minimum standards, room count, bathroom ratios, food service, safety facilities, accessibility, for each star category from General Tourist Standard through 5-Star Deluxe.

Tourism Industry Service Delivery Directory

2070 (2013)

Section 83 requires star-rated hotels to renew their DoT classification every 5 years. Section 83(2) mandates renewal application before expiry.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA)

2019 (2076 BS)

Primary FDI law. Hotels are NOT on the Negative List, foreign investment in hotels is permitted, including 100% foreign ownership. Governs FDI approval process, minimum investment threshold (NPR 20 million), investor rights, and repatriation of profits.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Rules (FITTR)

2021 (2077 BS)

Implements FITTA. Provides procedural details on FDI application, document requirements, the investment schedule (three-stage capital injection timeline), and automatic approval route for investments up to NPR 500 million.

Industrial Enterprises Act (IEA)

2076 (2020)

Requires industry registration after company incorporation. Hotels qualify as service industries under the IEA and must be registered at the Department of Industry. Operations must commence within 1 year of industry registration.

Companies Act (Kampani Ain)

2063 (2006)

Governs company incorporation at the OCR. All hotel businesses must be incorporated as companies before approaching any other regulatory authority.

Nepal Rastra Bank Act + FERA

2058 / 2019

Nepal Rastra Bank regulates foreign currency transactions. All FDI capital must be remitted through official banking channels and recorded with NRB within 6 months of injection. Profit repatriation requires NRB approval and tax clearance.

Income Tax Act

2058 (2002)

Hotel income is subject to corporate income tax. Special tax incentives apply for hotels in certain geographic areas. PAN registration and annual tax filing are mandatory.

⚖️ Key Distinction from Travel Agencies: The FITTA 2019 Negative List explicitly includes travel agencies, trekking agencies, and tour operators, these are closed to foreign investment. Hotels are NOT on this Negative List. A foreign investor can own 100% of a hotel company in Nepal without a Nepali partner. This is the single most important legal fact for any foreign investor evaluating Nepal’s hospitality sector.

Hotel Classification in Nepal: What Category Will Your Hotel Fall Into?

Before beginning any registration process, the foreign investor must understand Nepal’s hotel classification system. Your hotel’s category determines which specific construction standards apply, what facilities are mandatory, what fees you pay at the Department of Tourism, and how you will be marketed to incoming tourists.

Nepal’s Department of Tourism, through its Standard Fixation Committee, classifies hotels into the following categories as per the Hotel Standard 2077 and the HLRB Rules 2038:

📌 Classification Is Mandatory: Every hotel operating in Nepal must obtain a classification from the Department of Tourism’s Standard Fixation Committee before opening to guests. Operating without DoT classification is illegal under the Tourism Act 2035 and attracts penalties and forced closure. The classification also determines your legal right to call your property a “5-Star” or any other rated hotel, using a star rating without DoT classification is a misrepresentation.

3.1 The Standard Fixation Committee

The Standard Fixation Committee is a body established by the Government of Nepal under Section 11 of the Tourism Act 2035. It is responsible for recommending the classification or registration of hotels, lodges, restaurants, resorts, and bars as tourism standards. The Committee inspects proposed or completed hotel properties against the criteria established in the Hotel Standard 2077 and makes classification recommendations to the Department of Tourism.

For a new hotel project, the Standard Fixation Committee inspection typically occurs after construction is complete and the hotel is substantially ready for operation. The investor cannot receive the final hotel classification certificate until this inspection has been conducted and the Committee is satisfied that all applicable standards are met.

Foreign Investment Eligibility: Who Can Invest and How Much Is Required?

4.1 Eligible Foreign Investors

  • Foreign nationals: Any foreign national above 18 years of age from a country with which Nepal has diplomatic relations can invest in a hotel in Nepal.
  • Foreign companies: Any company registered and operating in a foreign country can invest in a Nepali hotel, subject to FITTA 2019 compliance.
  • 100% foreign ownership: Hotels are fully open to 100% foreign ownership. A Nepali joint venture partner is not legally required, though many foreign investors choose to partner with Nepali investors for local market knowledge and relationship networks.
  • No country-specific exclusions: There is no list of excluded countries for hotel investment in Nepal, subject to any applicable government sanctions or orders.

4.2 Minimum Investment Threshold

Under FITTA 2019, the minimum foreign investment in Nepal is NPR 20,000,000 (NPR 20 million, approximately USD 150,000) for most sectors. For hotels, this represents a very low floor relative to the actual cost of establishing any commercially viable hotel property. In practice, even a modest 3-star hotel in Kathmandu requires investment well above the NPR 20 million threshold.

Investment Size (NPR)

Approval Authority

Approval Route

NPR 20 million to NPR 500 million

Department of Industry (DoI), FITT Unit, OSSC

Automatic Route (7-day statutory processing window)

NPR 500 million to NPR 6 billion

Department of Industry (DoI)

Standard Route (30-45 days)

Above NPR 6 billion (~USD 45 million)

IBN Standard Route (60-90 days)

4.3 Forms of Foreign Investment Recognized Under FITTA 2019

Foreign investment in a Nepali hotel can take several forms, all recognized under Section 2(j) of FITTA 2019:

  • Equity investment: Purchase of shares in a Nepali hotel company. The most common FDI form.
  • Reinvestment of earnings: Reinvesting dividends or profits generated by the hotel back into the business.
  • Loan capital: Loans from foreign lenders to the hotel company, subject to NRB approval for foreign borrowing.
  • Technology transfer: Contribution of proprietary hotel management systems, brand licenses, or operational know-how in exchange for equity or royalties.
  • Franchise arrangements: International hotel brand franchise agreements (e.g. Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt franchise) constitute a form of technology/brand transfer recognized under FITTA.

A worked example

A foreign investor plans a boutique hotel in Pokhara. Foreign investment approval comes first, followed by incorporation, then the building approval, then the tourism registration, the municipal business registration, the kitchen hygiene permit and the liquor licence for the bar. Each one is modest. Together they decide whether the hotel can open on schedule.

Because the investor mapped the approvals before construction began, the kitchen and bar were compliant on the first day of operation. Had the approvals been sorted after opening, the first inspection would have closed the bar, and the cost of that delay would have exceeded the cost of the licences many times over.

We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

Frequently asked questions

Can a foreigner own 100% of a hotel in Nepal? Yes. Hotels are not on the negative list under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act 2019, unlike travel and trekking agencies, so full foreign ownership needs no Nepali partner. FDI approval from the Department of Industry still comes first.

How long does hotel registration take in Nepal? Allow two to three months for the full sequence. FDI approval through the Automatic Route takes seven working days for investments up to NPR 500 million, and the Department of Tourism classification follows inspection of the finished hotel.

What is the minimum investment for a foreign funded hotel? NPR 20 million under FITTA 2019, which is about USD 150,000. The Department of Industry approves investments up to NPR 6 billion, and larger projects go to Investment Board Nepal.

Who assigns the star rating to a hotel in Nepal? The Standard Fixation Committee, formed under Section 11 of the Tourism Act 2035, inspects the property against the Hotel Standard 2077 and recommends a category to the Department of Tourism. Using a star rating without that classification is a misrepresentation.

What is the correct order of hotel approvals? FDI approval at the Department of Industry, company registration at the Office of the Company Registrar, industry registration under the Industrial Enterprises Act 2020, then hotel registration and classification at the Department of Tourism. Municipal and hygiene permits run alongside.

How much does hotel classification cost? Department of Tourism fees run from NPR 5,000 for a one star hotel to NPR 60,000 for a five star deluxe property. Classification must be renewed every five years under the Tourism Industry Service Delivery Directory 2070.

Can I repatriate profits from my hotel? Yes, once the capital is recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank within six months of injection and tax clearance is obtained. FITTA 2019 allows dividends and returns on investment to be remitted abroad.

What reports must a registered hotel file? Semi annual returns go to the Department of Tourism under Section 47 of the Tourism Act 2035. Annual income tax filings and any VAT obligations with the Inland Revenue Department continue as well.

Is a liquor licence part of hotel registration? No. Building approval from the municipality, kitchen hygiene clearance, fire safety checks and a liquor licence for the bar are separate from the tourism licence. Secure them before opening day.

title: Establishing an Industry in Nepal as a Foreigner: FITTA 2019 Guide
content:
Establishing an industry as a foreigner is one of the more involved routes into Nepal, and one of the most rewarding when it is done properly. The country wants manufacturing and industrial investment, and the legal framework reflects that. What the framework also reflects, with equal clarity, is that industrial activity touches land, environment, labour and foreign exchange all at once, and each of those sits with a different authority.

This guide explains the full route in plain language, from the first approval to the day your plant is operating, so you can plan with realistic expectations rather than guesswork.

Quick answer

This guide covers everything a foreigner needs to know about establishing an industry in Nepal in 2025, including the legal framework (FITTA 2019, FITTR 2021, IEA 2020, Companies Act 2063), the nine forms of foreign investment, who qualifies as a foreign investor, the FITTA Negative List, the IEA classification of industries, the Automatic and Standard approval routes, company and industry registration steps, capital injection rules, government fees, tax incentives, investor protections, profit repatriation and post-registration compliance. Researched and verified against 2025 regulations.

Introduction: Why Nepal Is Attracting More Foreign Industrialists Than Ever

Something has genuinely shifted in Nepal’s investment story. In the first nine months of fiscal year 2024/25, Nepal recorded approximately NPR 58 billion in foreign investment commitments, with a remarkable 97% of those commitments flowing through the Automatic Route that the government introduced in 2023.

What does 'establishing an industry' mean in Nepal’s legal framework? It means more than opening a consulting office or a retail shop. In Nepal, an 'industry' is a specific category of business as defined by the Industrial Enterprises Act (IEA) 2020, one that produces goods, provides services, or engages in any activity classified as an industrial enterprise under the Act. This classification is the prerequisite for foreign investment: FITTA 2019 is explicit that foreign investment can only be made in businesses that qualify as an industry under the IEA. If your proposed activity does not meet the IEA’s definition, FDI approval cannot be granted.

The Legal Framework: Laws That Govern Foreign Industry Establishment in Nepal

Nepal’s foreign investment framework is built on four primary laws that work together.

Law

Year

What It Governs for Foreign Investors

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA)

2019 (2076 BS)

The cornerstone legislation. Defines foreign investment in nine distinct forms, eligible sectors, minimum thresholds, the Automatic and Standard approval routes, investor protections (national treatment, repatriation guarantee, dispute resolution), profit repatriation rules, and technology transfer provisions. Amended January 2025 to allow investment through venture capital funds registered with SEBON.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Regulations (FITTR)

2021 (2077 BS)

Implements FITTA procedurally. Provides document requirements, the critical 3-stage investment injection schedule under Rule 9, timelines for each stage, royalty payment limits for technology transfer agreements (capped at 5% of net annual sales), and operational guidance for the Automatic Route.

Industrial Enterprises Act (IEA)

2020 (2076 BS)

Defines what constitutes an 'industry' eligible for foreign investment. Classifies industries by fixed asset size (micro/cottage/small/medium/large) and by type (manufacturing/service/infrastructure/agro-processing/energy/mining). Foreign investment can ONLY be made in businesses that qualify as industries under this Act. Also provides the tax incentive framework by industry category and location.

Companies Act (Kampani Ain)

2063 (2006)

Governs company incorporation at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR). All foreign-invested industries must be incorporated as Private Limited or Public Limited companies. Company registration follows FDI approval and precedes industry registration. The CAMIS portal (camis.ocr.gov.np) is the online interface.

Income Tax Act

2058 (2002)

Corporate income tax at 25% standard rate. Specific reduced rates and multi-year full exemptions for certain industry types and geographic locations. PAN registration mandatory before any commercial operations.

Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA)

2019 BS (1962)

All FDI capital must enter Nepal through official banking channels (SWIFT). No cash investments permitted. Each foreign currency injection must be recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) within 6 months of receipt. Governs profit repatriation.

Special Economic Zone Act

2073 (2016)

Governs investment in Nepal’s SEZs (Bhairahawa, Simara, and others). Investors in SEZs receive enhanced incentives: 10-year full income tax exemption, duty-free import of raw materials, and dividend tax exemption for first 5 years. Key destination for export-oriented manufacturers.

⚖️ The One Stop Service Centre (OSSC): The OSSC at the Department of Industry (DoI), Tripureshwor, Kathmandu, is the primary interface for all FDI registration activities. It brings together the DoI, OCR, IRD, NRB, Department of Immigration, and other agencies under one roof. Online portal: imis.doind.gov.np. Office hours: Sunday, Friday, 10:00 AM, 5:00 PM. For investments above NPR 6 billion, approach the Investment Board Nepal (IBN) at Singha Durbar instead.

Who Qualifies as a Foreign Investor Under Nepal’s Law?

The definition of 'foreign investor' under FITTA 2019 Section 2(h) is deliberately broad. It encompasses far more than just passport-holding foreigners.

Investor Type

Definition Under FITTA 2019

Key Notes

Foreign individual

Any person who is not a Nepali citizen

Includes foreign nationals of any country with which Nepal has diplomatic relations

Foreign company / firm

Any company or business entity incorporated outside Nepal

Can be 100% foreign-owned. Must provide authenticated corporate documents.

Non-Resident Nepali (NRN)

Nepali citizen permanently residing abroad with NRN status

Classified as foreign investor but with some preferential provisions. Can invest in some sectors restricted to other foreigners.

Foreign government / agency

Sovereign wealth funds, development finance institutions, international agencies

Subject to specific sector restrictions based on Nepal’s bilateral agreements.

Institutional foreign investor

Foreign investment funds, private equity firms, venture capital funds

From January 2025: venture capital funds registered with SEBON in Nepal can be used as FDI vehicles (new FITTA amendment).

Nine Forms of Foreign Investment Recognised Under FITTA 2019

Section 2(j) of FITTA 2019 defines foreign investment to include nine distinct forms. The form your investment takes affects the approval process, NRB recording requirements, and applicable repatriation rules. Understanding this from the outset shapes your investment structure correctly.

Investment Form

Description

Key Considerations

Equity investment (shares)

Subscription or purchase of shares in a Nepali company

Most common form. Subject to the FITTR Rule 9 three-stage injection schedule. Ownership proportional to share percentage.

Convertible bonds / debentures

Investment through bonds convertible into equity shares

Subject to SEBON regulations. Useful for staged entry where investor wants debt-like instrument initially.

Loans from foreign financial institutions

Project loans from foreign banks or financial institutions

Requires Ministry of Industry recommendation + NRB approval. Cannot be from parent company, must be from a financial institution per FITTA Section 12.

Technology transfer

Contribution of proprietary technology, know-how, patents, or brand licences in exchange for equity or royalties

Royalties capped at 5% of net annual sales under FITTR. TTA must be registered with DoI. Subject to NRB approval for royalty remittance.

Lease investment

Investment through leasing of aircraft, ships, machinery, construction equipment

Introduced by FITTA 2019 (not in previous law). Useful for capital-intensive industries needing equipment without purchase capital.

Reinvestment of earnings

Reinvesting dividends or profits generated in Nepal back into the company

Treated as additional FDI. Counts toward approved investment schedule. Reduces need for further foreign currency injection.

Venture capital funds

Investment through VC funds or specialized investment funds registered with SEBON

Introduced by January 2025 FITTA amendment. Opens institutional investment pathways not previously available.

Merger and acquisition

Acquisition of shares or assets of an existing Nepali company

Requires FDI approval even for acquisitions of existing companies. Must respect foreign equity caps where they apply.

Other approved forms

Any other form approved by DoI or IBN

Requires specific regulatory approval and is assessed case by case.

What Industries Can Foreigners Invest In? The Open Sectors and the Negative List

FITTA 2019 uses a negative list approach: all sectors are open for foreign investment EXCEPT those specifically listed in the FITTA Schedule as prohibited or restricted. The March 2025 FITTA amendment further expanded the open sectors.

5.1 Prohibited and Restricted Sectors (The Negative List)

⚠️ These Sectors Cannot Accept Foreign Investment: Investing in any Negative List sector results in FDI approval denial. Attempting to circumvent these restrictions through nominee arrangements or mislabelled business activities constitutes fraud and carries criminal liability under Nepal’s laws.

Prohibited / Restricted Sector

Notes

Primary agriculture: animal husbandry, fish farming, beekeeping, fruits, vegetables, oilseeds, pulses, dairy, primary farming

Prohibited EXCEPT for large-scale agritech/mechanization that exports at least 75% of output

Cottage and traditional handicraft industries

Completely prohibited

Personal services: domestic work, personal care, hair salons, personal security

Completely prohibited

Arms, ammunition, gunpowder, explosives, NBC weapons manufacturing

Completely prohibited (national security)

Real estate trading (buying and selling of land)

Prohibited, NOTE: Hotel development, construction companies, and building projects are PERMITTED; only land trading is restricted

Retail business and domestic trading (below prescribed scale)

Prohibited

Internal courier services, local catering, money changing, remittance services

Completely prohibited

Travel agencies, tour guides, trekking companies, mountaineering guides, rural tourism, homestays

Completely prohibited, this is the key distinction from hotel investment (hotels ARE open)

Mass communication media in Nepali language (newspapers, radio, TV, online news)

Completely prohibited

Production of Nepali-language films

Completely prohibited

Ride-sharing services

Maximum 70% foreign ownership

Banking and financial institutions

Maximum 49-65% (sector-specific, NRB-regulated)

Telecommunications services

Maximum 80% foreign ownership

Domestic airlines

Maximum 49% foreign ownership

Consultancy services (management, legal, accounting, engineering)

Maximum 51% foreign ownership

IEA 2020 Industry Classification: Where Does Your Business Fit?

6.1 Classification by Fixed Assets (Capital Size)

Category

Fixed Assets (NPR)

Administering Authority

Micro Industry

Up to NPR 20 lakhs (2,000,000)

Local municipality / ward office

Cottage Industry

Up to NPR 50 lakhs (5,000,000)

District offices

Small Industry

NPR 50 lakhs to NPR 1.5 crore (150,000,000)

Department of Cottage and Small Industries

Medium Industry

NPR 1.5 crore to NPR 5 crore (500,000,000)

Department of Industry (DoI)

Large Industry

Above NPR 5 crore (500,000,000)

Department of Industry (DoI) or Investment Board Nepal

📌 Minimum FDI vs Industry Category: The NPR 20 million minimum FDI threshold places most foreign-invested businesses squarely in the Medium or Large category administered by the DoI. Micro, cottage, and small industries with fixed assets below NPR 5 million are generally inaccessible to foreign investors because they fall below the FITTA minimum threshold.

6.2 Classification by Business Type

Industry Type

Examples Relevant to Foreign Investors

Manufacturing

Food processing, garments, pharmaceuticals, electronics assembly, cement, steel, chemicals, packaging

Service

IT and software, healthcare, education, BPO/KPO, financial services (where permitted), media production

Infrastructure

Hydropower, roads, airports, tunnels, water supply, telecommunications networks

Agro-processing

Food manufacturing, dairy processing, beverages, oil extraction (NOT primary farming)

Energy

Solar, wind, hydropower, biogas, petroleum storage (downstream)

Mining

Mineral extraction, stone quarrying, mineral processing

Construction

Building construction, civil engineering, hotel development, industrial parks

The Two Approval Routes: Automatic vs Standard

Factor

Automatic Route

Standard Route

Investment size

Up to NPR 500 million (~USD 3.8 million)

Above NPR 500 million; or requiring sector-specific ministry review

Approval authority

Department of Industry (DoI), FITT Unit at OSSC

DoI for NPR 500M, 6B; Investment Board Nepal (IBN) for above NPR 6B (~USD 45M)

Statutory processing time

7 working days under FITTA Section 15(2)

30-45 working days (DoI); 60-90 days (IBN)

Application method

Online at imis.doind.gov.np + in-person at OSSC

Online + in-person; may require ministry consultations

Provincial recommendation

Eliminated in 2025 reforms (no longer required)

May be required for large or sensitive projects

IT sector minimum

No minimum capital (removed for Automatic Route)

NPR 20 million standard minimum applies

FY 2024/25 adoption

97% of all FDI commitments

Only 3% of commitments

Best suited for

Most manufacturing, service, IT, hospitality investments

Large infrastructure, power, mega projects

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to establish an industry in Nepal? Two to three months with a complete file. The Automatic Route at the Department of Industry gives seven working days for investments up to NPR 500 million, while larger standard route projects take 30 to 45 working days.

What is the minimum foreign investment to set up an industry? NPR 20 million under FITTA 2019 for most sectors. The IT sector has no minimum on the Automatic Route, and Investment Board Nepal takes over above NPR 6 billion.

Where do I file the foreign investment application? At the One Stop Service Centre of the Department of Industry in Tripureshwor, Kathmandu, which hosts the Office of the Company Registrar, Inland Revenue Department and Nepal Rastra Bank under one roof. Filing starts online at imis.doind.gov.np.

Can a foreigner own 100% of a Nepali company? Usually yes, because FITTA 2019 works on a negative list basis. Caps still apply in specific sectors, such as 49% in domestic airlines and 80% in telecom, while retail trade and travel agencies stay closed.

How must the investment money enter Nepal? Through official banking channels only, with no cash permitted, and each injection must be recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank within six months under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act. FITTR 2021 Rule 9 sets a three stage injection schedule.

What tax incentives can my industry claim? Industries in mountain regions can receive a full income tax exemption, and Special Economic Zone investors get a ten year income tax holiday plus duty free raw materials under the SEZ Act 2073. The standard corporate rate is 25%.

Do I need environmental clearance before I start? For manufacturing and other projects with real environmental impact, clearance from the Department of Environment under the Environment Protection Act 2076 sits alongside FDI approval and land acquisition. Sequence it early, because it is on the critical path.

How soon can I take profits out of Nepal? Once the investment is recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank and tax clearance obtained, dividends can be remitted, and FITTA 2019 guarantees repatriation processing within 15 days. Royalties under a technology transfer agreement are capped at 5% of net annual sales.

Do I still need provincial government approval for FDI? Not for Automatic Route applications, since the provincial recommendation requirement was removed in the 2025 reforms. Larger standard route projects may still need ministry or provincial consultation depending on scale and sensitivity.

title: Education Consultancy Registration in Nepal: Step-by-Step Guide
content:
Education consultancies are a popular way into the Nepali services market, and the sector is regulated precisely because the consequences of getting it wrong fall on students and their families. That regulation is not a barrier so much as a signal: done properly, a consultancy carries a credibility that an unregistered operation cannot claim.

This guide explains what registration involves, which approvals apply, and how to stay compliant once you are operating.

Quick answer

This article covers the complete registration and licensing process for starting an education consultancy in Nepal, including the legal framework, all 7 steps from company registration to MoSD license, required documents, government fees (NPR), timelines, TITI counselor requirements, MOU requirements, renewal rules, penalties for non-compliance, and FAQs. Researched and verified against 2025 regulations by Pluto Associates, Kathmandu.

Introduction: Nepal’s Booming Education Consultancy Sector

Nepal is one of the highest per-capita exporters of students for overseas higher education in Asia. Every year, hundreds of thousands of Nepali students aspire to study in countries such as Australia, the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, and Germany. This extraordinary demand has created a thriving education consultancy industry, one that has grown dramatically over the past decade and continues to expand.

An education consultancy in Nepal acts as the critical bridge between aspiring students and foreign universities and colleges. These firms provide services that range from country and course selection, application preparation, scholarship guidance, and visa filing support, to pre-departure orientation and post-arrival assistance. Given the life-altering nature of this guidance, the Government of Nepal has established a comprehensive regulatory framework to ensure that only properly qualified, licensed, and financially stable firms can operate in this sector.

The scale of enforcement has intensified dramatically in 2025. According to recent regulatory data, over 4,100 education consultancies were found operating across Nepal without proper registration or a valid license. In a single week during July 2025, the Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection collected fines totalling NPR 605,000 from unlicensed consultancies in Kathmandu alone. Operating without a valid license now carries penalties of NPR 50,000 to NPR 100,000 per violation, plus the risk of immediate closure.

Legal Framework: Laws and Governing Authorities

The education consultancy sector in Nepal is regulated by a layered set of laws that operate at both the national and provincial level. Following Nepal’s transition to a federal system, licensing authority has been transferred from the central government to provincial governments. Understanding this structure is essential before commencing the registration process.

2.1 Primary Legislation

Legislation

Year

Key Relevance

Companies Act

2063 (2006)

Governs the incorporation and operation of all private limited companies, including education consultancies.

Education Consultancy Service Directive

2073 (2016)

Sector-specific directive establishing licensing requirements, compliance standards, and operational obligations for education consultancies.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA)

2019

Regulates foreign direct investment; governs the maximum 51% foreign ownership permitted in education consultancy businesses.

Consumer Protection Act

2075 (2018)

Establishes service quality standards and consumer rights protections applicable to education consultancy services.

Province-level Social Development Ministry Regulations

Ongoing

Province-specific licensing, inspection, and compliance rules governing education consultancies in each province.

2.2 Licensing Authority: An Important Recent Change

A critically important regulatory change has taken effect in Nepal’s education consultancy sector. Licensing authority has been transferred from the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (MoEST) at the central level to the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) in each respective province.

For education consultancies operating in Bagmati Province (Kathmandu, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur): The Ministry of Social Development, Hetauda is now the sole licensing authority. All applications must be submitted through the official ECIS (Education Consultancy Information System) Bagmati portal.

Each of Nepal’s seven provinces has its own Ministry of Social Development that handles education consultancy licensing for that province. However, the process and requirements are substantially similar across all provinces.

⚠️ Critical Update: Applications submitted to the Ministry of Education or any other ministry for Bagmati Province will not be processed. The MoSD Hetauda is the only valid authority for Bagmati Province. This change came into effect in fiscal year 2082/83 (BS).

Who Can Register an Education Consultancy in Nepal?

Any Nepali citizen or eligible foreign national (subject to restrictions) may register an education consultancy in Nepal, provided they meet the eligibility and operational requirements set out by the applicable legislation and the Ministry of Social Development.

3.1 For Nepali Citizens

Any Nepali citizen holding a valid citizenship certificate is eligible to register and operate an education consultancy.

  • The company must be registered as a Private Limited (Pvt. Ltd.) company at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR).
  • The company must have a minimum authorized capital of NPR 5 Lakhs (NPR 500,000) and paid-up capital of NPR 5 Lakhs.

3.2 For Foreign Nationals

Foreign investment is permitted in Nepal’s education consultancy sector under FITTA 2019, but with significant restrictions:

  • Foreign nationals may invest in an education consultancy but are subject to a maximum ownership cap of 51%.
  • A Nepali partner must hold a minimum of 49% ownership in the company at all times.
  • Foreign investors must obtain Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) approval from the Department of Industry (DOI) or the Investment Board of Nepal, with prior approval from the Ministry of Education.
  • FDI approval in the education consultancy sector is subject to ministerial discretion and is not automatically granted upon application.

ℹ️ Note for Foreign Investors: Given the requirement for prior Ministry of Education approval before FDI is granted, foreign entrepreneurs are strongly advised to engage a qualified legal firm in Nepal before commencing the investment process.

Key Prerequisites Before You Begin

Before initiating the formal registration process, every prospective education consultancy owner must ensure that the following foundational requirements are in place. These are not optional add-ons, they are hard prerequisites that the Ministry of Social Development will verify during its inspection. Failure to meet any of these requirements at the time of inspection will result in rejection of the license application.

Prerequisite

Specific Requirement

Verified By

Company structure

Registered as a Private Limited (Pvt. Ltd.) company

OCR Certificate

Authorized & paid-up capital

Minimum NPR 5,00,000 (NPR 5 Lakhs) each

Share registry + bank records

Office premises

Commercial space with minimum 2-year rent agreement

Physical inspection by MoSD

TITI-certified counselors

At least 2 counselors with TITI certification from Sanothimi, Bhaktapur

TITI certificates + documents

Foreign university MOUs

Memoranda of Understanding with at least 2 foreign universities

MOU originals or certified copies

Tax registration

Valid PAN and VAT certificates from Inland Revenue Department

PAN/VAT certificates

Local ward registration

Business operation license from the relevant Ward Office

Ward office letter

Corporate bank account

Active company bank account in Nepal

Bank account certificate

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. Is an education consultancy license mandatory in Nepal?

Yes, absolutely. The Education Consultancy Service Directive 2073 (2016) requires every education consultancy operating in Nepal to hold a valid license from the relevant Provincial Ministry of Social Development. Operating without a license is a punishable offence.

2. Which ministry issues the education consultancy license in Kathmandu?

The Ministry of Social Development (MoSD), Hetauda, is the sole licensing authority for education consultancies in Bagmati Province, which includes Kathmandu, Lalitpur, and Bhaktapur. Applications must be submitted through the ECIS Bagmati portal.

3. Can I use my home address as the registered office?

Generally, no. The Ministry of Social Development requires education consultancies to operate from a commercial office space. Residential addresses are typically not acceptable. The office must be in a proper commercial location and the rent agreement must be for a minimum of 2 years.

4. What exactly is the TITI certification and where do I get it?

The TITI certification is a professional counselor qualification issued by the Training Institute for Technical Instruction (TITI) located in Sanothimi, Bhaktapur. It is obtained by completing a specialized training program at TITI. This is the only certification accepted by MoSD for education consultancy licensing, no other certification, however prestigious, is accepted as a substitute.

5. How many MOU agreements with foreign universities do I need?

A minimum of two (2) Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with foreign universities are required. These must be current, signed agreements that the MoSD can verify. Expired MOUs or unsigned draft agreements are not acceptable.

6. Can I run an education consultancy as a sole trader or partnership firm?

No. The regulatory framework explicitly requires that all education consultancies in Nepal be registered as Private Limited (Pvt. Ltd.) companies with the Office of the Company Registrar. Sole traders and partnership firms cannot obtain an education consultancy license.

7. How long does the complete registration process take?

With complete preparation (TITI-certified counselors already hired, MOUs already signed, office fully set up), the process typically takes 6-8 weeks. Without this advance preparation, the process commonly takes 2-4 months, primarily due to the time required for TITI counselor training and MOU procurement.

8. What happens if my application is rejected by MoSD?

If your application is rejected, MoSD will specify the reason(s) for rejection through the ECIS portal. The NPR 15,000 application fee is non-refundable. You may reapply after addressing all rejection reasons, but must pay the NPR 15,000 fee again upon reapplication.

9. Can I register an education consultancy as a foreign national?

Foreign nationals can invest in an education consultancy in Nepal under FITTA 2019, but with a maximum ownership of 51%. A Nepali partner must hold at least 49%. FDI approval from the Department of Industry (with prior Ministry of Education consent) is required. Given these complexities, foreign investors are strongly advised to engage a qualified Nepal law firm before proceeding.

10. How often must I renew the license?

The license must be renewed annually, within 3 months of the end of the Nepali fiscal year, specifically, before the end of Ashoj (mid-October). A 15-day grace period is available after expiry, but operating beyond this grace period is a punishable offence.

Conclusion: Invest in Compliance, Build a Lasting Business

Nepal’s education consultancy sector represents one of the country’s most dynamic and commercially promising service industries. With thousands of Nepali students seeking guidance about overseas education every year, a properly licensed and professionally managed education consultancy can build a highly profitable and meaningful business.

However, the regulatory framework governing this sector is detailed, sequential, and actively enforced. The seven-stage process, from company registration at the OCR through to license issuance by the Ministry of Social Development, demands careful preparation, complete documentation, TITI-certified professional staff, and genuine international university partnerships. Shortcuts or attempts to operate without full compliance carry significant financial and legal consequences.

At Pluto Associates, we provide end-to-end legal support for entrepreneurs seeking to register and license an education consultancy in Nepal. Our services cover company registration and documentation, PAN/VAT registration, MoSD licensing support, ECIS portal filing, inspection preparation, and annual renewal compliance. Our goal is to make the process as straightforward and efficient as possible for our clients, so they can focus on building a trusted, student-centric business from day one.

Disclaimer: This article is provided for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Regulations and fees are subject to change. Readers are advised to consult a qualified legal professional for advice specific to their circumstances. © 2025 Pluto Associates. All rights reserved.

A worked example

An aspiring consultancy wants to advise students on study abroad. The founders draft the constitution, register with the district administration office, and then discover that the activity itself carries its own approval, separate from the registration.

Had they mapped the sector approval alongside the company registration, both would have completed together. Because they treated them as one task rather than two, the business sat idle for several weeks. The lesson is worth carrying into every compliance question in Nepal: confirm which approvals your specific activity needs, and treat them as a set rather than a single step.

Pluto Associates advises clients on business registration and licensing in Nepal. If you would like a clear view of how this applies to your own situation, contact our team for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

Frequently asked questions

How much capital must an education consultancy company have? NPR 500,000 in both authorized and paid-up capital, which is 5 lakhs each. The Ministry of Social Development verifies this through the share registry and bank records during the licensing process.

How many TITI certified counselors must I employ? At least two counselors holding TITI certification from Sanothimi, Bhaktapur. Their certificates go into the license application, and no other qualification is accepted in their place.

Do I need PAN and VAT registration before applying for the license? Yes. Valid PAN and VAT certificates from the Inland Revenue Department are prerequisites that the Ministry of Social Development checks, alongside the company registration documents.

Is a ward office license also required? Yes. A business operation letter from the relevant Ward Office sits in the application file next to the OCR certificate and the corporate bank account certificate.

What are the penalties for running an unlicensed consultancy? Fines run from NPR 50,000 to NPR 100,000 per violation, with immediate closure a real risk. Enforcement intensified in 2025, when over 4,100 unlicensed consultancies were found operating nationwide and Kathmandu inspections alone collected NPR 605,000 in fines in a single week.

Which ministry licenses consultancies outside the Kathmandu valley? Each province has its own Ministry of Social Development, and the process and requirements are substantially similar across all seven provinces. The Bagmati authority is MoSD Hetauda, and applications filed elsewhere for Bagmati Province are simply not processed.

Must the company bank account already be open when I apply? Yes. An active corporate bank account in Nepal, evidenced by the bank account certificate, is one of the hard prerequisites verified at the inspection stage.

Does the Ministry inspect my office before issuing the license? Yes. MoSD conducts a physical inspection of the commercial premises and verifies the two year rent agreement, the counselors, the MOUs and the capital. Failure to meet any prerequisite at inspection results in rejection.

Which consumer protection rules apply once I am operating? The Consumer Protection Act 2075 applies to education consultancy services, covering service quality standards and client rights. Combined with annual license renewal, it forms the core of ongoing compliance.

faqs.q: Is a ward office license also required?
faqs.a: Yes. A business operation letter from the relevant Ward Office sits in the application file next to the OCR certificate and the corporate bank account certificate.

faqs.q: What are the penalties for running an unlicensed consultancy?
faqs.a: Fines run from NPR 50,000 to NPR 100,000 per violation, with immediate closure a real risk. Enforcement intensified in 2025, when over 4,100 unlicensed consultancies were found operating nationwide and Kathmandu inspections alone collected NPR 605,000 in fines in a single week.

faqs.q: Which ministry licenses consultancies outside the Kathmandu valley?
faqs.a: Each province has its own Ministry of Social Development, and the process and requirements are substantially similar across all seven provinces. The Bagmati authority is MoSD Hetauda, and applications filed elsewhere for Bagmati Province are simply not processed.

faqs.q: Must the company bank account already be open when I apply?
faqs.a: Yes. An active corporate bank account in Nepal, evidenced by the bank account certificate, is one of the hard prerequisites verified at the inspection stage.

faqs.q: Does the Ministry inspect my office before issuing the license?
faqs.a: Yes. MoSD conducts a physical inspection of the commercial premises and verifies the two year rent agreement, the counselors, the MOUs and the capital. Failure to meet any prerequisite at inspection results in rejection.

faqs.q: Which consumer protection rules apply once I am operating?
faqs.a: The Consumer Protection Act 2075 applies to education consultancy services, covering service quality standards and client rights. Combined with annual license renewal, it forms the core of ongoing compliance.

title: Registering a Travel, Tours & Trekking Agency in Nepal
content:
Trekking agencies belong to a category that looks simple from the outside and is not. The sector is open and well established, and Nepal has spent decades welcoming visitors who want to walk its mountains. At the same time, tourism is one of the areas the law reserves most carefully, because the work involves safety, foreign visitors and the country’s most treasured landscapes.

This guide explains what registration actually involves, who may own a trekking agency, and where the common assumptions do not hold.

Quick answer

This guide covers the complete registration process for travel, tours, and trekking agencies in Nepal, including the legal framework (Tourism Act 2035, Travel and Trekking Agency Rules 2062), the 5 agency categories (Travel Agency, Tour Operator, Trekking Agency, Mountain Guide Agency, Rafting Agency), the key fact that tourism is on FITTA’s Negative List (foreigners cannot register directly), minimum paid-up capital (NPR 25 lakhs) and bank guarantee (NPR 5 lakhs) requirements, office space standards, the complete 7-step registration process from OCR to Department of Tourism license, the full document checklist, government fees (NPR 25,000 tourism license fee), 5-year license validity and renewal rules, TAAN membership, the restricted trekking areas permit system, annual compliance obligations, penalties for non-compliance, and 12 FAQs. Researched and verified against 2025 regulations by the Pluto Associates legal team, Kathmandu.

Introduction: Nepal’s Tourism Sector and Why Proper Registration Matters

Nepal’s mountains are among the most sought-after destinations on earth. Mount Everest, Annapurna, Langtang, Mustang, Kanchenjunga, the names alone carry a gravitational pull that brings trekkers, climbers, cultural travellers, and adventure seekers from over 100 countries every year. Tourism contributes approximately 7.9% of Nepal’s GDP and supports over one million jobs directly and indirectly. It is, without exaggeration, one of the most important pillars of Nepal’s economy.

Behind every successful trekking expedition, every cultural tour, every helicopter ride to Everest Base Camp, and every whitewater rafting adventure, there is a registered agency. These agencies are not just commercial entities, they are the legally accountable intermediaries between Nepal’s extraordinary natural and cultural landscape and the travellers who come to experience it. They arrange permits, hire licensed guides, book lodges, coordinate logistics, and ensure that visitors are safe and supported throughout their journey.

Operating a travel, tours, or trekking agency in Nepal without proper registration is not just a legal risk, it is a practical one. Unregistered agencies cannot issue official receipts, cannot apply for restricted area trekking permits on behalf of their clients, cannot be listed on the Nepal Tourism Board or official platforms, and cannot build the institutional credibility that international tour operators and travel companies require before partnering with Nepal-based agencies.

The regulatory landscape: Tourism in Nepal is a highly regulated sector. The primary licensing authority is the Department of Tourism (DoT) under the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation. The registration process involves multiple government offices, specific capital requirements, physical office standards, qualified staff requirements, and a bank guarantee that demonstrates the agency’s financial credibility. This guide walks through every step of that process in plain language.

Legal Framework: Laws Governing Travel, Tours, and Trekking Agencies

The registration and operation of travel, tours, and trekking agencies in Nepal is governed by a layered set of laws. Understanding which law governs which aspect of your agency’s operations prevents costly mistakes later.

Law

Year

Relevance to Agency Registration

Tourism Act (Paryatan Ain)

2035 (1978)

Primary legislation governing all tourism-related activities in Nepal. Establishes the Department of Tourism as the licensing and regulatory authority. Defines permitted tourism activities and the legal obligations of registered agencies.

Travel and Trekking Agency Rules (Pravas tatha Bhramanpath Sanstha Niyamawali)

2062 (2005)

The most operationally important law for agency registration. Sets out the detailed rules for license application, required documents, minimum capital, bank guarantee, office requirements, license duration (5 years), renewal procedures, and penalties for violations.

Tourism Act Amendment

2053 (1997)

Updated provisions relating to tour guides, safety standards, and the regulatory framework for adventure tourism.

Companies Act (Kampani Ain)

2063 (2006)

Governs the company registration process at the OCR. All tourism businesses must first be incorporated as a Private Limited Company before approaching the Department of Tourism.

Industrial Enterprises Act (IEA)

2076 (2020)

Requires tourism businesses to register as an industry at the Department of Industry (DoI). This is a mandatory step between OCR registration and DoT licensing.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA)

2019 (2076 BS)

Critically: Tourism agencies (travel, tours, trekking) are listed on the FITTA Negative List. This means foreign nationals CANNOT directly own or register a travel, tours, or trekking agency in Nepal. This is a hard prohibition, not a procedural requirement.

Labour Act

2074 (2017)

Governs employment of guides, staff, and all workers engaged by the agency. Mandatory compliance from the first hire.

Income Tax Act

2058 (2002)

PAN registration and annual tax compliance. VAT registration is mandatory for tourism agencies.

National Parks and Conservation Areas Act

2029 (1973)

Governs trekking permits for national parks and conservation areas where many popular trekking routes pass through.

⚖️ Primary Regulatory Authority: The Department of Tourism (DoT), located at Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, under the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, is the competent authority for issuing, renewing, and regulating tourism agency licenses in Nepal. The DoT operates from Sunday to Friday, 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM.

Types of Tourism Agencies: Which License Do You Need?

Before approaching any government office, you must decide which type of tourism agency you want to establish. The Department of Tourism categorizes tourism businesses into several types, each with specific activities, capital requirements, and staffing qualifications. Choosing the wrong type means either under-licensing your agency (leaving you unable to offer certain services) or over-registering (paying more than necessary for services you won’t offer).

Agency Type

Primary Activities

Min. Capital

Key Additional Requirement

Travel Agency

Air ticketing, hotel reservations, ground transportation, visa assistance, foreign exchange (if licensed)

NPR 25 Lakhs (2,500,000)

IATA accreditation strongly recommended for international ticketing

Tour Operator

Comprehensive tour packages (accommodation + transport + guided tours), domestic and inbound tourism

NPR 25 Lakhs (2,500,000)

Qualified tour guides; vehicle coordination; package pricing compliance

Trekking Agency

Trekking expeditions across Nepal’s trail networks, trekking permit facilitation, porter and guide management

NPR 25 Lakhs (2,500,000)

TAAN membership recommended; licensed trekking guides mandatory; restricted area permits for certain routes

Mountain Guide Agency

High-altitude mountaineering expeditions, peak climbing arrangements

Higher, as specified by DoT

Certified mountain guides (NMA licensed); equipment standards; expedition permits from Ministry of Tourism

Rafting and Kayak Agency

River rafting and kayaking expeditions on Nepal’s rivers

Higher, as specified by DoT

Rafting permits from DoT; certified river guides; safety equipment standards

Combined Agency (Travel + Trekking)

Both travel agency and trekking services under one registration

NPR 25 Lakhs (2,500,000)

Satisfying requirements of both categories simultaneously

Foreign Nationals and Tourism Agencies: A Critical Legal Restriction

This section addresses one of the most important, and most frequently misunderstood, aspects of Nepal’s tourism agency registration framework. If you are a foreign national considering registering a travel, tours, or trekking agency in Nepal, read this section carefully before proceeding.

⚠️ Tourism Is on the FITTA Negative List: Travel agencies, tour operators, and trekking agencies are explicitly listed on the Negative List of the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA) 2019. This means that foreign nationals and foreign companies CANNOT directly invest in, own, or register a travel, tours, or trekking agency in Nepal. This is not a restriction that can be waived, worked around, or negotiated. It is a statutory prohibition.

4.1 What Foreign Nationals Cannot Do

  • Directly register a travel, tours, or trekking agency as a sole owner
  • Hold a majority share in a travel or trekking agency
  • Form a joint venture with a Nepali partner while holding any ownership share in a tourism agency
  • Use a Nepali nominee as a front while retaining beneficial ownership, this constitutes fraud and exposes both parties to criminal liability

4.2 What Foreign Nationals Can Do

  • Appoint a distributor or agent: Foreign tour operators and travel companies can market their services in Nepal by executing a formal distributorship or agency agreement with a registered Nepali tourism agency. The Nepali agency acts as the local representative and is responsible for regulatory compliance.
  • Employ foreign staff: A Nepali-owned tourism agency can employ qualified foreign nationals in specialist roles (mountain guides, specialist instructors, etc.) subject to work permit and visa requirements.
  • Partner with registered Nepali agencies: Foreign tourism companies commonly partner with Nepali agencies through commercial agreements for ground handling, tour packages, and trekking logistics. The Nepali agency handles all government-facing activities, while the foreign partner focuses on marketing and client acquisition abroad.

✅ Foreign Entrepreneurs’ Realistic Option: If you are a foreign national who wants to build a tourism business focused on Nepal, the practical route is to build a strong commercial partnership with a properly registered Nepali agency rather than attempting direct ownership. Many of Nepal’s most successful tourism agencies operate in exactly this model.

Prerequisites: What You Must Have Before You Apply

The Department of Tourism will not accept an agency registration application unless all of the following prerequisites are already in place. These are not suggestions, they are hard requirements that will be verified during the DoT inspection. Attempting to apply before these are ready wastes time and the NPR 25,000 license fee.

Prerequisite

Specific Requirement

Where Verified

Company registration

Private Limited Company registered at the OCR with tourism-related business objectives in the MOA

OCR Certificate

Minimum paid-up capital

NPR 25,00,000 (NPR 25 lakhs) paid-up share capital deposited in the company’s corporate bank account

Bank certificate + share registry

Bank guarantee

NPR 5,00,000 (NPR 5 lakhs) bank guarantee issued in favour of the Department of Tourism, Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, Nepal by a licensed commercial bank

Bank guarantee letter, mandatory document

Physical office

Commercial office space (not residential). Minimum 200 sq. ft. with proper signage, furniture, communication facilities, and a separate toilet/washroom

DoT physical inspection

Office lease agreement

Minimum 5-year lease agreement for the office premises

Lease document submitted with application

PAN and VAT registration

PAN certificate from IRD. VAT registration mandatory for tourism agencies

PAN + VAT certificates

Qualified staff

At least one key staff member with a tourism-related degree, diploma, or recognized certification. For trekking agencies: at least one licensed and certified trekking guide on staff

Staff CVs + certificates submitted

Ward office registration

Business operation permit from the local ward office

Ward permit certificate

Industry registration

Registration at the Department of Industry (DoI) as an industry under the IEA 2076

Industry registration certificate

⚠️ The Bank Guarantee Is Non-Negotiable: The NPR 5 lakh bank guarantee in favour of the Department of Tourism is not a deposit in your own account, it is a formal guarantee instrument issued by a commercial bank that the DoT can call upon if the agency fails to meet its obligations to clients. Without this guarantee letter, the DoT application will not be processed. Allow 5-10 working days for your commercial bank to prepare this document.

A worked example

Two entrepreneurs want to run trekking operations. One assumes a foreign investor can simply open an agency and takes a lease and hired guides before checking ownership rules. The other confirms first whether the activity is open to foreign ownership, and then structures the business accordingly.

The first discovers mid-way that the ownership position does not permit what it planned, and the investment is restructured at a cost. The second proceeds without a surprise. The difference was a single question asked at the beginning rather than months later, and it is the question this guide is written to help you answer.

Frequently asked questions

Can a foreigner own a trekking agency in Nepal? No. Travel, tour and trekking agencies sit on the FITTA 2019 Negative List as a hard statutory prohibition, so foreign nationals cannot own shares directly or through a joint venture. The lawful route for foreign tour operators is a distributorship agreement with a registered Nepali agency.

How much capital is required to register a trekking agency? NPR 25 lakhs of paid-up capital, which is 2,500,000 rupees, plus a bank guarantee of NPR 5 lakhs to demonstrate financial credibility to the Department of Tourism.

Can one company offer both travel services and trekking? Yes. The combined Travel and Trekking Agency registration covers both under a single licence, as long as the requirements of both categories are satisfied simultaneously. It is the most common structure chosen by new tourism entrepreneurs.

Which government office issues the tourism agency licence? The Department of Tourism at Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, operating under the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, issues, renews and regulates all tourism agency licences.

How long is a tourism agency licence valid? Five years under the Travel and Trekking Agency Rules 2062, after which the licence must be renewed with the Department of Tourism.

Is TAAN membership mandatory for a trekking agency? TAAN membership is recommended rather than a statutory condition of licensing. Licensed trekking guides, by contrast, are mandatory under the rules.

Do I have to register my company as an industry as well? Yes. The Industrial Enterprises Act 2020 requires tourism businesses to register their industry at the Department of Industry, and that step sits between OCR company registration and the Department of Tourism licence.

What permits does my agency need for restricted trekking areas? Agencies apply for restricted area permits on behalf of clients, and routes inside national parks and conservation areas require permits under the National Parks and Conservation Areas Act 2029. An unregistered agency cannot apply for these permits at all.

Is VAT registration compulsory for a tourism agency? Yes. The Income Tax Act 2058 requires PAN registration and annual tax compliance, and VAT registration is mandatory for tourism agencies from the outset.
