title: Key Corporate Law Reforms in Nepal: What Directors Need to Know
content:
Directors in Nepal often assume that their duties are settled, set out once in the Companies Act and unlikely to change. The reality is gentler and more demanding at the same time. The core duties are stable, but the way regulators and courts expect them to be applied keeps moving, particularly around disclosure and personal accountability. A board that ran cleanly five years ago can be quietly out of step today.

This guide explains what directors are expected to do, and where the scrutiny has shifted. It covers the legal foundation, key areas of focus, practical governance steps, timelines, risks and the common mistakes to avoid.

Quick answer

Directors of Nepali companies operate under the Companies Act, 2063, which codifies fiduciary duties to act in good faith, avoid conflicts of interest, and exercise the care of a reasonably prudent person. Around this, regulatory practice has tightened disclosure, related-party dealings and beneficial ownership reporting, and courts have shown a willingness to hold directors personally accountable in distress situations. Staying current is part of the job.

The Companies Act as the foundation

The Companies Act, 2063 remains the primary source of directors' duties. It requires directors to act honestly and in the company's interest, to avoid putting themselves in a position where duty and personal interest conflict, and to bring reasonable care and skill to their role. These duties are owed to the company itself, which matters when a director later tries to argue that a decision was good for shareholders or for a particular family.

Directors must also exercise independent judgment and act within the powers conferred by the company's memorandum and articles of association and by law. Breaching these duties can lead to civil liability, disqualification in certain cases, and, in insolvency contexts, personal liability to creditors. The duty to act within powers means a director cannot simply approve transactions that fall outside what the company is authorised to do, even if all directors agree.

Where scrutiny has increased

- Timely and accurate financial reporting to shareholders and the Office of the Company Registrar.

- Proper maintenance of statutory registers and minutes of board meetings.

- Disclosure of transactions with related parties and connected persons.

- Compliance with beneficial ownership reporting under anti-money-laundering rules.

- Approval of significant asset transfers and major financing arrangements.

- Accuracy of information filed with regulators and timely response to queries.

- Oversight of risk management, internal controls and tax compliance.

The common thread is transparency. Regulators increasingly treat the quality of a board's records as a measure of the board itself. A well documented board can demonstrate that it took reasonable care, even where a commercial decision later proves unsuccessful. A poorly documented board cannot.

Conflicts of interest

A director with an interest in a transaction must disclose it and, in most cases, step back from the relevant resolution. Failing to do so can expose the director to personal liability and allow the transaction to be unwound at the company's instance. The practical habit that prevents most problems is a standing conflict-of-interest item at every board meeting, recorded in the minutes.

Related party transactions require particular care. The board should consider whether the transaction is on arm's length terms, document the basis for approval, and ensure the minutes clearly record disclosure, abstention and the rationale. Where required by law, shareholder approval may also be necessary. Proper documentation protects both the company and the individual directors. Disclosure should be specific, not generic, naming the interest and the relationship.

Indirect interests also count. A director whose family member, partner, or controlled entity stands to benefit from a transaction is interested, even if the director is not named in the transaction documents. The test is whether a reasonable observer would see a conflict, not whether the director subjectively feels conflicted.

Insolvency and personal liability

Judicial trends have made directors personally accountable for trading while the company is insolvent and for preferences that disadvantage creditors. A board that suspects the company is in difficulty should take advice before continuing to trade, because the decision to keep going is itself a decision the law scrutinises.

Directors should monitor key indicators such as cash flow, creditor pressure, overdue taxes and mounting liabilities. If insolvency is likely, the duty shifts in emphasis towards protecting creditor interests. Taking early professional advice can help the board consider restructuring, refinancing or other options and document the basis for decisions made in that context.

Personal liability can also arise from breaches of duty that cause loss to the company, from misapplication of company assets, and from certain tax or regulatory offences. Directors should understand that limited liability protects the company's shareholders, not the personal conduct of directors acting improperly or recklessly.

Financial reporting and audit

Directors are responsible for ensuring that financial statements give a true and fair view and are prepared in accordance with applicable standards. They must also ensure timely filing with the Office of the Company Registrar and compliance with audit requirements under the Companies Act. Inaccurate or late filings attract penalties and can trigger further scrutiny.

Reviewing draft financials in detail, questioning assumptions, and ensuring adequate disclosures are part of the board's oversight role. The audit committee, where established, plays an important part, but the ultimate responsibility rests with the board. Directors should not simply accept management's explanations without testing them, particularly around estimates, provisions and related party balances.

Statutory registers, minutes and records

Maintaining up to date statutory registers, minutes of board and shareholder meetings, and resolutions is not a formality. These are the primary evidence of board decisions and compliance. Regulators routinely ask for these documents during inspections or investigations. Missing or backdated records undermine credibility and make it difficult to defend decisions.

Minutes should record attendance, disclosures of interest, the matters discussed, the decisions made, dissenting views if any, and the rationale for key decisions. They should be approved at the next meeting and filed promptly. Digital record keeping is acceptable if secure and retrievable. Keeping minutes contemporaneously, rather than reconstructing them later, is both a legal safeguard and a governance discipline.

Beneficial ownership and AML compliance

Companies are required to disclose their beneficial owners under anti-money laundering rules. Directors must ensure that the company identifies its beneficial owners, keeps the register up to date, and files the required information with the relevant authorities. Failure to comply can result in penalties and increased regulatory scrutiny.

Beneficial ownership disclosure requires ongoing vigilance, particularly when shareholding changes or when ownership structures become complex. The board should have a process to verify and update this information at least annually, or more frequently if changes occur. Nominee arrangements and layered structures require especially careful review, as regulators look through them to the natural persons who ultimately control the company.

Practical steps for the year ahead

1. Schedule an annual governance review so duties and filings are checked, not assumed.

2. Update the company's internal bylaws to reflect current practice and regulatory expectations.

3. Verify that statutory filings and registers are current and complete.

4. Put related-party and beneficial ownership disclosures on a standing agenda for every board meeting.

5. Have external counsel audit board practices against current expectations at least once every few years.

6. Maintain a compliance calendar for key filing deadlines and renewal dates.

7. Provide periodic governance training for directors, especially new appointees.

8. Document delegation of authority clearly to avoid confusion about who can bind the company.

9. Review the company's insurance, including directors and officers cover, in light of the increasing focus on personal accountability.

Common mistakes to avoid

Assuming duties are static is a mistake. Failing to disclose conflicts, approving related party transactions without documentation, trading while insolvent without advice, and keeping inadequate minutes are frequent issues. Backdating documents, relying on oral approvals for material decisions, and neglecting beneficial ownership filings can all lead to serious consequences. Directors should document decisions contemporaneously and seek advice when in doubt.

A worked example

A family-owned company wants to lease premises owned by its managing director. Done properly, the director discloses the interest, takes no part in the vote, and the remaining directors approve the lease on documented market terms. The minutes record all of it. Done casually, with the same director voting, the lease can later be challenged, and the director can be called to account. The substance of the two situations is nearly identical. The difference is the paper trail, and that is exactly what regulators and courts look at.

The same discipline applies to financing, asset transfers and any transaction where a director has a personal interest. Consistent process is the best protection.

Frequently asked questions

What are a director's basic duties in Nepal?

To act in good faith in the company's interest, avoid conflicts of interest, and exercise reasonable care and diligence under the Companies Act, 2063.

Can a director be personally liable?

Yes. Personal liability can arise from undisclosed conflicts, trading while insolvent, preferences to creditors, and breaches of statutory duties.

What must be disclosed in a related-party transaction?

The interest must be disclosed, and the director should abstain from the relevant resolution in most cases. The board should document the terms and rationale for approval.

Are minutes and registers really that important?

Yes. They are the evidence of how a board made its decisions, and regulators treat them as a measure of governance.

What is beneficial ownership reporting?

A requirement to disclose the natural persons who ultimately own or control the company, under anti-money laundering rules.

What should a board do when the company is in difficulty?

Take advice early. The decision to keep trading can itself attract scrutiny, and duties may shift towards protecting creditors.

How often should governance be reviewed?

At least annually, with a more detailed review by external counsel every few years or when regulations change significantly.

Can directors delegate their duties?

Directors can delegate certain functions, but they remain responsible for oversight. The delegation should be clearly documented and monitored.

What happens if filings are late?

Late filings attract penalties under the Companies Act and can lead to compliance notices or other enforcement action.

Do nominee directors have special duties?

Yes. Nominee directors owe the same duties to the company as other directors. They cannot simply follow the instructions of the nominating party if that conflicts with the company's interests.

Can a director vote on a matter they are conflicted on?

Generally no. A conflicted director should disclose the interest and abstain from voting. Voting on a matter in which you have an undisclosed interest is a common ground for challenge.

Is there a minimum number of directors?

Companies Act requirements apply. A private limited company must meet the minimum number of directors prescribed by the Act. Check the current requirement before incorporation or appointment.

Our corporate team advises boards on governance, compliance and director duties across Nepal. If you would like a clear view of your situation, send us a note through our contact page for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp at +977 9802356987, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

title: Trademark Registration in Nepal: A Practical Guide for Businesses
content:
A brand is often worth more than the premises it is sold from, yet plenty of businesses in Nepal trade for years without ever registering their name. Nothing goes wrong until it does: a copycat opens nearby, a former partner launches under a similar mark, or an online listing uses your name to draw your customers. Registration is what turns a name you use into a right you can enforce.

This guide explains how trademark registration works in Nepal and why the timing of your filing matters. It covers the legal framework, the step by step process, costs, timelines, enforcement, and the practical pitfalls that catch even well-run businesses.

Quick answer

Trademarks in Nepal are registered with the Department of Industry under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act, 2022. Registration grants a statutory monopoly over the mark and a clear basis to act against counterfeiters and copycats. The process runs from a preliminary search, through examination, to publication and registration. A registered mark is valid for seven years and can be renewed for successive periods. Protection is territorial, so a mark registered abroad does not automatically cover Nepal.

Where you file

The Department of Industry administers patents, industrial designs and trademarks from its office in Kathmandu. Because one office handles all three, the system is centralised, which makes the filing route predictable. The trade-off is that a busy office rewards a well-prepared application over a rushed one. Applications are processed in line with the Act and the relevant rules, so complete submissions tend to move faster than incomplete ones.

Applicants can file themselves or through a registered agent. Using an experienced agent is often worthwhile, because the agent understands classification practice, examination objections and the documentation that the Department expects. Whatever route you choose, keeping a clear record of the application number, filing date and all correspondence is essential for follow up.

The registration process

1. Preliminary search. Check for conflicting marks already on the register before you commit to a name or a filing. This is the single most effective way to avoid objections and delay. A search should cover identical and similar marks in the relevant classes.

2. File the application. Include a representation of the mark, the applicant's details, a clear description of goods or services, and the correct class or classes under the classification system used. Incomplete applications attract objections.

3. Examination. The Department of Industry examines the mark for distinctiveness, formal requirements and conflicts with earlier marks. If objections are raised, the applicant has a window to respond with arguments or amendments.

4. Publication. If accepted, the mark is published in the official journal, opening a window for opposition by interested parties. Third parties can oppose if they believe the mark conflicts with their earlier rights.

5. Registration. If no opposition succeeds, or if any opposition is resolved in favour of the applicant, the mark is registered and a certificate of registration is issued. The registration certificate is the document you will rely on for enforcement.

Why distinctiveness matters

A mark must be capable of distinguishing your goods or services from those of others. Descriptive words, common surnames and generic terms are frequently rejected, unless they have acquired a distinct meaning through long use. A name that describes exactly what you sell is easy to market and hard to protect. A name that is distinctive may need a little more explanation, but it is the one that can be defended.

Invented words, arbitrary marks and suggestive marks are generally easier to register. Combinations of letters or stylised logos can also be registrable, depending on their distinctiveness. If a mark is borderline, evidence of use, advertising spend, market recognition and sales figures can help show acquired distinctiveness, though this is not guaranteed and depends on the strength of the evidence.

Classes of goods and services

Trademarks are registered in specific classes of goods and services. Filing in the wrong class or filing too narrowly can leave gaps that competitors exploit. Filing too broadly can increase the risk of objections and slow the process down. A proper search should cover the classes relevant to your business, and your application should list only the goods or services you actually intend to offer, or plan to offer in the near term.

Many businesses file in multiple classes where they operate or plan to expand. Each class requires a separate fee, so the decision involves both strategy and budget. Filing in the core class first and expanding later is a common approach, but it carries the risk that someone else registers the mark in the additional class in the meantime.

Duration and renewal

A registered trademark is initially valid for seven years and can be renewed for successive periods of seven years. Renewal is a simple filing, but missing the deadline can remove the mark from the register, and rebuilding protection after a lapse is far harder than keeping it alive. The Department of Industry publishes deadlines and there is usually a prescribed renewal window, so maintaining a renewal calendar for all registered marks is essential.

After renewal, the mark continues to enjoy statutory protection. Failure to use a mark for a prolonged period can, in certain circumstances, expose it to non-use cancellation, so using the mark in trade and keeping evidence of use is important to preserve rights. Good records of packaging, invoices, advertising and online listings all help demonstrate genuine use if challenged.

Costs and timelines

Costs vary depending on whether you file for one class or multiple classes, and on professional fees if you use an agent. Government fees are published by the Department of Industry. Timelines depend on the workload at the Department, the completeness of the application, any office actions, and whether any opposition is filed.

A straightforward, well-prepared application with no conflicts can move through the process in a reasonable time, but objections or oppositions will extend it. Budget for renewal fees and monitoring costs as well, as a trademark portfolio needs ongoing attention. The cost of filing early is modest compared to the cost of a dispute after a competitor has registered a similar mark.

Enforcing your rights

A registered proprietor can oppose conflicting applications, demand that infringing use stop, and pursue civil remedies or criminal action under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act, 2022. An unregistered mark can only rely on passing off, which requires proving goodwill and misrepresentation and is both harder and costlier. Registration does not remove the need to police a mark, but it changes the odds decisively in your favour.

Effective enforcement starts with monitoring. Watch for new applications that conflict with your mark, monitor marketplaces and domain names, and act promptly when infringement appears. Cease and desist letters are often effective if backed by a registration certificate. Where negotiation fails, civil proceedings or criminal complaints may be necessary. The strength of your registration certificate, combined with clear evidence of use and ownership, is your strongest asset.

International considerations

Trademark protection is territorial. A mark registered abroad does not protect you in Nepal. If you plan to expand beyond Nepal, you will need to consider protection in other jurisdictions separately. Conversely, foreign brands entering Nepal should register their marks here before launching, as prior use by others in Nepal can complicate matters.

If you rely on well-known marks, there are additional considerations under the law, but registration is still the clearest route to enforceable rights. Businesses with regional ambitions often file in several jurisdictions at once or in a planned sequence, coordinating through local counsel in each country. Nepal is not a member of the Madrid Protocol as of the time of writing, so a separate national filing is required.

Common mistakes to avoid

Delaying registration until after someone else files is the most expensive mistake. Filing without a proper search leads to avoidable objections. Choosing a descriptive name makes registration difficult. Failing to renew on time results in loss of rights. Filing in the wrong class leaves gaps in protection. Not policing the mark allows dilution and makes later enforcement harder. Finally, assuming foreign registration covers Nepal is a frequent error. Addressing these points at the start prevents most problems.

A worked example

Two cafes open in the same district within a year of each other, both called something close to a well-known coffee brand. Neither registered. When the original brand owner enters Nepal, both are served notice. The owner who filed a trademark application early is in a strong position to oppose the copy or to license the mark. The owner who relied on the common law of passing off must prove reputation and confusion, which is slower and more expensive, and the outcome is less certain. The cost of the filing, paid early, is trivial next to the cost of the dispute.

Had the earlier user filed a proper trademark application in the relevant class, the later entrant would have faced an opposition based on a registered right rather than a passing off claim based on disputed evidence of reputation. The difference in outcome, cost and speed is substantial, and it comes down to a decision taken years earlier.

Frequently asked questions

How long does trademark registration take in Nepal?

It varies with examination, office workload and any opposition, but a complete application typically takes several months. A search before filing avoids the most common delays.

How long is a trademark valid?

Seven years initially, renewable for successive periods of seven years.

Can I register a descriptive name?

Usually not, unless it has acquired a distinct meaning through use. Evidence of use and recognition is needed to support such an application.

What can I do if someone copies my mark?

If registered, you can oppose their application and act against their use through civil or criminal remedies. If unregistered, you depend on passing off, which is harder to prove.

Do I need the mark registered before I use it?

You can use a mark before registering it, but you gain enforceable rights only on registration. Prior use can help in some contexts, but registration is far stronger.

Does a foreign trademark cover me in Nepal?

No. Protection is territorial, so a mark registered abroad does not protect you in Nepal. You must register in Nepal separately.

What happens if I miss the renewal deadline?

The mark may be removed from the register. Restoration or re-registration is possible only in limited cases and is far more difficult than renewing on time.

Can I oppose someone else's trademark application?

Yes. If you have prior rights, you can file an opposition within the prescribed period after publication.

Do I need to use my trademark after registration?

Yes. Continued use is important. Non-use for an extended period can expose the mark to cancellation proceedings.

Should I register my logo and name separately?

It depends on how you use them. Registering both gives broader protection, but each requires a separate application and fee.

Can I license my trademark to another business?

Yes. Licensing is common and permitted, but the licence should be documented and, depending on quality control provisions, may need to be recorded. Licensing without quality control can put the mark at risk.

How much does a trademark search cost?

The cost varies by agent and by how many classes are searched. A proper search is a small investment compared to the cost of rebranding after a dispute.

faqs.a: The mark may be removed from the register. Restoration or re-registration is possible only in limited cases and is far more difficult than renewing on time.

faqs.q: Can I oppose someone else's trademark application?
faqs.a: Yes. If you have prior rights, you can file an opposition within the prescribed period after publication.

faqs.q: Do I need to use my trademark after registration?
faqs.a: Yes. Continued use is important. Non-use for an extended period can expose the mark to cancellation proceedings.

faqs.q: Should I register my logo and name separately?
faqs.a: It depends on how you use them. Registering both gives broader protection, but each requires a separate application and fee.

faqs.q: Can I license my trademark to another business?
faqs.a: Yes. Licensing is common and permitted, but the licence should be documented and, depending on quality control provisions, may need to be recorded. Licensing without quality control can put the mark at risk.

faqs.q: How much does a trademark search cost?
faqs.a: The cost varies by agent and by how many classes are searched. A proper search is a small investment compared to the cost of rebranding after a dispute.

title: Renewable Energy Projects in Nepal: Legal and Regulatory Overview
content:
Nepal's rivers have powered the country for generations, and they remain the centre of its energy ambitions. A hydropower project is also one of the most heavily regulated investments anyone can make here, not because the law is hostile, but because a river is a shared resource and a large dam touches land, forests, communities and the national grid at once. Developers who understand the licensing chain early move faster than those who learn it by trial.

This guide gives an overview of the legal and regulatory framework for renewable energy projects in Nepal, with a focus on hydropower. It covers the main legislation, licensing, power purchase agreements, financing, environmental and social compliance, timelines, costs, and the common pitfalls that delay even well-planned projects.

Quick answer

Renewable energy projects in Nepal are governed mainly by the Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050, with larger priority projects falling under the Investment Board Act. A developer needs a survey licence, then a generation licence, plus environmental approval. Power is normally sold to the Nepal Electricity Authority under a power purchase agreement. Foreign investment adds approval and repatriation requirements under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA) and Nepal Rastra Bank's foreign exchange framework.

The primary legislation

The Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050 govern the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity. The Investment Board Act applies to projects that fall within the national priority thresholds and are handled by the Investment Board Nepal. Alongside these sit environmental law, land and forest rules, and, for foreign investors, FITTA and Nepal Rastra Bank's foreign exchange framework. Local government rules may also apply depending on the location of the project.

Hydropower is the dominant source, but other renewables such as solar, wind and biomass are also covered by the same electricity framework, with scale-based differences in licensing and environmental requirements. Understanding which regime applies at the outset prevents unnecessary delays and helps the developer plan the approval sequence properly.

Licensing requirements

A project typically needs these in sequence:

- A survey licence to carry out studies and feasibility assessments.

- An electricity generation licence once the survey and studies are complete.

- Approval of an environmental impact assessment (EIA), or an initial environmental examination (IEE) for smaller projects, as determined by the applicable thresholds.

- Where a dedicated transmission line is needed, related approvals from the transmission authority.

Each stage depends on the one before it, which is why a project can be delayed substantially by an incomplete study or an environmental file that is submitted too early. For larger projects, additional approvals may be needed from sector bodies and the Investment Board Nepal. Transmission line approvals may also be required if a dedicated line is needed.

The survey licence gives the right to enter land for investigation, subject to compensation for any damage. Securing land access agreements in parallel is prudent, as landowner consent can become contentious even during the survey stage.

Power purchase agreements

The Nepal Electricity Authority is the principal off-taker. The terms of the power purchase agreement, including tariffs, take-or-pay obligations, payment security, force majeure, dispute resolution and termination, are negotiated against the prevailing regulatory framework and often decide whether a project is bankable. Because the PPA sits at the centre of project revenue, its negotiation deserves as much care as the technical design.

Tariff structures vary by project type and timing. Developers should be clear on the tariff applicable to their project, the currency and indexation provisions, and any conditions precedent. Lenders will scrutinise the PPA carefully, so it should be as bankable as possible without compromising the project's economics. Negotiating the PPA in parallel with financing discussions, rather than after, often speeds up the overall timeline.

Project finance

Lenders typically require a complete chain of land rights, generation and transmission licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance before they will commit. Foreign investors should confirm whether their project needs Investment Board Nepal approval or a sectoral licence. Most financing delays trace back to a gap in the licence chain rather than to the money itself.

Equity, debt and mezzanine structures are all used. Due diligence covers technical, legal, environmental, social and commercial aspects. Security packages, step in rights, and intercreditor arrangements take time to negotiate. Developers should engage lenders and their legal advisers early, and prepare a financing timeline that aligns with the licensing sequence to avoid expiry of commitments.

For foreign currency loans and hedging, Nepal Rastra Bank rules may apply. Currency convertibility and repatriation provisions need to be considered in the financing documents and in the foreign investment approval. Lenders will also want assurance that the project company can meet its tax and regulatory obligations throughout the loan term.

Environmental and social compliance

Hydropower and renewable projects face close environmental and social scrutiny. Resettlement, forest clearance, biodiversity impacts and river-flow obligations must be addressed in the EIA and monitored through the life of the project. These are not only legal requirements. They are also, increasingly, what a project's lenders and off-takers expect to see properly handled.

Public consultation is a key part of the EIA process. Early engagement with affected communities helps identify concerns and build workable mitigation measures. Forest clearance requires separate approvals from the relevant forest authorities. Compensation for land acquisition and resettlement must be carried out in accordance with the applicable legal framework and with due process.

Environmental monitoring, compliance reporting and implementation of the environmental management plan are ongoing obligations after approval. Non-compliance can lead to suspension of licences or other enforcement action, so developers should budget for long term monitoring and community liaison. A dedicated social and environmental team within the project company is common for larger developments.

Grid connection and transmission

Connecting to the national grid requires coordination with the Nepal Electricity Authority and, for larger projects, compliance with grid codes and technical standards. The interconnection agreement governs the technical and commercial relationship between the project and the grid. Transmission upgrades, if required, may be shared with other projects or funded by the developer, and the cost allocation should be clear before financial close.

Delays in grid connection are common, particularly in areas where the transmission network is weak. Developers should engage with the Nepal Electricity Authority early in the study phase, not after the generation licence is applied for. Understanding the evacuation capacity available at the point of interconnection can avoid costly redesigns later.

Hydropower specific considerations

Hydropower projects carry a distinct set of issues that other renewables do not. River flow data, hydrology studies, sediment management, dam safety, and downstream impacts all form part of the technical and environmental file. The design flood, dam height and reservoir capacity decisions affect both the licence and the environmental approvals, so they should be settled before the EIA is finalised.

Land acquisition for hydropower, including the headworks, transmission line and access roads, is often the most sensitive part of the project. Securing land rights early, with documented agreements and compensation where required, prevents delays at the generation licence stage. Forest clearance for the transmission line corridor is a separate process and should be started in parallel, not after.

For run-of-river projects, environmental flow requirements must be met to protect downstream users and ecosystems. These are specified in the EIA and monitored over the life of the project. Failure to maintain environmental flows can lead to complaints, enforcement action and reputational damage with lenders and off-takers.

Timelines and costs

Timelines vary widely with project size and the completeness of the studies and environmental file. The sequence, not the calendar, is the main variable. Survey licences are time limited, so feasibility studies must be completed within that window. Generation licence applications require full technical studies and land rights documentation. EIA approval timelines depend on the completeness of the submission and the level of review required.

Costs include government fees, consultant fees for technical and environmental studies, legal fees, land acquisition and resettlement costs, forest clearance fees, insurance, and financing costs. Currency exposure, escalation and interest during construction should all be factored into the financial model. A realistic budget includes contingencies for delays, as licensing slippage is common if the sequence is not managed tightly.

A common source of cost overrun is scope change driven by incomplete surveys. A thorough feasibility study, even if more expensive upfront, reduces the risk of redesign during construction and of licence conditions that require costly mitigation. The investment in good studies pays for itself.

Common mistakes to avoid

Applying for the generation licence before securing land rights or before the environmental file is ready is a frequent error. Underestimating the time needed for forest clearance or local consultations causes avoidable delays. Treating the PPA as an afterthought rather than a bankability issue leads to financing problems. For foreign investors, failing to align foreign investment approval with the project structure and capital remittance plan creates unnecessary friction. Finally, inadequate community engagement often leads to opposition that can halt progress even when all technical approvals are in place.

A worked example

A foreign developer identifies a run-of-river site and secures a survey licence. The feasibility study is thorough, and the land rights chain is assembled before the environmental file is finalised, so the generation licence and EIA approval are not held up by a missing link. The PPA is negotiated with a clear tariff and take-or-pay terms, and the lenders are satisfied. A second developer moves faster and applies for the generation licence before land rights are settled. The file stalls for months, the PPA window narrows, and the financing costs rise. The technical projects are similar. The disciplined sequence is what separates them.

The first developer also invests in early community engagement, so the EIA consultation phase proceeds without major objections. The second developer leaves community engagement until the file is already in the system, and faces organised opposition that delays approval further. The lesson is consistent across hydropower projects: process discipline, not technical sophistication alone, determines outcomes.

Frequently asked questions

What licences does a hydropower project need?

A survey licence, an electricity generation licence, and environmental approval (EIA or IEE as applicable), in sequence.

Who buys the electricity?

The Nepal Electricity Authority is the principal off-taker, under a power purchase agreement.

Is environmental approval always required?

Yes, in some form. Larger projects need a full EIA, while smaller projects may qualify for an IEE based on the prescribed thresholds.

Do foreign investors need separate approval?

Often yes, especially for larger projects under the Investment Board Nepal, and always under FITTA for the foreign investment itself. Nepal Rastra Bank approval is also needed for capital inflow and repatriation.

What do lenders require?

A complete land rights chain, the relevant licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance. They will also require due diligence on environmental, social and technical aspects.

How long does licensing take?

It varies widely with project size and the completeness of the studies and environmental file. The sequence, not the calendar, is the main variable.

Can a project sell power to private buyers?

Yes, subject to the applicable regulatory framework and licensing requirements. However, most grid-connected projects sell to the Nepal Electricity Authority.

What about forest clearance?

If the project affects forest land, separate forest clearance approvals are required. This can take time and should be factored into the schedule.

Are there restrictions on repatriation of profits?

Repatriation is allowed after tax clearance and Nepal Rastra Bank approval, provided the investment was properly documented under FITTA.

How early should legal advice be sought?

As early as site identification. Getting the sequence right from the start avoids the majority of delays and cost overruns.

What is a power purchase agreement?

A long term contract under which the Nepal Electricity Authority agrees to buy the project's electricity at agreed terms. It is central to project bankability and financing.

Can licenses be transferred?

Yes, subject to regulatory approval. The transferee must meet the same eligibility requirements, and the Department must be notified and approve the transfer.

Our energy and infrastructure team advises developers, lenders and investors across the project lifecycle, from licensing to power purchase agreements and foreign investment approvals. If you would like a clear view of your project, send us a note through our contact page for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp at +977 9802356987, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

title: Employment Law in Nepal: Employee Rights and Employer Obligations
content:
Hiring your first employee in Nepal feels simple until the paperwork arrives. The Labour Act sets minimum standards that apply whether or not an employer has thought about them, and the obligations mostly fall on the employer by default. A business that treats employment as a handshake tends to discover the rules only when a dispute or an inspection forces the question.

This guide explains the main employer obligations under the Labour Act, 2074, and how to stay compliant without overcomplicating the basics. It covers contracts, working hours, leave, termination, social security, and practical steps that help businesses avoid the mistakes that lead to avoidable disputes.

Quick answer

The Labour Act, 2074 governs employment in Nepal and applies to most private sector employers. It prescribes minimum standards for written contracts, working hours, leave, termination and social security. Employers must issue written contracts, keep proper records, contribute to the Social Security Fund, and follow the statutory procedure before terminating employment. These are legal minimums and cannot be waived, even if both parties agree to do so.

Written employment contracts

An employer must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee. The document should set out the nature of the work, the remuneration, the working hours, and the grounds and procedure for termination. A clear contract protects both sides, and it is the first thing a labour office will ask to see if there is a complaint.

At a minimum, the contract should state the employee's designation, the department or reporting line, the place of work, the date of commencement, the duration if fixed term, the probation period if any, the salary structure and payment cycle, working hours, leave entitlements, grounds for termination, the notice period, and any specific duties. It is also helpful to record the mode of payment and whether accommodation or other benefits are provided. Vague clauses create room for disagreement later, so clarity at the outset saves time and cost.

Fixed term contracts are used for project work or seasonal employment, but employers should not use repeated fixed term contracts to avoid the protections of permanent employment. The Labour Act looks at the substance of the relationship, not just the label. Where work is continuous and ongoing, the employee is likely to be treated as a regular employee for the purpose of statutory rights, regardless of how the contract is named.

Probation periods are common, but they must still comply with the minimum standards of the Act. During probation, the employer can assess suitability, but the employee remains entitled to the basic protections set out in the law. If employment continues after probation, those rights remain in place without needing to be reissued in most cases, though a confirmation letter is good practice.

Working hours and leave

The standard working week is limited to 48 hours, with overtime payable for additional work. Employees are entitled to annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, along with maternity and paternity leave as prescribed by the statute. These are minimums, not suggestions, and they cannot be traded away in a contract.

Working hours should be clearly recorded through attendance registers or approved timekeeping systems. Where employees work beyond the normal hours, overtime must be calculated and paid in accordance with the Labour Act. Employers should keep a record of overtime authorisations, as claims for unpaid overtime are a common source of disputes. Rest breaks during the day and weekly rest periods must also be respected where applicable to the nature of work.

Leave entitlements under the Act include annual leave, sick leave, public holidays declared by the government, and special leave as provided by law. Maternity leave and paternity leave are granted as prescribed. Leave must be properly recorded in a leave register, and requests should be documented. Carry forward rules and encashment on termination depend on the category of leave and the specific provisions of the Act, so employers should track leave balances accurately.

Public holidays are observed as notified. If work is required on a public holiday, the additional compensation prescribed by law applies. Employers should maintain a holiday calendar each year and communicate it to staff in advance to avoid confusion and unplanned overtime.

Termination and severance

Termination must follow the procedure in the Labour Act. An employee whose services are terminated, other than for misconduct, is entitled to notice or pay in lieu, and to gratuity and leave encashment where applicable. The procedural steps matter as much as the money: a termination that is fair in substance but wrong in process can still be found unlawful.

For termination on grounds other than misconduct, the employer must follow the statutory process, including providing the required notice in writing or payment in lieu, stating the reasons clearly, and giving the employee an opportunity to be heard where required. The notice period and entitlements depend on the length of service and the circumstances of termination. Dismissal for misconduct requires a proper inquiry in line with the procedure set out in the Act. Hasty dismissals without following procedure often lead to reinstatement orders or compensation.

Gratuity and leave encashment apply where the employee qualifies under the Act. Final settlement should include all outstanding wages, overtime, leave encashment, gratuity and any other dues. Employers should prepare a full settlement statement and obtain a discharge where appropriate, while ensuring compliance with statutory timelines. Full and accurate documentation of the process, including show cause letters, inquiry records, notices and final payments, is essential to defend any claim.

Redundancy situations must also follow the law. If positions are abolished for genuine business reasons, the procedure and entitlements under the Labour Act must be observed. Employers should document the business rationale and ensure selection criteria are fair and non-discriminatory.

Social security

Registered employers must contribute to the Social Security Fund on behalf of their employees. Contributions cover medical, accident, dependency and pension benefits, and late or non-payment attracts penalties. Enrolling new staff promptly, rather than in a batch at year end, avoids both the penalty and the administrative scramble.

Employers must register with the Social Security Fund and make regular contributions for all eligible employees. The contribution rates and coverage are as prescribed under the relevant rules. It is important to maintain accurate records of contributions, including employee details, salary on which contributions are calculated, and payment receipts. Late payments accrue penalties and interest in addition to the principal amount, so timely compliance is both a legal and financial necessity.

When an employee joins or leaves, the employer must update records with the Social Security Fund within the prescribed timeframes. Final settlement should account for any outstanding contributions before closure of employment. Keeping a compliance calendar for monthly or periodic payments helps prevent missed deadlines and the resulting enforcement action.

Workplace safety and non-discrimination

Employers have an obligation to provide a safe and healthy workplace. Occupational safety and health duties require taking reasonable steps to prevent accidents and protect employees from foreseeable risks. Depending on the nature of the business, specific safety measures, training and first aid provisions may apply. Maintaining incident records and conducting basic safety checks is prudent for all employers.

Discrimination on grounds prohibited by law is not allowed in recruitment, promotion, training, pay or termination. Equal treatment and fair process reduce the risk of claims and help build a stable workplace. Policies should be applied consistently to avoid claims of unequal treatment, and any disciplinary action must be based on documented facts and fair procedure.

Employee records must be kept confidential and maintained for the period required by law. Attendance, payroll, leave, contracts, disciplinary records and Social Security Fund records should be securely stored and readily retrievable if requested by a labour inspector.

Practical compliance steps

Maintain attendance records, payroll documentation and statutory registers. Issue written contracts and keep signed copies on file. Enrol employees in the Social Security Fund on time. Ensure workplace policies meet anti-discrimination and occupational safety obligations. Follow the statutory process before any termination. Conduct periodic reviews of employment documentation to catch gaps before they become disputes.

Create a simple compliance checklist for each new hire: prepare contract, get signatures, collect required documents, enrol in Social Security Fund, record in attendance and payroll, explain leave policy, and provide workplace safety briefing. For exits, use a checklist covering notice, final dues calculation, return of company property, clearance, Social Security Fund update and issuance of experience letter where appropriate.

Common mistakes to avoid

Many employment disputes in Nepal arise from avoidable errors. Issuing only an offer letter without a full employment contract, omitting the termination procedure, failing to document misconduct before dismissal, delaying Social Security Fund enrolment, not recording overtime, and paying final dues late are frequent issues. Another common mistake is treating regular employees as contractors to avoid statutory obligations, which is unlikely to succeed if the actual working relationship shows control and subordination. Avoid shortcuts and document decisions contemporaneously.

A worked example

A growing marketing firm hires eight staff in a year and, being busy, issues offer letters that omit the termination procedure and working hours. When one employee's performance fails to improve, the firm dismisses him with immediate effect. The dismissal is overturned as procedurally flawed, and the firm pays compensation it could have avoided. A one-page contract drafted at the start, with the statutory procedure spelled out, would have made the same decision defensible. The lesson is common to most labour disputes: the paperwork you disliked at the beginning is the paperwork that protects you at the end.

Had the firm documented performance warnings, given the required notice or pay in lieu, conducted a fair process and calculated final dues correctly, the outcome would have been different. The cost of proper documentation at hiring and during employment is minimal compared to litigation costs and reputational damage.

Frequently asked questions

Is a written contract required?

Yes. Employers must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee under the Labour Act, 2074.

What is the maximum working week?

48 hours, with overtime payable beyond that as prescribed by law.

What is an employee entitled to on termination?

Notice or pay in lieu, and gratuity and leave encashment where applicable, unless the termination is for misconduct.

Must employers contribute to the Social Security Fund?

Yes. Registered employers must contribute on behalf of their employees for the prescribed benefits.

What happens if contributions are late?

Penalties apply, and the arrears remain payable along with any interest as prescribed.

Does the Labour Act apply to all employers?

It applies to most private sector employers, with limited exceptions as set out in the Act.

Can an employer dismiss an employee immediately?

Only in cases of serious misconduct and only after following the proper inquiry procedure set out in the Labour Act. Immediate dismissal without due process is risky.

Should part time employees get the same minimums?

Part time employees are entitled to the applicable minimums on a pro rata basis as per the Act. Employers must still issue written terms and comply with statutory obligations.

How long should employment records be kept?

Employment records should be kept for at least the period prescribed by law and in any case long enough to respond to potential claims. Good practice is to retain key records for several years after employment ends.

Can employment terms be changed unilaterally?

Material changes to employment terms generally require the employee's consent. Unilateral changes that reduce statutory or agreed benefits can be challenged.

Our labour and employment team assists employers with contracts, workplace policies, termination procedures and Social Security Fund compliance. If you would like a clear view of your situation, send us a note through our contact page for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp at +977 9802356987, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

title: Divorce in Nepal: Process, Cost and Timeline Explained
content:
Deciding to end a marriage is rarely a single moment. For most people it follows a long period of trying to make things work, and by the time they speak to a lawyer they are carrying both the emotional weight of the decision and a set of practical fears about money, children and paperwork. The law in Nepal is clearer than many expect, but it moves along two very different tracks, and knowing which one you are on early makes the whole process easier to bear.

This guide explains both tracks, what each involves, and how to prepare, so you can make decisions calmly rather than under pressure.

Quick answer

There are two routes to divorce in Nepal. A mutual consent divorce, under Section 93 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, is when both spouses agree to end the marriage and settle the terms. A contested divorce, based on a recognised ground, is when one spouse does not agree or the terms cannot be settled. Mutual cases are faster and cheaper. Contested cases take longer, because the court must decide custody, maintenance and property along the way.

The law behind it

Divorce in Nepal is governed by Chapter 3 of the National Civil Code, 2074 (the Muluki Civil Code), and by the National Civil Procedure Code for the process itself. The case is filed in the Family Court, or in the District Court with jurisdiction over the respondent's locality. Because the route and the outcome both turn on the facts, the advice worth having is advice about your facts, not about divorce in the abstract.

Grounds for divorce

Under Section 94, either spouse may petition on grounds such as adultery, desertion, physical or mental cruelty, or having lived apart for three or more consecutive years. Section 95 gives a wife additional grounds, including polygamy by the husband and marital rape. If your situation does not fall neatly into one of these, a mutual consent filing may be the more honest route.

How a mutual consent divorce works

Both spouses file a joint petition and agree the terms. Where children, maintenance or property are involved, those terms should be written into the petition so they are settled, not left for a later dispute. In practice this is the route most couples choose when the relationship has ended without open conflict, because it closes the matter in weeks rather than years. The court can decree the divorce after the prescribed period, which is designed to give both parties time to reconsider.

How a contested divorce works

When only one spouse wants the divorce, or the two cannot agree, the petition must state a recognised ground and the case proceeds through hearings, evidence and, frequently, reconciliation attempts. The court will decide custody, maintenance and how jointly acquired property is divided. Because these decisions are discretionary, the quality of the evidence prepared at the start often decides the outcome more than anything said in the final hearing.

How long it takes

Route Typical timeframe
Mutual consent A few weeks to two to three months after the court accepts the petition
Contested, no major disputes Around one to two years from filing
Contested with custody or property disputes Longer still, and longer again if the respondent cannot be traced

These are realistic ranges, not promises. Court load and the cooperation of both parties move the timeline more than anything else.

Documents you will normally need

  • Citizenship certificates of both spouses
  • The marriage registration certificate, or court marriage certificate
  • Birth certificates for any children
  • Evidence supporting any claim over property or maintenance
  • A properly authenticated power of attorney if a spouse lives abroad

What it costs

The court fee on a divorce plaint in a district court is modest, often a few hundred rupees. The larger cost is professional fees, which depend on whether the matter is mutual or contested and how much negotiation and hearing time it needs. A mutual file can usually be handled on a fixed fee. A contested matter with property and custody issues is typically billed on milestones. Whichever applies, ask for a written fee structure before you engage anyone.

A worked example

A couple who married in Kathmandu and now live in Australia want to divorce by agreement, but neither can easily return. They sign a power of attorney before a notary in Australia, have it attested by the Nepali embassy, and their Nepali lawyer files a mutual consent petition in Kathmandu. The terms on their apartment and on child maintenance are set out in the petition, so there is nothing left to argue about later. The matter is done without either of them flying home. Had one of them opposed the divorce, the same facts would have taken a much longer and more expensive route, and at least one appearance would likely have been required.

Divorce when a spouse lives abroad

Nepali couples living overseas can often complete a mutual consent divorce by power of attorney, avoiding a return to Nepal. Contested cases are harder to run remotely and usually need at least one appearance by the petitioner, or cross-examination of a witness.

Custody, maintenance and property

The court decides custody in the interest of the child, weighing the child's welfare and age against the care each parent can provide. Maintenance reflects the needs of the dependent spouse and children and the ability of the person paying. Property acquired during the marriage through joint effort is generally divided, while ancestral and individually owned property is treated separately. These questions are where most of the emotion in a case sits, and where calm, early advice pays off most.

Practical steps to take

  1. Speak to a family lawyer before filing, so the right route and grounds are chosen.
  2. Gather the documents above, including the original marriage certificate.
  3. If the divorce is mutual, put the terms on custody, maintenance and property in writing first.
  4. File with the correct court and attend the required hearings.
  5. After the decree, update your records and register any new marriage.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a divorce take in Nepal? A mutual consent divorce is typically finalised within a few weeks to two to three months once the court accepts the petition. A contested divorce generally takes one to two years, and longer where custody or property is disputed.

Can I divorce without going to court? No. Even a mutual consent divorce requires a court decree. The agreement shapes the case, but the court issues the order.

Can we divorce in Nepal if we married abroad? Often yes, depending on your citizenship and where the respondent lives. A Nepali couple who married abroad can generally proceed in Nepal, and the marriage may need to be registered here first.

Do I need my spouse's agreement to divorce? No. A contested divorce is available on a recognised ground without the other spouse's consent, though it takes longer.

What happens to property on divorce? Property acquired during the marriage through joint effort is generally divided. Ancestral and individually owned property is treated separately.

Can a spouse abroad be divorced without returning? In mutual cases, usually yes, through an authenticated power of attorney. Contested cases often require an appearance.

How Pluto Associates can help

Our family law team handles mutual and contested divorces, custody and maintenance across Nepal, and for Nepali couples living abroad. If you would like a clear view of your situation, contact our team for a confidential consultation, message us on WhatsApp, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

title: How to Register an NGO in Nepal: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
People who set out to do good in Nepal often hit a wall they did not expect, and it is rarely about the cause. It is about paperwork. The registration route for a non-profit depends on whom you intend to serve and where your funding comes from, and choosing the wrong route at the start can stall an organisation before it has done any work at all.

This guide explains the two main routes for non-profits in Nepal, the third path for international organisations, and how to keep a registration in good standing once it is granted.

Quick answer

There are two domestic routes and one international one. A local non-profit registers with the District Administration Office (DAO) if it will work within Nepal under domestic funding. An organisation that operates nationally or receives foreign funding affiliates with the Social Welfare Council (SWC) as well. An International NGO (INGO) enters Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and an agreement with the SWC, and must work through local partners rather than operating directly in the community.

A fourth route deserves mention because it is often overlooked: a non-profit can also be structured as a company limited by guarantee or a not-for-profit company and registered at the Office of the Company Registrar under the Companies Act 2063. That route suits organisations that expect contractual work, foreign institutional funding or a corporate form of governance. The right choice among these depends on three questions: where the money comes from, how wide the work reaches, and how the founders intend to govern the body. Answer those first and the paperwork becomes a straight line.

NGO and INGO: what the words mean in practice

In everyday use, an NGO is a domestic non-profit registered with the DAO and affiliated with the Social Welfare Council. An INGO is a foreign non-profit that enters Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and an agreement with the SWC. The distinction matters because an INGO cannot simply run its own projects here. It channels its work through local NGO partners, and its approval process is more regulated.

The practical consequences of the distinction show up in daily operations. A domestic NGO hires staff, signs leases and opens accounts in its own name throughout Nepal. An INGO's agreement with the Social Welfare Council defines which sectors it may work in, with whom it must partner, and how funds are transferred to and accounted for by those partners. Foreign funding is the other dividing line. An NGO that has registered only with the DAO and then accepts a grant from an overseas foundation has moved into territory that requires Social Welfare Council involvement, and doing that after the money has been committed is far harder than doing it before.

Step 1: Form the founding committee

You need a group of founding members, usually five or more Nepali citizens, who will form the general assembly and elect an executive committee. Their citizenship certificates, and in most cases passports, are required. Getting the founding group right at this stage saves redoing the documents later.

Choose founders who will actually stay. Every change of office bearer means a fresh set of documents, a fresh signature specimen and, in some offices, a fresh round of scrutiny. The general assembly is the organisation's supreme body, and its first meeting should produce proper minutes: the date, the attendees, the decisions taken, the constitution adopted and the executive committee elected. Those minutes are part of the application file, and they are also the document you will rely on years later when a bank or a funder asks who is authorised to act.

Step 2: Draft the constitution

The constitution is the heart of the application. It should set out the organisation's name, objectives, area of operation, membership, the composition and tenure of the executive committee, how decisions are taken, and how funds are managed. Supporting documents include the minutes of the formation meeting, the election of office bearers, and the PAN application of the institution. A constitution that is vague about objectives or about how funds are controlled is the most common reason a file is sent back.

Write the objectives with care, because they define what the organisation may lawfully do. Narrow objectives make future projects awkward; sweeping objectives invite questions. The fund management clause deserves equal attention. It should say how bank accounts are opened, who may sign, how expenditure is approved, how accounts are kept and how they are audited. Funders read this clause before they read anything else, and a constitution that is silent on audit and signatory rules will be questioned later by the Social Welfare Council, the bank, or both. Keep the language plain. An application written in precise, simple terms moves faster than one written in ornate generalities.

Step 3: Register at the District Administration Office

The complete file goes to the DAO of the district where the organisation is based. The DAO reviews the constitution and documents and, once satisfied, issues the registration. This registration gives the organisation legal personality, which it needs before it can open a bank account or sign agreements in its own name.

Depending on where the organisation is based and the nature of its work, registration or recognition at the local government level may also apply alongside the DAO route, so it is worth confirming the current practice in your district before filing. Once registration is issued, check it immediately for errors in the name, address and objectives. A registration certificate is the document every subsequent application will quote, and a mistake in it propagates through every later filing. Store the original safely and keep certified copies, because the original will be requested repeatedly.

Step 4: Affiliate with the Social Welfare Council

A registered NGO that intends to receive foreign funding, or to operate beyond the local level, typically registers with and seeks affiliation from the Social Welfare Council. Affiliation is what unlocks access to funding and to formal national recognition. The SWC reviews the constitution, the DAO registration and the organisation's work plan.

Practically, the SWC process asks an organisation to show what it intends to do, where, with what budget and under whose management. A clear work plan with realistic figures moves through review more smoothly than a broad aspiration. Affiliation also brings ongoing duties: project approvals for funded work, reporting on implementation, and coordination where foreign personnel or funds are involved. Organisations that treat affiliation as a one-time paperwork exercise, rather than as an ongoing relationship, are the ones that later find a grant cannot be received or disbursed without further SWC steps.

Step 5: Bank account and PAN

With the DAO registration and, where applicable, SWC affiliation in hand, the organisation can open a bank account in its own name and complete its tax registration to receive a PAN. These are the prerequisites for receiving funding, issuing receipts and employing staff.

Open the account with a clear signatory rule from the constitution, and make sure the bank's mandate matches the office bearers recorded in your registration. Tax registration then determines how the organisation handles withholding on salaries and payments, and whether it has filing obligations even in years with no taxable income. Many non-profits assume that because they are non-profit, tax filings stop. They do not. Filing discipline from the first year prevents a build-up of outstanding returns later, which is exactly the kind of thing a funder's audit finds.

Costs and realistic timelines

The direct costs are modest. Registration at the DAO, affiliation with the Social Welfare Council, PAN registration and the bank account each carry small official fees, and professional preparation, if you use it, is usually the larger part of the budget. The real cost is time. A complete, well-drafted file is measured in weeks. A file returned for a constitutional amendment or a missing minute is measured in months, because it must be corrected and re-queued rather than simply resubmitted.

Timelines depend mostly on readiness. Founders who arrive with citizenship documents, a settled name, agreed objectives and signed minutes move quickly. Founders still debating the name and objectives at the filing stage do not. The single most effective thing a founding group can do is settle the substance, name, objectives, area, office bearers, fund rules, before anyone starts drafting forms.

A worked example

A group in Lalitpur wants to run a literacy programme funded entirely by local donors. It follows the DAO route, publishes a clear constitution, and keeps its work within the district. A second group wants to run the same programme but with a European foundation as its funder. That funding brings the Social Welfare Council into the picture, and with it a stricter review of the constitution and work plan. Had the second group registered only with the DAO and then accepted foreign funding, it would have had to pause and restructure mid-programme. Deciding at the outset which route fits your funding is the single most useful early choice.

The second group's experience contains a further lesson. Because its grant agreement with the overseas foundation specified a twelve-month reporting cycle, the SWC affiliation and the work plan had to be aligned to that calendar from the start. Funder deadlines and regulatory deadlines do not automatically match, and reconciling them is much easier before signature than afterwards. Where foreign personnel are involved, or where funds must flow to partner organisations, the approval steps should be built into the grant's own timetable rather than discovered during implementation.

Ongoing compliance

A non-profit must file annual reports and financial statements with the DAO and, where affiliated, with the Social Welfare Council to keep its registration current. Falling behind on reporting is the most common reason an organisation's status lapses and funding is interrupted. Renewal and reporting dates vary by office, so a compliance calendar from day one is worth the small effort.

Good standing also has a practical face. Keep the executive committee current, hold and minute general assembly meetings on the cycle your constitution requires, have accounts prepared annually, and update the DAO and SWC whenever office bearers or the address change. When a funder or a partner bank asks for proof of status, the answer should be a single folder containing the registration certificate, the affiliation, the PAN, the latest annual report and the audit. Organisations that can produce that folder quickly attract funding; organisations that cannot spend weeks reconstructing it.

Common mistakes

Most NGO registration problems are variations of a few errors. Choosing the DAO-only route while actively courting foreign grants. Drafting objectives so broadly that the reviewing office queries them, or so narrowly that the first project falls outside them. Filing before the founding meeting minutes and office bearer elections are properly documented. Accepting foreign funding before SWC affiliation is in place. Letting the annual report deadline pass because the organisation was busy with fieldwork. And keeping the registration certificate details out of sync with reality after office bearers or the registered address change.

Each is avoidable with a short checklist at the start and a calendar that runs in the background afterwards.

Frequently asked questions

How many founding members are needed?

Usually five or more Nepali citizens, who form the general assembly and elect the executive committee. Their citizenship certificates, and passports in some cases, form part of the application file.

Do I need Social Welfare Council affiliation?

If you intend to receive foreign funding or operate beyond the local level, yes. It is central to accessing funding and national recognition, and it is harder to obtain after a grant has already been signed.

What is the difference between an NGO and an INGO?

An NGO is a domestic non-profit registered with the DAO. An INGO is a foreign non-profit entering Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and working through local partners.

Can an INGO operate directly in Nepal?

Generally it must work through local NGO partners rather than operating directly in the community, and its agreement with the Social Welfare Council defines the sectors, partners and modality of its work.

Does an NGO need a PAN?

Yes. A PAN is required for receiving funding, issuing receipts and employing staff, and filing obligations can apply even in years without taxable income.

What happens if annual reports are missed?

The registration and affiliation can lapse, which interrupts funding. Reporting discipline keeps the organisation in good standing, and a compliance calendar from day one is the simplest way to maintain it.

Can an NGO be registered as a company instead?

Yes. A not-for-profit or company limited by guarantee can be registered at the Office of the Company Registrar under the Companies Act 2063. That route can suit organisations doing contractual work or seeking institutional funding, and the choice should be made before drafting.

Can an NGO receive foreign currency into its account?

Where foreign funding is involved, Social Welfare Council affiliation and the applicable approvals come first. The bank will ask for the affiliation documents before remitting funds, so this should be settled before a grant agreement is signed.

How long does registration take?

With a complete file, a constitution settled in advance, and minutes ready, it is typically a matter of weeks. Returned files add months, because the constitution or documents must be corrected and the application re-queued.

What does an INGO need to enter Nepal?

Entry and operation under the Social Welfare Act, an agreement with the Social Welfare Council, and local NGO partners through whom the work is carried out. The agreement defines scope, duration and reporting duties.

How Pluto Associates can help

Our NGO and INGO practice prepares the constitution and formation documents, manages the DAO registration and Social Welfare Council affiliation, and keeps annual reporting on track. If you would like a clear view of your situation, [contact our team](/contact) for a consultation, message us on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/9779802356987), or call [+977 9802356987](tel:+9779802356987). We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.
