title: NRN Investment in Nepal: How Non-Resident Nepalis Can Invest
content:
For many non-resident Nepalis, investing back home is both a financial decision and an emotional one. There is a family business to support, or a plot of land to develop, or simply a wish to keep a stake in the country you grew up in. The good news is that NRNs are welcome to invest, and the framework exists. The part that trips people up is the same one that catches every foreign investor: the approvals come before the money, not after.

This guide explains how NRN investment works in Nepal, where the diaspora route differs from ordinary foreign investment, what the process costs and requires, and what to get right so your capital is not stranded when you want it back.

Quick answer

Non-resident Nepalis can invest in Nepal under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), which treats NRNs as permitted foreign investors. The usual approvals apply: sector eligibility, approval from the Department of Industry, and registration with the Office of the Company Registrar. In some cases the NRN route carries a lower entry threshold than the general foreign investment minimum, so it is worth confirming the current policy before you structure anything.

Is the NRN route different?

NRNs are foreign investors under FITTA, so the framework is familiar. What differs is treatment. Certain concessions are available to the diaspora, and some technology-based or smaller investments can qualify for a lower threshold than the general minimum. These are policy details that change, which is exactly why they should be checked at the time you invest rather than assumed from something read a year ago.

First, a word on who counts as an NRN. The Non-Resident Nepalis Act covers Nepali citizens residing abroad, and also persons of Nepali origin who have taken foreign citizenship. Both categories are generally eligible to hold an NRN card, issued through the designated Nepali authorities, and holding that card is worth doing before you invest rather than after. It is the document that evidences your status to banks, regulators and later to the tax authorities when you want funds to leave the country. An NRN who invests without keeping the status paperwork current often discovers the gap at exactly the wrong moment, when a dividend or capital payment is queued for remittance.

The card itself does not confer investment rights. Those come from FITTA and the applicable policies. But in the mechanics of banking and approvals, being able to prove status cleanly removes a layer of friction that otherwise slows every step.

Ways an NRN can invest

  • A new company in an eligible sector, usually a private limited company with the NRN as shareholder. This is the most common route.
  • Investment in an existing company, by subscribing to new shares, subject to sector limits and the company's approval. Buying shares from an existing shareholder is a different transaction again, requiring its own approvals.
  • Listed securities, meaning portfolio investment in shares on the Nepal Stock Exchange, which follows separate rules for non-residents.
  • A branch or joint venture, where the NRN invests alongside Nepali or other partners.
  • Technology and knowledge contributions, where the NRN's expertise is valued as part of the investment, which in some cases affects the minimum capital that must be brought in.

Each of these routes has its own filing path. The new company route is the cleanest for first-time investors because everything is created fresh and the paper trail is unambiguous. Buying into an existing company is perfectly workable but introduces the diligence questions that come with any secondary purchase: what are you actually buying, and do the company's records say the same thing as its promoters.

Minimum investment and sector eligibility

The general minimum foreign investment threshold in Nepal is currently NPR 20 million, and individual sectors carry their own limits or are reserved for Nepali citizens. Energy, tourism, IT and manufacturing are broadly open. Some service and retail activities are reserved. Technology-based investments in certain cases benefit from a lower or waived threshold. Confirm sector eligibility before committing money, because a structure that cannot be approved wastes both the filing cost and months of time.

A few practical notes on eligibility. The negative list, meaning sectors closed or restricted to foreign investment, includes certain retail trade, personal service activities and locally oriented small-scale businesses. Where a sector is open but capped, the cap applies to the foreign shareholding percentage, so a joint venture with a Nepali partner may be the only viable structure rather than a preference. And approval authority depends on the size and nature of the project: the Department of Industry handles most applications, while larger or certain strategic projects go to the Investment Board Nepal. Knowing which door to knock on before you file saves a month of redirection.

Sector rules are the single most common cause of wasted effort in this space. An NRN reads that a sector is open, commits to a lease and a business plan, and only then discovers that the precise activity, as distinct from the broad industry, is reserved. A short eligibility check at the start, ideally with someone who reads the current policy rather than a summary from a forum, prevents this entirely.

The process, step by step

  1. Confirm sector eligibility and the minimum investment that applies to an NRN.
  2. Submit the foreign investment application to the Department of Industry and obtain approval. This is the step that must precede the money, not follow it.
  3. Reserve the company name and prepare the memorandum and articles of association, with the shareholding structured exactly as the approval specifies.
  4. Incorporate at the Office of the Company Registrar and obtain the certificate.
  5. Register for PAN and, where applicable, VAT.
  6. Open a corporate bank account and route the investment through authorised banking channels, so the capital inflow is recorded properly from the first remittance.

Timelines vary with the completeness of the file and the season, but applicants who have their documents in order, including notarised and authenticated papers from abroad, generally move through the stages in a matter of weeks rather than months. The stage that most often slips is the foreign investment approval, because any gap in the paperwork sends the file back into the queue.

Do you need to be in Nepal?

Much of the process can be handled remotely. A shareholder resolution and a power of attorney can be notarised abroad and authenticated, and a local representative can complete the filings. In practice, being available for one visit at the key banking stage smooths things out, but it is not always essential.

A few points for those managing this from abroad. Documents executed overseas generally need notarisation and authentication, or consular legalisation, before Nepali authorities will accept them, and this takes time in itself, so start it early. Appointing a representative with a clean power of attorney is essential, and the document should be drafted to cover the specific acts needed, including banking, registration and tax filings, rather than a vague authorisation. And keep clear communication channels with whoever is filing, because the most common cause of delay in remote setups is a query from an office that nobody reads for a week. Our guide to setting up a company in Nepal walks through the incorporation step by step.

A worked example

An NRN in the United States wants to buy 30% of an existing Nepali software company. Because the sector is open and the investment meets the threshold, the route is manageable. He starts by confirming eligibility, then files for foreign investment approval, then subscribes to new shares. The capital enters through his bank, not hand to hand, and is recorded at the central bank.

Two years later, when he wants to repatriate a dividend, the paper trail from that original transfer is what makes the remittance smooth. The company's records show the shareholding, the tax filings show the dividend, and the bank can trace the original inflow against the outgoing payment. An NRN who wires money informally in year one often finds the same funds impossible to send back in year three. The money is not lost, but it is stuck, and unsticking it costs far more in professional fees than doing it properly at the start would have.

Repatriation of profits and capital

Profits, dividends and, on winding up, capital can be repatriated subject to Nepal Rastra Bank approval and the company's tax obligations. The key is documentation: funds should enter through the banking system and the equity should be reflected in the company's records. Keep your NRN status and papers current, because repatriation depends on being able to show exactly where the money came from.

A few things to understand about how this works in practice. Dividends can normally be remitted after the company has cleared its tax liabilities for the relevant year, and the remittance is processed through the banking system with the approval trail in place. Capital repatriation on winding up follows liquidation and tax clearance, and requires that the original investment, plus any approved increases, is documented. Royalty and technical fee remittances follow their own rules under the foreign exchange framework. In every case, the currency question resolves itself if the inflow was clean, and becomes a problem if it was not.

Nepal Rastra Bank's foreign exchange guidelines are the operative document here, and they are updated from time to time. Confirming the current position before you structure the investment, particularly where repatriation is a priority rather than an eventual possibility, is worth the conversation.

Costs and timelines

Budget for more than government fees. The line items typically include government filing fees for investment approval and incorporation, notarisation and authentication costs for documents executed abroad, professional fees for legal and advisory work, and the cost of your own time or travel if you visit. None of these are large individually, and the aggregate is modest relative to the investment most NRNs make.

The timeline is usually measured in weeks for a straightforward new company, longer where the sector requires additional clearance or where documents from abroad need consular processing. The expensive timeline is the one that starts twice, because a structure that cannot be approved had to be rebuilt. That is where the real cost lives, and it is entirely avoidable with an eligibility check before commitment.

Common pitfalls

  • Committing to a sector that is closed to foreign investment.
  • Bringing funds in informally, which then blocks repatriation.
  • Skipping notarisation and authentication, causing delays at the registrar or the bank.
  • Confusing company registration with foreign investment approval, when both are required.
  • Investing without current NRN status documentation, which surfaces at the remittance stage.
  • Relying on policy summaries that are a year or two out of date, when thresholds and sector rules change.
  • Structuring around a minimum investment figure without checking whether the specific sector has its own requirement.

Frequently asked questions

Can an NRN own 100% of a Nepali company?

In sectors not on the negative list, generally yes. Where a sector is capped for foreign shareholding, a joint venture structure may be required, so eligibility should be confirmed for the specific activity before structuring.

Is the minimum investment lower for NRNs?

Sometimes, depending on the sector and the type of investment, including technology-based cases where the threshold can be lower or waived. Confirm the current policy before structuring, because these details change.

Can an NRN invest while living abroad?

Yes, largely. Notarised and authenticated documents and a local representative allow most of the process to be handled remotely, though being available for the key banking stage can help.

Can an NRN repatriate profits?

Yes, after tax clearance and Nepal Rastra Bank approval, provided the original investment was documented and entered through the banking system. An informally funded investment creates problems here.

Does an NRN need foreign investment approval?

Yes. NRNs are treated as foreign investors under FITTA and require approval from the Department of Industry, or the Investment Board Nepal for larger projects, before the capital is brought in.

Can an NRN buy land in Nepal?

An NRN who holds Nepali citizenship generally can. An NRN who has taken foreign citizenship faces the same property restrictions as other foreign nationals. See our guide on foreigners buying property.

What is an NRN card and do I need one?

The NRN card is issued to eligible non-resident Nepalis and persons of Nepali origin through the designated Nepali authorities. It is not itself an investment licence, but it evidences your status to banks and authorities, and holding one smooths both investment and remittance.

Do I have to visit Nepal to complete the investment?

Usually not for the full process. Most filings can be done by a local representative under a power of attorney, with documents notarised and authenticated abroad. A visit at the banking stage is helpful but not always essential.

How long does the approval process take?

For a complete file in an open sector, approval and incorporation typically take weeks rather than months. Incomplete documents, or documents from abroad that have not been properly authenticated, are the most common cause of delay.

What happens if I send money to Nepal before approval?

This is the classic mistake, and it creates lasting problems. Unapproved inflows are difficult to record as equity, and the same funds become hard to repatriate later. Approval must precede the money, always.

How Pluto Associates can help

We advise non-resident Nepalis on eligibility, structuring, approvals and compliance, and can manage the full incorporation from abroad. If you would like a clear view of your situation, contact our team for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

faqs.a: In sectors not on the negative list, generally yes. Where a sector is capped for foreign shareholding, a joint venture structure may be required, so eligibility should be confirmed for the specific activity before structuring.

faqs.q: Is the minimum investment lower for NRNs?
faqs.a: Sometimes, depending on the sector and the type of investment, including technology-based cases where the threshold can be lower or waived. Confirm the current policy before structuring, because these details change.

faqs.q: Can an NRN invest while living abroad?
faqs.a: Yes, largely. Notarised and authenticated documents and a local representative allow most of the process to be handled remotely, though being available for the key banking stage can help.

faqs.q: Can an NRN repatriate profits?
faqs.a: Yes, after tax clearance and Nepal Rastra Bank approval, provided the original investment was documented and entered through the banking system. An informally funded investment creates problems here.

faqs.q: Does an NRN need foreign investment approval?
faqs.a: Yes. NRNs are treated as foreign investors under FITTA and require approval from the Department of Industry, or the Investment Board Nepal for larger projects, before the capital is brought in.

faqs.q: Can an NRN buy land in Nepal?
faqs.a: An NRN who holds Nepali citizenship generally can. An NRN who has taken foreign citizenship faces the same property restrictions as other foreign nationals. See our guide on foreigners buying property.

faqs.q: What is an NRN card and do I need one?
faqs.a: The NRN card is issued to eligible non-resident Nepalis and persons of Nepali origin through the designated Nepali authorities. It is not itself an investment licence, but it evidences your status to banks and authorities, and holding one smooths both investment and remittance.

faqs.q: Do I have to visit Nepal to complete the investment?
faqs.a: Usually not for the full process. Most filings can be done by a local representative under a power of attorney, with documents notarised and authenticated abroad. A visit at the banking stage is helpful but not always essential.

faqs.q: How long does the approval process take?
faqs.a: For a complete file in an open sector, approval and incorporation typically take weeks rather than months. Incomplete documents, or documents from abroad that have not been properly authenticated, are the most common cause of delay.

faqs.q: What happens if I send money to Nepal before approval?
faqs.a: This is the classic mistake, and it creates lasting problems. Unapproved inflows are difficult to record as equity, and the same funds become hard to repatriate later. Approval must precede the money, always.

title: Can Foreigners Buy Property in Nepal? The Rules Explained
content:
Foreigners are often surprised by how much of the answer to this question depends on what they actually want the property for. Owning the land outright and having secure, long-term use of it are two different things in Nepal, and the law treats them very differently. Understanding that distinction early saves both money and heartache.

This guide explains what a foreign national can and cannot do with property in Nepal, and the routes that genuinely work.

Quick answer

In general, a foreign national cannot own land in Nepal in their own name. Land ownership is reserved for Nepali citizens. There is no simple path to individual freehold ownership for a foreigner. That does not close the door on property altogether. Foreign-invested businesses can lease, can hold property for their own operations in eligible circumstances, and in narrow situations can buy apartments. The structure you choose matters far more here than in most countries.

The useful way to think about it is to separate three questions. First, what is your legal status, foreign citizen, Nepali citizen living abroad, or Nepali citizen who has taken foreign citizenship, because citizenship rather than residency decides your rights. Second, what do you need the property for, a home, premises for a business, or an investment, because the answers differ. Third, how will it be held, personally, through a company, or under a registered lease, because that choice determines your security, your taxes and your exit. Settle those three questions before any negotiation begins.

The legal position

Nepal's land rules reserve ownership to Nepali citizens. A foreign individual buying land in their own name is not viable, and arrangements that try to hold land through a local nominee carry serious legal and reputational risk, including the risk that the nominee's own creditors or heirs take the land. The workable routes for a foreign national or a foreign company are leasing, corporate holding in eligible circumstances, and limited apartment ownership.

The nominee problem deserves a closer look, because it comes up constantly. A foreign buyer pays for land, the deed is registered in the name of a Nepali friend, relative or employee, and everyone relies on trust. Legally, the registered owner owns the land. Their divorce, their debts, their death or simply a change of heart can all reach the property, and the foreign buyer's claim rests on side agreements that are difficult to enforce and easy to deny. Successors who were not party to those agreements are not bound by them. For these reasons we advise against nominee arrangements in every case, and lawful alternatives achieve the same practical result.

Property rules also interact with investment rules. Where the aim is to hold property through a business, the foreign investment framework applies alongside the land rules, and approvals for the investment shape what the company may do with the property. Reading both together, rather than either alone, is what produces a structure that survives due diligence.

Option 1: Long-term leasing

For a foreign business that needs premises, a registered lease is the most common and safest route. Foreign-invested companies use commercial leases for offices, restaurants, factories and hotels. Register the lease so it is secure, and set the terms, permitted use and renewal rights out precisely. Leasing gives you reliable use of the property for the term without the complications of ownership. For a twenty-year industrial lease, the lease document is effectively your asset, and it deserves the same care as a purchase deed.

What makes a lease strong is the detail. Specify the permitted use, because a lease silent on use invites a dispute when the business changes. Set the rent review mechanism, so increases are predictable rather than negotiated annually under pressure. Include the right to renew or an option to renew at a stated rent, which is what protects a business that has built its location, its customer base and its fittings into one address. Address registration at the Land Revenue Office, because a registered lease is enforceable against third parties, including a subsequent purchaser of the land. Add clear provisions for repairs, insurance, early termination and the condition of handback at the end. A landlord who resists registration of a long lease is telling you something worth knowing before you sign.

Option 2: A foreign-invested company holding property

A company incorporated in Nepal, even with foreign shareholders, is a Nepali legal entity. In eligible circumstances it can acquire and hold property for its own business operations. This route is regulated and depends on the sector and the nature of the use, so it should be structured with advice rather than assumed. The important point is that the company holds the property, not the foreign shareholder personally. If you sell your shares, you sell the company that owns the land, which is a different transaction with different tax consequences.

Practically, this route works well for genuine operating needs: a factory site, a warehouse, an office floor, a hotel property. It works poorly as a way of acquiring land for personal use, because the property must serve the company's business, and a regulatory review will ask exactly that question. Keep the corporate records clean. The land ownership certificate should sit with the company's statutory documents, the acquisition should be approved and minuted properly, and any use of the premises by a shareholder personally should be documented at arm's length. When the time comes to exit, you are choosing between selling the shares and having the company sell the property, and the tax and registration consequences of each differ, so that choice should be made deliberately rather than by default.

Option 3: Apartments and residential ownership

Specific rules allow foreign nationals to purchase apartments and flats in limited situations, but the conditions are narrow and often misunderstood. Availability depends on your citizenship and residency status and on the particular development. Confirm the current position before any purchase commitment, because a scheme that sounds straightforward can turn out not to apply to you.

Two checks prevent disappointment. The first is eligibility: confirm in writing, ideally through the authority administering the rule, that your particular citizenship and residency status qualifies. The second is the project itself: confirm that the development is approved for sale to foreign buyers and that the title, building permit and completion position are all in order. Rules in this area can change, so a position confirmed two years ago is not one to rely on today. Any purchase should proceed only after the current position is verified and written into the agreement as a condition.

A worked example

A foreign investor wants a home in Kathmandu and a factory outside it. The home is the harder problem. Rather than attempting ownership through a Nepali friend, which would leave the investment exposed, the practical route is a long registered lease or an apartment under the limited framework, whichever fits. The factory is different: the investor's Nepali company can hold industrial land for its own operations where the sector and use qualify. Two goals, two structures, and getting them the wrong way round is the classic mistake.

The investor did one more thing correctly: sequence. Eligibility was confirmed first, then the title and boundary checks on the two sites, then the structures, a registered residential lease on one and a company acquisition on the other, and only then did money move. Buying in a hurry and structuring afterwards is where foreign buyers lose time and, occasionally, the property itself. An orderly sequence costs patience and saves almost everything else.

What every buyer or lessee should verify first

  • Confirm the land record (kitta) at the land revenue office shows the correct owner.
  • Check for mortgages, loans and other encumbrances.
  • Verify the land category and any public restrictions.
  • Confirm the tax and valuation position before registration.

A clean title check before you commit is the cheapest protection any property transaction can buy.

For a foreign party, add three checks to that list. Confirm your own legal capacity to hold the right you are buying, whether ownership, lease or shares, before negotiations go far. Confirm that any approval your structure needs, foreign investment approval for example, is either in place or can be obtained within the timetable of the deal. And confirm how money will move: the remittance route for the purchase, the account into which funds will be received, and the tax that will be deducted at registration. Payments made from outside Nepal without a clean documented trail cause problems at the bank and at the tax office later, so the banking route should be settled before the deed is drafted.

Taxes, fees and practical costs

Property transactions in Nepal carry registration fees at the Land Revenue Office, based on the government valuation of the land or building, and those fees are payable at registration rather than later. A registered lease also attracts a registration fee. Beyond the transaction itself, income from property, rent or the eventual disposal, is taxable, and a company disposing of property accounts for the gain in its tax return. Where the property will be leased out, the lease should state who bears which tax, because surprises at that stage tend to become disputes.

Budget also for the professional work: title verification, drafting or review of the deed or lease, and any survey where boundaries are unclear. These costs are modest against the value of the asset, and skipping them to move quickly is rarely economical.

Can an NRN buy property in Nepal?

Non-resident Nepalis are treated differently. An NRN who remains a Nepali citizen can generally acquire property, and many NRNs buy land or a house for family use or investment. An NRN who has taken foreign citizenship faces the same restrictions as any other foreign national. Because citizenship, not residency, decides your rights, this is the first point to clarify with a lawyer before you negotiate anything.

NRN purchases still carry conditions and practical checks. The route for bringing funds into Nepal, the applicable investment channels, and any ceiling or condition attached to the acquisition should all be confirmed against current law and Nepal Rastra Bank's instructions before commitment. Where an NRN holds foreign citizenship and wants property in Nepal, the same alternatives discussed above, leasing, corporate holding, or an eligible apartment purchase, apply in the same way.

Practical steps

  1. Establish your legal capacity to own or lease before negotiating.
  2. Run the title, encumbrance and land-category checks at the relevant office.
  3. Structure the deal through a registered lease or a corporate entity, with advice.
  4. Prepare and register the deed or lease, and pay the applicable taxes and fees.
  5. Update the records so the transaction is reflected at the land office.

Each step has a failure mode worth naming. Negotiating before capacity is settled produces agreements that cannot be performed. Skipping the record check produces surprises at registration. Structuring without advice produces a company or lease that fails its own purpose. Registering late or partially produces a transaction that binds the parties but not the world, and forgetting to update the records leaves a file that contradicts itself for years. The sequence above avoids all of these without slowing a genuine transaction.

Common mistakes

The recurring errors are consistent. Proceeding with a nominee because it seems faster, and discovering the risk only when the nominee's circumstances change. Assuming a lease is secure because it is signed, without registering it. Treating a foreign-invested company as a personal ownership vehicle rather than a business holding property for its own operations. Relying on an apartment rule heard second-hand rather than confirmed in writing for the buyer's specific status. Moving money into Nepal before the banking route and approvals are settled. And negotiating on price first, with structure and due diligence left for later, by which point the seller has little incentive to cooperate with either.

Avoiding these is not complicated. It simply requires the structure and the checks to come before the money, in that order, every time.

Frequently asked questions

Can a foreigner buy land in Nepal?

Generally no. Land ownership is reserved for Nepali citizens, and there is no simple path to individual freehold ownership for a foreign national.

Can a foreigner buy an apartment in Nepal?

In limited situations, under specific rules, depending on citizenship, residency and the development. This should be confirmed case by case, and in writing, before any purchase commitment because the position is administered by instruction and can change.

Can a foreign company own property in Nepal?

A Nepali company with foreign shareholders can hold property for its own operations in eligible circumstances. The company owns it, not the foreign shareholder, and the use must serve the company's business.

Is leasing a safe alternative?

Yes. A registered long-term lease is the most common and safest route for a foreign business, provided it is registered, precisely drafted and clear on permitted use, term, renewal and rent review.

Can an NRN own property?

An NRN who holds Nepali citizenship generally can. One who has taken foreign citizenship cannot, on the same terms as other foreigners, because citizenship rather than residency decides the right.

What happens if I buy through a Nepali nominee?

It is legally risky and can result in the loss of the property if the nominee's circumstances change, including through their debts, inheritance or a change of mind. We advise against it in every case.

Do I need foreign investment approval to hold property through a company?

Where the company has foreign investment, the investment approval framework applies alongside the land rules, and the permitted use of the property should be checked against the conditions attached to that approval.

What taxes and fees should I expect?

Registration fees at the Land Revenue Office on transfer or on a registered lease, based on government valuation, plus income tax on rent or gains as applicable. The deed or lease should also state clearly which party bears which tax.

Should a lease be registered?

Yes, for anything beyond a short or casual arrangement. Registration at the Land Revenue Office makes the lease enforceable against third parties, including a subsequent purchaser, which is precisely the protection a long-term tenant needs.

How long does a property transaction take?

It depends on readiness. With a clean title, capacity confirmed and documents prepared, registration itself is straightforward. Title problems, approvals or funding routes left unresolved are what extend the timeline, and all of them should be settled before the signing date is set.

How Pluto Associates can help

Our real estate team advises foreign investors, NRNs and companies on ownership, leases, corporate holding structures and property transfers in Nepal. If you would like a clear view of your situation, [contact our team](/contact) for a consultation, message us on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/9779802356987), or call [+977 9802356987](tel:+9779802356987). We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

title: PAN and VAT Registration in Nepal: What Businesses Need to Know
content:
Of all the post-incorporation steps, PAN and VAT cause the most needless difficulty. Neither is complicated on its own. What catches founders out is the timing, and the fact that a company's tax responsibilities begin on the day of incorporation, whether or not it has earned a rupee. A company that treats tax registration as a task for "later" usually ends up paying for the delay, either in penalties or in invoices a customer cannot use.

This guide explains what PAN and VAT are, when each applies, how the registration process works in practice, and what it costs in time and money to do both properly from day one.

Quick answer

Every company in Nepal needs a Permanent Account Number (PAN), issued by the Inland Revenue Department. Businesses whose taxable turnover crosses the legal threshold must also register for Value Added Tax (VAT). A company's PAN is obtained soon after incorporation and quickly. VAT registration, and the separate registration of each branch, are the steps first-time founders most often miss.

As a working rule: start the PAN process the week the certificate of incorporation is issued, decide deliberately whether to register for VAT voluntarily, and never issue an invoice without the company's tax numbers on it.

What a PAN is

The PAN is the tax identification number for individuals and businesses in Nepal. Companies obtain it as a post-incorporation step, typically within a short window of receiving the certificate of incorporation. Salaried employees, landlords and self-employed professionals also hold personal PANs for withholding and filing. The number attaches to the person or entity, not to a trade name, so a company that later changes its name keeps its PAN.

For a company, the PAN is the spine of everything that follows. Corporate income tax returns are filed against it. VAT registration is linked to it. Withholding tax deducted by customers is reported under it. Banks ask for it when opening the corporate account, and most established clients will not pay an invoice that does not show it. In practice, a company without a PAN cannot invoice properly, cannot open some banking facilities without difficulty, and cannot file the returns that keep it in good standing.

Individuals need PANs too, and this is the part employees and landlords often miss. Any person earning taxable income, including salary, rent or professional fees, is required to obtain a PAN and many payments are subject to withholding tax at source unless the payee provides one. A landlord who cannot produce a PAN may find tax deducted from rent at a higher rate. A freelance consultant billing a registered company will find the company compelled to withhold. Getting a personal PAN is inexpensive and quick, and it avoids these frictions entirely.

What VAT registration is

VAT applies once taxable turnover reaches the legal threshold, and registration is completed at the Inland Revenue Office. Once registered, the business charges VAT on its sales and claims input VAT on its purchases, filing periodic returns to settle the difference. Businesses below the threshold may register voluntarily, and many B2B suppliers do, because it lets their customers claim input credit on the invoices they receive. For a business selling mainly to other registered businesses, voluntary registration is often a commercial advantage rather than a burden.

Under the VAT Act 2074, the mandatory registration threshold is annual turnover of NPR 5 million, and the standard VAT rate is 13 percent. Certain supplies are zero-rated or exempt, which matters when you plan pricing, so it is worth checking how your particular revenue stream is treated before you commit to numbers in a contract.

The mechanics of a VAT registration are worth understanding before you file. A registered business charges VAT on taxable sales, collects it, and pays the net amount (tax collected minus tax paid on inputs, known as input credit) to the Inland Revenue Department with each periodic return. Input credit is only available where the supplier has issued a valid VAT invoice and the purchase is properly recorded, which is why the quality of your invoicing and bookkeeping directly determines your tax bill. Poorly kept purchase records are one of the most common reasons input credit claims are disallowed on audit.

Voluntary registration deserves a moment of thought rather than a reflex yes or no. It is usually right for businesses selling mainly to other registered companies, because those customers want creditable invoices and will often prefer a registered supplier even at a slightly higher price. It is usually wrong for businesses selling mainly to consumers or to unregistered small buyers, because the business then carries the administrative burden of filing and record-keeping with little offsetting benefit. The decision is commercial as much as legal, and it is worth modelling before you commit, since deregistration is not a simple matter of changing your mind.

Documents you will need

  • The certificate of incorporation, or the registration certificate for another entity type
  • The memorandum and articles of association, where applicable
  • Details of the business premises, including address and ownership or rental documents
  • Identification of the authorised representatives and directors
  • The business bank account details
  • Photographs and citizenship or passport copies of the directors and authorised signatory, as requested by the local office
  • The company seal, where your practice uses one on filings

Requirements vary slightly between Inland Revenue Offices, and papers that are perfectly acceptable in one office can draw a request for one extra document in another. Confirming the list with your office, or with counsel, before you submit saves a wasted trip.

The steps for a new company

  1. Incorporate with the Office of the Company Registrar.
  2. Apply for the PAN at the Inland Revenue Office soon after incorporation. This is typically straightforward and is often completed within a few working days when the papers are in order.
  3. Register for VAT once turnover will cross the threshold, or apply voluntarily, with the supporting documents for the business premises and bank account.
  4. Register each branch or permanent establishment separately, because VAT registration follows premises, not just the head office entity.
  5. Build the PAN and VAT numbers into invoices, contracts and accounts from day one, so that no billing cycle passes without them.

If the company will import goods or deal with customs, the PAN is also needed for customs clearance, and banks will request it when opening letters of credit or remitting payments abroad. Getting it early prevents a shipment sitting at the port for a paperwork reason.

Costs and timelines

Government fees for PAN registration and for VAT registration are modest, and the larger cost is usually professional fees if you engage a consultant, plus the cost of your own time. The real cost, however, lives in delay. A PAN is generally issued within days of a clean application. VAT registration takes longer, and incomplete premises documentation is the most common cause of the file being sent back.

From the company's side, the useful discipline is to treat tax registration as part of the incorporation sprint rather than a task for the first quiet month. In our experience, founders who file for PAN in the same week they receive their certificate are never the ones calling in a panic about an invoice a client has refused to pay.

A worked example

A technology consultancy incorporates in Kathmandu and plans to bill clients in Nepal and abroad. Because most of its clients are VAT-registered businesses that want input credit, the firm registers for VAT voluntarily even before crossing the threshold. Its PAN is issued within days of incorporation, and the same numbers appear on every invoice. Later, when the consultancy opens a second office in Pokhara, it knows the branch must be registered separately.

A competitor that waits until turnover forces the issue finds that invoices issued in the meantime cannot support the customer's input claim, leaving an awkward hole in its early bookkeeping. Two of its larger clients quietly move to registered suppliers. The competitor's eventual registration is not late in any legal sense, but the commercial cost of the gap was real and entirely avoidable. That contrast is the single most useful thing to take from this guide.

Consequences of late registration

Operating without a PAN where one is required attracts penalties, and VAT carries the same risk. The Inland Revenue Department can impose fines for failure to register within the prescribed period, and for a registered business that fails to file returns or pays late, penalties and interest accrue quickly and can exceed the underlying tax for smaller amounts.

Late VAT registration also means the business could not issue valid VAT invoices for the period before registration, which complicates both customer billing and input claims. Customers who discover after the fact that invoices they paid cannot support an input credit often ask for that credit to be made good, and the supplier has little legal ground to refuse.

Because the tax obligations of a company run from incorporation even before revenue begins, registering early is cheaper and simpler than catching up. A catch-up filing also tends to arrive with a request for explanation, which invites a wider look at the accounts than most new businesses would want.

Annual compliance after registration

With PAN and VAT in place, the ongoing obligations begin: periodic VAT returns, social security contributions if you employ staff, and the annual corporate income tax return supported by audited financial statements. Missing a filing date attracts fines quickly and invites scrutiny. Most businesses keep a compliance calendar from the start rather than tracking deadlines by memory.

A few points worth building into that calendar. VAT returns are generally filed on a monthly cycle, commonly due by the 25th of the following month, and must be accompanied by payment of any net tax due. Books of account must be maintained in accordance with the company and tax laws, and audited statements prepared for the annual return. Withholding tax deducted during the year must be deposited and reported on its own cycle. If staff are employed, contributions to the Social Security Fund are monthly obligations in their own right.

Businesses that appoint a accountant or bookkeeper still benefit from one partner or director understanding the calendar. The deadline that slips is almost always the one nobody owned.

Common mistakes

  • Treating PAN as something to arrange after the first invoice, and then stalling a payment because the invoice lacks the number.
  • Registering for VAT purely because a competitor did, without checking whether the customer base can actually use the credit.
  • Opening a second branch and assuming the head office registration covers it, when each permanent establishment requires its own registration.
  • Issuing invoices without the prescribed particulars, which customers then reject or which fail on audit.
  • Filing VAT returns without reconciling input credit properly, leading to claims being disallowed later.
  • Letting the annual return creep up as a surprise, rather than preparing audited accounts through the year.

None of these are exotic errors. They are the ordinary ones, and each is avoidable with a little discipline in the first few months.

Frequently asked questions

Is PAN registration mandatory for every company?

Yes. Every company in Nepal must obtain a PAN. It is required for tax filing, for VAT registration, for proper invoicing and for most banking arrangements.

When must a company get its PAN?

Soon after incorporation, within the short window set by the Inland Revenue Department. In practice, filing in the same week you receive the certificate avoids almost every downstream problem.

When does VAT registration become mandatory?

Once taxable turnover reaches the legal threshold, currently NPR 5 million in annual turnover under the VAT Act 2074. Below it, registration is voluntary but often worthwhile for B2B suppliers.

Can I register for VAT voluntarily?

Yes. Many businesses do, so their customers can input credit on their invoices. It is most useful where your buyers are registered businesses, and less useful where you sell mainly to consumers.

Does each branch need its own registration?

Yes. Each branch or permanent establishment is registered separately for VAT, because the registration is tied to the premises from which taxable supplies are made.

What happens if I register late?

Penalties apply, and invoices issued before registration cannot support a customer's VAT claim. Customers may ask that the credit be made good, and the delay invites a closer look at the accounts.

How often are VAT returns filed?

Returns are filed on a periodic cycle, commonly monthly and generally due by the 25th of the following month. Confirm the cycle that applies to you and build it into your compliance calendar.

Do employees and landlords need PANs too?

Yes, individuals with taxable income including salary, rent and professional fees are required to hold PAN, and many payments are subject to withholding at source unless the payee provides one.

Can a company deregister from VAT if it was registered voluntarily?

Deregistration is possible in principle but is not a simple about-face. The rules restrict frequent switching, and the Inland Revenue Department examines the application. Decide deliberately before registering rather than assuming you can easily undo it.

What records must a VAT-registered business keep?

Sales and purchase records, VAT invoices, input credit documentation, and books of account maintained in the prescribed form. The quality of these records determines whether input credit claims survive an audit.

How Pluto Associates can help

We handle PAN and VAT registration for companies, branches and foreign-invested entities, and support the ongoing filing and compliance that keeps a business in good standing with the Inland Revenue Department. If you would like a clear view of your situation, contact our team for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

faqs.q: How often are VAT returns filed?
faqs.a: Returns are filed on a periodic cycle, commonly monthly and generally due by the 25th of the following month. Confirm the cycle that applies to you and build it into your compliance calendar.

faqs.q: Do employees and landlords need PANs too?
faqs.a: Yes, individuals with taxable income including salary, rent and professional fees are required to hold PAN, and many payments are subject to withholding at source unless the payee provides one.

faqs.q: Can a company deregister from VAT if it was registered voluntarily?
faqs.a: Deregistration is possible in principle but is not a simple about-face. The rules restrict frequent switching, and the Inland Revenue Department examines the application. Decide deliberately before registering rather than assuming you can easily undo it.

faqs.q: What records must a VAT-registered business keep?
faqs.a: Sales and purchase records, VAT invoices, input credit documentation, and books of account maintained in the prescribed form. The quality of these records determines whether input credit claims survive an audit.

title: Bail in Nepal: How to Apply and What the Court Considers
content:
When someone is arrested in Nepal, the hours that follow decide more about the case than almost anything that comes later. Families usually call a lawyer in a state of alarm, unsure whether bail is even possible and what it would take. The honest answer is that bail is the default for many offences, but not all, and the difference lies in how the case is classified and how the application is made.

This guide explains how bail works under Nepali law, what the court weighs, what the application needs to contain, and what a family should do in the first critical window after an arrest.

Quick answer

Bail is the legal route to release from custody while a case is pending. It is not automatic, but it is the norm where the offence is not serious and the accused is not a flight risk. The court considers the nature of the offence, the strength of the evidence, the risk of flight or witness interference, and any prior record. How quickly bail is granted depends on the court, the classification of the offence, and how well the application is presented.

How bail works

Bail is decided by the court handling the case, under the Criminal Procedure Code 2074. At the early stage, the question of release is normally considered when the case first comes before the court after arrest, at the production or first hearing. The court weighs how serious the offence is, how strong the evidence appears, whether the accused might flee or interfere with witnesses, and whether there is a criminal record. For minor offences the accused is usually released on bail, or where no remand is warranted, on a simple recognisance.

Nepali criminal law divides offences into bailable and non-bailable categories. For bailable offences, release is closer to a right: the accused is entitled to bail, and either the police or the court grants it as a matter of course on the required surety. For non-bailable offences, bail becomes a matter for judicial discretion. The court must still consider it, and for many mid-range offences it is routinely granted, but the accused cannot demand it. For the most serious offences, particularly those carrying long terms of imprisonment or life imprisonment, bail is granted sparingly and the application has to answer the specific anxieties the court will have.

It is worth saying plainly what bail is not. It is not an acquittal, and it is not a promise that charges will be dropped. It is release on conditions while the case runs its course, and it comes with obligations, chiefly the obligation to attend every hearing. Breaching those conditions can lead to cancellation of bail and re-arrest, which is precisely the outcome a family under stress sometimes brings about by advising the accused to miss a hearing and lie low.

When bail is routinely available

  • Offences classified as not serious, where the accused is unlikely to interfere with the case.
  • Where the accused has no criminal record and a fixed residence in Nepal.
  • Where detention has run past the legal limit without a proper extension.
  • Where the accused has strong community ties, a family to support, or a business to run, and the court can be satisfied these tie them to the jurisdiction.
  • Where the prosecution itself does not oppose release, which often happens once the investigation has taken the statements it needs.

For these categories the application tends to be procedural rather than argumentative. The work is in the preparation and the timing, not in lengthy submissions.

When bail is harder to obtain

For serious offences, particularly those carrying long prison terms, bail is opposed and the court scrutinises the evidence closely. In these cases the onus shifts to showing why the accused should be released, and the application must answer the court's specific concerns rather than repeat general arguments.

Certain categories make bail genuinely difficult. Offences involving organised crime, those under special statutes with their own detention and bail provisions, and cases where the accused is alleged to have interfered with witnesses or tampered with evidence in the past all draw closer scrutiny. Repeat applicants, meaning someone who has sought bail before on similar facts, find the court reads the pattern.

Flight risk deserves particular attention, because it is the concern Nepali courts take most seriously in practice and the one most often under-addressed in applications. A foreign national, a person with substantial assets abroad, or someone with no fixed property or family in Nepal will be presumed a flight risk unless the application gives the court concrete reasons not to worry. Saying the accused will not flee is worth nothing. Offering something that makes fleeing costly or difficult is worth a great deal.

What the court expects from an application

  1. Identify the correct court and file promptly, with the specific facts of the case, including the exact allegation, the section of law invoked and the stage of investigation.
  2. Address the recognised factors: seriousness, evidence, flight risk and witness interference. Each should be answered on its own terms with facts, not slogans.
  3. Offer conditions that reassure the court, such as a fixed residence, regular attendance, a passport deposit where relevant, and a suitable surety of credible standing.
  4. Attend the hearing on the fixed date and respond to any objection. A defence counsel who is present and prepared on the hearing date signals a case that will not collapse into absconding.
  5. Keep the papers tidy. Courts notice applications that are disorganised, and the impression formed in the first minute carries into the order.

A practical note on sureties. The court wants a person of substance who will genuinely ensure attendance, not a relative of no means who signs because they were asked. A surety with a fixed address, an income and a reputation in the community reassures the court far more than a long list of names.

A worked example

A foreign businessperson is detained after a commercial dispute is reported as fraud. The first instinct, to explain everything to the police, is the wrong one. Instead, the person confirms identity, asks for a lawyer, and says nothing further. The lawyer files a bail application that directly addresses the court's likely concern, that a foreign national might leave the country, by offering a local address, a passport deposit and a Nepali surety. Framing the application around that single worry is what gets the release. A generic application, filed a week later, often does not.

Compare the other outcome. The family, panicking, hires a local fixer who files a template petition full of generalities about liberty and human rights, with no address offered and no surety arranged. The court, with a foreign national before it and a fraud allegation on file, refuses and remands. Two weeks later a better application finally reaches the court, by which time the accused has spent a fortnight in custody that better preparation would have avoided. The law did not change between the two applications. Only the quality of the preparation did.

If bail is refused

A refusal is not the end. Depending on the stage, the decision can be challenged by a review before the same court, an application to a higher court, or a writ petition. Timing matters, because the review window is short and the longer a person stays in custody the harder the case becomes. Someone who tracks the deadlines in the file is essential at this point.

A practical strategy on refusal is to make the next application materially different rather than merely repeated. If the first application failed on flight risk, the second should arrive with a passport deposit, a fixed address verified by documents, and a surety who did not appear last time. If it failed on the gravity of the offence, the second should develop the mitigating picture: employment, family responsibilities, medical circumstances, prior good character. Courts are far more receptive to a second application that demonstrates something new than to a reprint of the first.

What to do immediately after an arrest

The period between arrest and the first court appearance is the most consequential part of any case. The accused should avoid statements beyond confirming identity, should exercise the right to a lawyer, and should not agree to anything under pressure. Anything said at the police stage can resurface at trial, so the discipline shown in the first 48 hours often sets the course of the whole case.

For the family, three things matter in the first day. First, find out where the accused is held and under what provision, because that single fact determines the bail strategy. Second, instruct a lawyer immediately rather than waiting to see what the police advise. Third, do not attempt to influence witnesses, retrieve documents or move assets in a panic. Interventions of that kind, if noticed, become the basis for allegations of interference that will be used against the bail application.

White-collar and corporate cases

In fraud, money-laundering and regulatory matters the bail analysis is different again. These cases often turn on documentary evidence, the nature of the financial harm, and the risk that a financially mobile accused might abscond. A company facing a regulatory and criminal investigation at the same time should treat its defence as a single strategy from day one rather than responding piecemeal.

A few features of these cases are worth knowing. The investigation often runs longer, because documents take time to seize and analyse, which means more applications and more chances for the defence to show good faith through cooperation. The accused's own business records can be both an asset and a liability, so preserving and organising them early helps. And in cases involving companies, the question of which individuals bear personal criminal exposure, as distinct from corporate liability, is often worth clarifying sooner rather than later, because it shapes who needs the strongest bail case.

Costs and timelines

Legal fees for bail work vary with the complexity of the case and the court involved, and it is fair to ask for an estimate at the outset rather than discovering the bill later. The application itself, once prepared, is usually heard within days in the district courts, though timing depends on the court's calendar. The more expensive variable is delay: every day in custody carries a cost that no fee structure captures, which is why the premium in this area of law is on speed of preparation rather than length of argument.

Common mistakes

  • Allowing the accused to give a detailed statement to the police in the belief it will help.
  • Filing a generic bail petition that does not engage the specific concern the court will have.
  • Offering a surety who cannot demonstrate means.
  • Missing a hearing date, which invites cancellation of bail even after release.
  • Waiting for the investigation to conclude before seeking release, when the law contemplates release while it runs.
  • Treating a refusal as final and letting the review window lapse.

Frequently asked questions

Is bail a right in Nepal?

For bailable offences, release on bail is essentially entitlement. For non-bailable offences, it is the norm for many charges but not automatic. The court decides based on the offence, the evidence and the risk factors.

How quickly can bail be granted?

It is usually considered at the first appearance after arrest. A well-prepared application filed promptly improves the chances of an early release, and delay itself works against the applicant.

Can a foreign national get bail in Nepal?

Yes, though flight risk is examined closely. Offering a local address, a passport deposit and a Nepali surety with genuine means helps, and addressing the concern head-on rather than in generalities is what tends to succeed.

What if bail is denied?

It can be challenged by review, by application to a higher court, or by writ petition, depending on the stage. The review window is short, so the file should be watched carefully from the day of the order.

Should the accused speak to the police?

Beyond confirming identity, no. Statements made at the police stage can be used at trial, and the temptation to explain everything in the first hours is one of the most damaging mistakes families make.

Does a prior record affect bail?

Yes. A prior record weighs against release, particularly for similar offences. Where a record exists, the application should address it squarely with evidence of rehabilitation rather than ignoring it.

Can bail be cancelled after it is granted?

Yes. If the accused breaches conditions, absconds, interferes with witnesses or commits an offence while on bail, the court can cancel it. Attending every hearing and keeping the conditions is the whole of the obligation.

What is the difference between police bail and court bail?

For bailable offences the police may grant bail themselves at the station. For non-bailable offences, release is a matter for the court, and only the court can order it.

Does the seriousness of the charge alone decide bail?

No. The charge matters, but so do the evidence strength, flight risk, ties to the community, the accused's record and the conditions offered. Serious charges make bail harder, not impossible.

What should a family do in the first 24 hours after an arrest?

Establish where the person is held and under what provision, instruct a lawyer immediately, and avoid any attempt to contact witnesses or move assets. The first day shapes both the case and the bail application.

How Pluto Associates can help

Our team prepares and argues bail applications in district, high and appellate courts across Nepal, and acts quickly when the statutory limits on detention are breached. If you need urgent help, contact our team now, message us on WhatsApp, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how quickly it can move.

title: Company Registration in Nepal 2026: Costs, Documents, Timeline
content:
Most founders arrive in Nepal expecting the hard part to be the registration itself. In practice, the registration is the easy part. It usually takes days. What surprises people is everything around it: clearing a name that satisfies the registrar, opening a corporate bank account, and, for foreign investors, a separate investment approval that sits before the company can even be incorporated.

This guide explains the whole picture in plain terms, so you know what you are committing to before you start.

Quick answer

A private limited company is registered at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) under the Companies Act, 2063. For a straightforward domestic company, the paperwork is light, the government fees are modest, and incorporation can be done in days once the name is cleared. Add PAN and VAT, a bank account and any sector licence, and the realistic timeline is three to six weeks. If there is foreign investment involved, a further approval stage applies before incorporation, and we cover that separately in our guide for foreign investors.

Which company type fits you?

The structure you choose affects cost, compliance and how easily you can raise money later. Most businesses fall into one of four buckets.

A private limited company is the default. Shareholders' liability is limited, the company is a separate legal person, and the number of shareholders is capped, with no public offering. It suits virtually every startup, trading business, consultancy and foreign subsidiary.

A public limited company is for larger businesses that intend to raise capital from the public. The regulation and reporting are heavier, so it rarely makes sense at the start.

A not-for-profit company is used for non-profit objectives. This is different from the NGO route, which is governed by separate social-welfare law.

A branch or liaison office lets a foreign company operate in Nepal without incorporating a local subsidiary. A branch can trade; a liaison office cannot. Both need approval from the Department of Industry first.

The registration process, step by step

Name clearance. The proposed name is submitted to the OCR for availability. Names that are too close to an existing company, or that mislead, are rejected, which is the most common reason founders are sent back to the start. It is worth preparing two or three alternatives.

Draft the constitutional documents. The memorandum and articles of association set out the name, objectives, capital, shareholders and governance. These documents govern how the company runs, so the drafting deserves attention now, not later when a dispute forces the question.

Filing and registration. The incorporation application and documents are filed with the OCR. Once approved, the certificate of incorporation issues and the company exists as a legal person.

Tax registration. The company obtains a Permanent Account Number from the Inland Revenue Office and registers for VAT if it expects to cross the turnover threshold.

Bank account. The corporate bank account is opened, and where foreign investment is involved, the capital is remitted through banking channels and recorded at Nepal Rastra Bank.

Sector approvals. If the business is an industry, it registers with the Department of Industry. Sector licences, such as those for tourism or education, are obtained where they apply.

What it costs

The government side is genuinely modest: a name-clearance application fee, a registration fee based on authorised capital, and a small PAN registration charge. Authorised capital drives the registration fee, and setting it higher than you need means paying more for no benefit.

The larger line item is professional fees. These vary with the capital structure, the drafting required, and the sector approvals involved, and we agree them up front before any work starts. For a foreign-owned company, the separate investment approval adds both time and cost to the file.

How long it takes

Stage Realistic duration
Name clearance One to three days
Document preparation Three to seven days
Registration at the OCR A few days to two weeks
PAN and VAT One to two days
Bank account Three to five days
Total Three to six weeks

Foreign investment cases run longer, because the approval stage comes first. Expect several weeks to a couple of months depending on the sector.

Documents you will need

  • Citizenship, passport or company documents for every shareholder and director
  • The proposed company name and registered office address
  • The memorandum and articles of association
  • Details of authorised and issued capital
  • Identification and PAN details of the directors
  • For a foreign parent, a board resolution authorising the subsidiary

A worked example

Two founders, one based in Kathmandu and one in Dubai, want to set up an IT services company. Because the Dubai founder is a foreign investor, the process starts not at the OCR but at the Department of Industry, where the investment is approved. Only then is the company incorporated, capital is remitted through banking channels and recorded at Nepal Rastra Bank, and PAN and VAT follow. The Kathmandu founder's citizenship documents handle the local side, while the Dubai founder's documents are apostilled and translated. Had they incorporated first in the belief that registration came before approval, they would have had to redo the memorandum to match an approval that arrived later.

Life after incorporation

Incorporation is the beginning of compliance, not the end. The company must keep statutory registers, hold board and general meetings, maintain share records, and file annual returns. This is the work that quietly slips in year one, and it is exactly when slip-ups become expensive to correct. Putting the statutory calendar in place early avoids that. Our annual compliance guide sets out the recurring filings.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to register a company in Nepal? Once the name is cleared and documents are ready, registration itself is quick. The full set-up, including PAN, VAT, the bank account and any sector approvals, is realistically three to six weeks.

Can one person own a company? Yes. A private limited company can be formed with a single shareholder.

Is there a minimum capital requirement? There is no fixed minimum for an ordinary private company. Capital should be realistic and aligned with the business, and higher authorised capital means higher registration fees.

Can a foreigner register a company in Nepal? Yes, but a foreign investor needs approval under the foreign investment law before incorporation. See our FDI registration guide for the full sequence.

What is the difference between authorised and issued capital? Authorised capital is the maximum the company may issue; issued capital is what shareholders have actually subscribed. The registration fee follows authorised capital.

Do I need to be physically present? Not necessarily. A power of attorney lets a representative file on your behalf, though banking formalities often require the directors in person.

What happens if I ignore annual compliance? Late filings attract penalties, and persistent non-compliance can lead to the company being struck off. It is far cheaper to keep the calendar current than to fix a lapse later.

Related guides: FDI registration process in Nepal, minimum foreign investment, branch, liaison or subsidiary office.

How Pluto Associates can help

We prepare and file company registrations at the OCR, draft the memorandum and articles, and manage the post-incorporation steps including PAN, VAT and year-one compliance. If you would like a clear view of your own situation, contact our team for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.
