title: Obtaining Business Licences and Approvals in Nepal
content:
Company registration is where a business in Nepal begins, but it is rarely where compliance ends. Almost every worthwhile activity carries a second layer: an operating licence, a sector permit, or an approval that gives you the standing to actually do the work. Banks, landlords, buyers and regulators all look for these documents, and a missing one tends to surface at the worst possible moment, often when a payment, an import or a deal depends on it.

This guide explains how to work out which licences apply to you, and how to keep them current.

Quick answer

Beyond incorporation, most businesses need one or more operating licences or sector approvals. Which ones apply depends on what you sell and where you operate. The practical approach is to map your activity against the responsible ministries and departments first, apply to the right authority the first time, and then track renewals so nothing lapses.

Start from the activity, not the company. Two businesses with identical articles of association can need completely different permits, because Nepali regulation follows what you do rather than what you are called. A manufacturing company, an importer, a restaurant and a clinic incorporated on the same day will each face a different authority, a different document list and a different renewal cycle. Mapping those before you open is the difference between a smooth first month and a first month spent visiting offices.

Why the second layer exists

Incorporation makes a company exist. Licences make it lawful to do a particular thing. A company can be perfectly incorporated and still be unable to serve food, import goods, build a structure or operate a clinic without the specific permission for that activity. Regulators in Nepal are activity-based, so the licence follows the work, not the entity.

The logic behind this is straightforward. The state separates the question of whether an entity may exist, handled by the Office of the Company Registrar under the Companies Act 2063, from the question of whether it may perform a given activity safely. Food hygiene, structural safety, environmental impact, financial soundness and public health each have their own regulator with its own standards, and none of them is satisfied by a certificate of incorporation. For a business owner, this means the licence list is a workstream of its own, running alongside payroll, tax and premises from day one.

Working out what applies to you

The answer depends on your sector. A few examples show the pattern:

  • A restaurant needs a hygiene permit and, if it serves alcohol, a liquor licence.
  • A manufacturer needs industry registration and environmental clearances.
  • An importer needs an import authorisation tied to its PAN and VAT accounts.
  • A tourism business needs registration with the relevant tourism authority.
  • A healthcare provider needs sector approval from the health regulator.

The practical method is to list what your business will actually do, then match each activity to the department or agency responsible for it. Doing that mapping before you open avoids applying to the wrong office and discovering the error through a refusal.

Reading the examples closely

The restaurant example shows how layers stack. Food handling sits with the food quality and safety authorities, while the premises themselves need municipal business registration, and alcohol adds an excise and local permission layer on top. The manufacturer's list typically includes industry registration with the Department of Industry or the relevant provincial body, an environmental clearance scaled to the size and type of the project under the Environment Protection Act 2076, and fire safety clearance for the premises. An importer's authorisation is tied to the company's tax accounts and to the customs regime, and businesses with foreign investment will also have conditions attached to their investment approval that shape what may be imported and for what purpose.

Tourism and healthcare follow the same pattern with different regulators. Trekking and travel operations register with the tourism authorities, hotels with classification bodies, and healthcare facilities with the health services regulator, alongside professional registration for the practitioners themselves. The point is not the specific office in each case. The point is that almost every sector has one, and the licence list can be built reliably by asking one question per activity: who regulates this.

Where multiple approvals interact

Some licences depend on others. A construction-related approval usually needs the building permit in place first. A manufacturing licence often waits for environmental clearance. A hotel classification may follow municipal registration and fire clearance. When approvals are sequential, the order matters as much as the papers, because applying out of sequence wastes the fee and the queue position. Mapping dependencies before applying is what keeps the process moving in weeks rather than months.

Getting the application right the first time

Most licence delays are document delays. Applications stall because a supporting paper is missing, a fee was paid to the wrong office, or a form was completed for the wrong category. Preparing a complete file, with the correct fee and the right category, is what turns a weeks-long process into a short one. Where approvals depend on one another, the sequence matters as much as the papers.

A complete file usually contains the company registration certificate from the Office of the Company Registrar, PAN and, where applicable, VAT registration, proof of premises such as a lease or ownership document, citizenship or passport documents of the directors, the activity-specific documents, and the fee receipt. Consistency matters as much as completeness: names, addresses and the description of activity should read the same across every document, because mismatches are the most common reason a file is queried. Where an application involves a foreign director or shareholder, translated and notarised documents are often required, and they take longer to obtain than they look on paper, so they should be started early.

Renewals and the calendar

Licences expire. Some renew annually, others on a fixed cycle, and the penalty for a lapse is not only a fine. An expired permit can suspend your ability to operate, freeze a payment, or block a transaction while a buyer waits for proof that you are compliant. Mapping every licence to its renewal date, and starting each renewal in good time, is the simplest protection a business can put in place.

The renewal file should be treated as a standing folder rather than a fresh exercise. Keep the previous year's application, the receipts, the inspection reports and any correspondence together, so renewal becomes a matter of updating rather than rebuilding. Many renewals also require evidence that the underlying conditions still hold: the premises are still the same, the qualified staff are still in place, the tax status is current. Checking those conditions a month before the renewal date, rather than on it, prevents the common scenario of a renewal refused because one supporting certificate had itself expired.

Costs and realistic timelines

Licence costs fall into three parts: the application or issuance fee set by the authority, the supporting work such as drawings, reports, testing or notarisation, and the renewal fees that recur. Fees vary widely by activity and by the scale of the operation, so the honest budgeting approach is to price each licence individually using the authority's current tariff rather than a rule of thumb. Industry registration with an environmental component will cost several times what a municipal trade registration costs, largely because of the assessment work behind it.

Timelines follow the same logic. A municipal business registration may take days when the file is complete. A sector licence with an inspection, such as food handling or a health facility, takes longer because a visit to the premises is involved. Environmental clearance and industry registration are measured in weeks to months depending on the category of assessment. The practical rule is to build the licence schedule backwards from your intended opening date, adding contingency for anything that requires an inspection, and never announcing an opening date that depends on a permit still being applied for.

A worked example

A foreign-invested company opens a boutique hotel. Incorporation and PAN are straightforward, and the owners assume the rest will follow. But the hotel needs a tourism registration, a municipal business registration, a hygiene permit for its kitchen and a liquor licence for its bar. Each sits with a different authority. Because the owners mapped the licences before opening, the kitchen and bar were compliant on day one. Had they opened first and sorted the paperwork later, the first inspection would have closed the bar and the delay would have cost far more than the licences themselves.

The owners also did two quieter things well. They applied in dependency order, municipal registration first because other files referenced it, then hygiene, then tourism, then alcohol, so no application had to be refiled. And they built a renewal sheet at the same time, with each licence, its cycle, its lead time and its owner. Six months later a routine inspection found a missing document, and the renewal folder produced it in one afternoon. That is what organised licensing looks like in practice: unremarkable, boring, and far cheaper than the alternative.

Common mistakes

The familiar errors are worth naming because they are so easy to avoid. Opening first and applying later, on the assumption that inspections are rare. Applying to the authority that regulates the company rather than the one that regulates the activity. Paying a fee for the wrong category and waiting weeks to discover it. Letting one licence lapse because its renewal date was held by a staff member who left. And treating a licence as a one-off project rather than a standing obligation attached to premises, staff and tax status.

There is also a quieter mistake: never checking whether the licence you hold still matches what the business actually does. A company that started with one product line and added another, or moved premises, or took on a foreign shareholder, may find that its existing licence no longer covers its real activity. A short annual review against the current activity list catches this while it is still a filing matter rather than a compliance problem.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need more than company registration?

Usually yes. Most activities need at least one operating licence or sector approval on top of incorporation. Registration makes the company exist; the licence makes the specific activity lawful.

How do I know which licences apply to me?

Map what your business actually does against the responsible ministries and departments, then apply accordingly. List each activity separately, because one company frequently needs approvals from several different regulators.

Can I operate while a licence is pending?

Generally no, for the licensed activity. Operating without it risks fines, closure of the activity, and problems with landlords, banks and buyers who ask to see the permit.

Do licences expire?

Yes. Renewal cycles vary, so track each licence to its due date, with a lead time for gathering the supporting documents before the renewal window.

What happens if a licence lapses?

Penalties apply, and operations for the licensed activity may have to stop until it is restored. A lapse can also surface at the worst moment, such as during a contract signing or a bank review.

Is this different for foreign-invested companies?

The licences are activity-based and apply to any company, though foreign investment adds its own approval layer. Documents for foreign directors, such as notarised passports and translations, also lengthen the preparation time.

Which authorities handle common licences?

Local government for business registration and many operating permissions, the Department of Industry and related bodies for industrial registration, the environment authorities for clearances under the Environment Protection Act 2076, customs and trade authorities for import rights, and the relevant sector regulator for tourism, health, finance and similar activities.

How long does a licence application take?

It depends on the activity. A complete municipal registration may take days. Anything requiring a premises inspection or an environmental assessment takes weeks to months. Budget the schedule backwards from your opening date and keep contingency for inspections.

How much do licences cost?

There is no single figure. Budget the authority's fee, the supporting work such as reports or drawings, and the recurring renewal fees, each priced from the current tariff for your activity and scale.

Can Pluto Associates check which licences my business needs?

Yes. That mapping is the natural starting point. We identify the approvals your activity requires, prepare the applications, and set up the renewal tracking so nothing lapses.

title: Real Estate Licensing and Project Approvals in Nepal
content:
Land in Nepal is rarely bought or developed on title alone. Behind every project that actually gets built sit land-use and zoning rules, building permits, developer registrations and, for larger or commercial projects, approvals at the municipal and sometimes central level. A missing layer rarely announces itself at the start. It surfaces later, as a hard stop when a completion certificate, a sale registration or a mortgage is on the line.

This guide explains the approvals that matter most for a property project in Nepal, and the order in which they should be secured.

Quick answer

Real estate projects in Nepal require land-use and zoning compliance, building permits before construction, developer registration and project approval for advertised or sold units, and, for larger or commercial schemes, further municipal or central approvals. Buyers should also complete a title and boundary verification. Securing these in the right order is what keeps a project deliverable.

Four ideas do most of the work. Land use decides whether your intended purpose is allowed on that plot at all. The building permit, issued by your municipality or rural municipality against national standards, allows construction to begin. Developer registration and project approval protect the buyers who will see your units advertised. And a title and boundary check at the Land Revenue Office tells you whether the ground beneath all of it is sound. Skip one layer and the others become much harder to defend later.

The approvals that matter most

  • Land-use and zoning compliance, confirming the land may lawfully be used for the intended purpose.
  • Building permits, obtained before construction begins.
  • Developer registration and project approval, confirmed before units are advertised or sold.
  • Title and boundary verification, so a buyer knows exactly what is being acquired.

Each one depends on the integrity of the last. A building permit issued on land that cannot lawfully be used for that purpose is worthless when a buyer's lender examines the file.

Land-use and zoning compliance

Every plot in Nepal sits inside a land category under the Land Use Act 2074 and the local master plan or land-use plan of the concerned local government. Categories such as residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural and public purpose each carry their own rules about what may be built, how high, and how far from the boundary. Before any drawing is prepared, confirm with the ward office and the municipality that your intended use matches the category shown on the plan. Where it does not, an application to change the land use must be filed and approved first. Building on the wrong category is the single most expensive early mistake, because everything downstream, the permit, the loan, the sale, inherits the defect.

Zoning rules also control the practical details that shape a design: road frontage and road width, setbacks on each side, ground coverage, and height limits. A commercial building on a narrow residential lane may be permitted in principle and still fail on frontage. Checking these points before engaging an architect costs a conversation and saves a redesign.

Building permits

A building permit is granted by the municipality or rural municipality where the land sits, applying the Local Government Operation Act 2074 and the National Building Code. The application is normally supported by drawings prepared by a registered architect or engineer, the land ownership certificate, the citizenship documents of the owner, the approved land-use position, recent tax clearance, and the prescribed fee, which is usually calculated on built-up area. The authority examines the drawings for structural adequacy, setbacks, fire and ventilation norms, and only then issues the permit.

The permit is not the end of the authority's interest. Most local governments expect inspections at key stages, for example at plinth level and at frame or roof completion, and a completion or occupation certificate follows only when the built work matches what was approved. That certificate is what buyers, banks and future registrars ask for. Construction that finishes without it is finished, legally speaking, in limbo.

Developer registration and project approval

A company that builds to sell is doing more than construction, it is offering units to the public. Local authorities require housing and commercial developers to register the project and obtain approval for the scheme before units are advertised, booked or sold. The company itself must be in good standing at the Office of the Company Registrar under the Companies Act 2063, with its PAN and, where applicable, VAT registration current. Project approval typically covers the approved plan, the number and type of units, common areas, and the developer's commitment to deliver against that plan.

Marketing before approval is a risk with two edges. The authority can stop the campaign, and a buyer who discovers the unit was offered without approval has a claim against the developer that no later paperwork will fully cure. Registration and approval are also what serious buyers, and the banks financing them, look for first.

Title and boundary verification

Verification is carried out at the Land Revenue Office (malpot) and, where a cadastral map exists, against the survey record. The check confirms three things: that the seller is the person recorded as owner, that there is no mortgage, court dispute, lien or other encumbrance, and that the physical boundaries match the deed. In practice this means reading the chain of transfers, confirming the land category, checking access to a public road, and reconciling the plot with the field. A clean title check before commitment remains the cheapest protection available in any Nepali property transaction.

Why the sequence matters

Property approvals in Nepal form a chain, not a checklist. Land-use comes before design, design before the building permit, and the permit before construction. A developer who starts building while a permit is pending is not merely late. The construction may be unauthorised, and remedying that can mean demolition or a costly regularisation process, where the authority accepts completed work in exchange for a penalty and a corrected file. Regularisation is never guaranteed, it depends on the breach and the local government's policy at the time.

Doing the steps in order is faster than doing them out of order and repairing the consequences. It is also cheaper. Fees, professional charges and financing costs all rise when a project restarts, and the delay tends to arrive at the worst moment: after units have been promised to buyers and a contractor is on site.

For developers

A developer should confirm zoning and land-use first, secure the building permit before breaking ground, and register the developer and obtain project approval before advertising or selling any unit. Where a project is financed, lenders will examine the whole chain, from land rights to permits, before releasing funds. Foreign investment adds a further layer, because Nepal Rastra Bank and the Department of Industry will want to see that the investment is approved under the foreign investment framework before funds arrive for construction. A clean chain is what makes a project fundable and saleable.

Practically, this means building a documents folder from day one and keeping it current: the land record and map, the land-use confirmation, the architect's drawings and their approval, the permit, inspection sign-offs, the project registration, and correspondence with the ward and municipality. When a buyer's lawyer or a bank asks for the file, the folder answers the question in one sitting rather than across several weeks.

Costs and timelines

Costs fall into three groups. Government fees include the building permit fee, usually a percentage of construction cost or built-up area set by the local government's building byelaw, inspection charges, and later the registration fees at the Land Revenue Office when a unit or plot is transferred. Professional fees cover the architect, structural engineer and, for larger projects, the environmental assessment. Then there is the cost of time: design and approval cycles, inspection appointments, and the periodic renewals that apply to project approvals held open while construction runs.

As a rough working shape, a straightforward permit application with complete drawings is measured in weeks, while an incomplete file, a land-use change or an environmental clearance for a larger scheme is measured in months. Project approval and developer registration should be budgeted before marketing begins, not after a launch date has been announced. The most reliable way to cost a project accurately is to price each approval as its own line item with its own deadline, the same discipline a compliance calendar brings to a trading company.

A worked example

Two developers start projects on adjacent plots. The first confirms zoning, finalises the design to match the permitted use, and takes the building permit before construction. The second, eager to move, begins construction while the permit is pending and discovers the design breaches a setback rule. The first reaches completion and sells units with clean paperwork. The second faces rework, a fresh approval cycle and nervous buyers. The land and the market were the same. The difference was the order of the approvals.

The second developer's problems compounded. Because construction had started without a permit, the completed portion could not simply be signed off, it had to be adjusted to satisfy the setback or argued through a regularisation application. Buyers who had paid bookings asked for refunds, and the bank that had promised construction finance paused until the file was regularised. Eight months later the first developer's project was registered and occupied, while the second was still revising drawings. None of the second developer's errors were unusual or unlucky. Each one was the predictable result of starting the chain in the middle.

For buyers

A buyer's protection comes from verification before commitment. Complete a title and boundary check so you know the seller owns what is being sold, that the land is not encumbered, and that the boundaries match the deed. Whether you are buying a completed unit or land to develop, this check is the cheapest insurance available.

For an apartment or a unit in a project, add four questions to the file. Is the project registered and approved before it was marketed. Does the building permit match the plan you were shown. Has a completion or occupation certificate been issued. And will the transfer be registered at the Land Revenue Office in your name, with all taxes and fees settled by the seller as the agreement provides. If the seller proposes to register later, or to hand over possession without registration, treat that as a warning rather than a convenience.

Common mistakes

Most approval problems in Nepali real estate are variations of a few familiar errors. Beginning construction on the strength of an assurance from a ward office rather than a printed permit. Assuming a use is permitted because neighbouring buildings do it, when those buildings predate the current plan. Marketing units before project approval because the launch date was already announced. Buying on an agreement to sell and never registering the transfer, which leaves the seller on the record for years. Relying on a boundary description in the deed without a physical check, only to find a fence or a road where the kitchen was drawn. And treating a completion certificate as an administrative formality rather than a condition of sale, mortgage or resale.

Each of these is avoidable with a short list of checks done at the start. The cost of the checks is small next to the cost of unwinding a project after money has moved.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a building permit before construction?

Yes. Construction should not begin before the building permit is issued by the municipality or rural municipality. Building first and regularising afterwards risks penalties, forced adjustment of the work, or demolition of the unauthorised portion.

What is land-use or zoning compliance?

It is confirmation that the land may lawfully be used for the intended purpose under the Land Use Act 2074 and the local master plan. It covers the land category, setbacks, ground coverage, height, road frontage and access, and it must be settled before the design is finalised.

Does a developer need to be registered?

Yes. A developer should be registered and the project approved before units are advertised or sold. The company must also be in good standing at the Office of the Company Registrar with its tax registrations current.

What should a buyer verify?

Title, encumbrances and boundaries, through a proper title and boundary check at the Land Revenue Office before committing. For a unit in a project, also confirm the project approval, the building permit, and the completion or occupation certificate.

Can approvals be obtained after construction?

It is risky and often impossible to regularise. Obtaining them in order is far safer, and regularisation is granted at the discretion of the authority depending on the breach and local policy.

Do commercial projects need extra approvals?

Larger or commercial projects typically require additional municipal, and sometimes central, approvals. These can include environmental assessment under the Environment Protection Act 2076, fire clearance, and sector approvals where the building will house a licensed activity.

Who issues the building permit in Nepal?

The municipality or rural municipality where the land is located, applying the Local Government Operation Act 2074 and the National Building Code. National standards are set centrally, but the permission is local.

How long does the approval process take?

It depends on completeness. A complete permit file with approved drawings is usually measured in weeks. A land-use change, an environmental assessment or an incomplete submission can extend the process to several months.

What happens if my boundaries do not match the deed?

The mismatch must be resolved before purchase, through the survey and land records process, because an unregistered or disputed boundary will block transfer, financing and future sale. Do not rely on a verbal assurance that it can be fixed later.

Is a title search enough on its own?

It is the essential first step, but for a project purchase it should be joined by permit and project approval checks, and by a physical inspection that the built or promised work matches the approved plan.

How Pluto Associates can help

We walk the process from the first due-diligence check to the final permit, in English and Nepali, and we carry the correspondence with planning and land authorities so nothing is lost in translation. If you would like a clear view of your project, [contact our team](/contact) for a consultation, message us on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/9779802356987), or call [+977 9802356987](tel:+9779802356987). We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

title: Business Approvals Every Company in Nepal Should Track
content:
Once a company is incorporated in Nepal, its obligations multiply quietly. PAN and VAT registrations, provident fund and social security enrolment, municipal business registration, and any industry-specific permits begin landing on different calendars, each with its own deadline and penalty clock. None of them is hard on its own. Together, they are exactly the kind of administrative load that slips when a business is busy growing.

This guide explains why a compliance calendar is one of the most useful things a company can build, and what belongs on it.

Quick answer

After incorporation, a company in Nepal faces a recurring set of registrations, filings and renewals, each handled by a different authority and each with its own due date. A compliance calendar that maps every obligation to its deadline turns a scattered set of risks into a manageable routine. The approach is simple: list every obligation, assign each a date and an owner, and review the calendar regularly.

The obligations come from at least four directions. The Inland Revenue Department collects tax registrations and returns. The Social Security Fund and, for some staff, the provident fund collect contributions on a payroll cycle. The Office of the Company Registrar collects annual company filings. Your municipality collects business registration and local fees. Layer any regulated activity on top, and a sector regulator joins the list. None of these offices synchronise with each other, which is precisely why the synchronising has to happen inside the company.

The obligations that build up

  • PAN registration, and VAT registration where applicable.
  • Periodic VAT returns and the annual corporate income tax return.
  • Social security and provident fund enrolment and contributions.
  • Municipal business registration.
  • Industry-specific permits and their renewals.
  • Annual filings at the Office of the Company Registrar.

Individually these are routine. Collectively, they are the reason so many businesses discover a problem only after a deadline has passed.

Tax registrations and returns

PAN is the anchor document. It is needed for bank accounts, contracts, invoicing and payroll, and most other obligations hang off it. VAT registration follows once turnover crosses the statutory threshold or once a business chooses to register voluntarily, which many exporters and suppliers to registered companies do because it makes them claimable. Registered businesses file VAT returns on the cycle set by the Inland Revenue Department, and the corporate income tax return follows the fiscal year, which ends in mid-July. Beyond returns, there are withholding obligations: tax deducted at source on rent, professional payments, contracts and salaries has to be deposited and reported, even in months when the company itself sells nothing. Missing a withholding deposit is one of the most common and most avoidable assessments a small company receives.

Social security and payroll contributions

The Social Security Act 2074 brought employed staff into the Social Security Fund, with contributions calculated as a set percentage of salary costs and paid on a monthly cycle. Where an employer operates a provident fund scheme instead, contributions follow that scheme's rules. Both require accurate monthly payroll data, and both penalise late payment. Payroll obligations are the easiest to automate and the easiest to forget when a finance person is on leave, which is exactly why they should sit on the calendar with a named owner and a reminder ahead of the due date.

Company filings and municipal registration

Each year, companies registered at the Office of the Company Registrar must file their annual returns with supporting documents under the Companies Act 2063, and keep particulars such as directors, addresses and share capital current as they change. Separately, the municipal business registration that lets a business operate from a premises is renewed with the local government on its own cycle, with its own fee. Neither of these is difficult. Both become expensive when a renewal window closes while attention is elsewhere, because a lapsed filing can surface during a bank due-diligence exercise or a contract vetting.

Why the calendar matters

The companies that run into trouble are rarely the ones with a single large problem. More often they are the ones where a renewal lapsed, a filing was missed by two days, or a permit expired in the middle of signing a contract. A missed date is rarely catastrophic on its own, but the penalty, the reinstatement and the disruption to a live transaction can easily outweigh the cost of the underlying obligation many times over. A calendar changes the arithmetic.

There is a second, quieter benefit. A calendar converts compliance from a series of surprises into a known budget. Once every obligation has a date, the fees, the professional charges and the staff hours can be planned into the year rather than absorbed as emergencies. For a business raising finance or preparing for an audit, the ability to show a clean twelve-month record of filings is itself an asset.

What belongs on the calendar

  1. Every registration, with the date it was obtained and any renewal date.
  2. Every recurring filing, with its frequency and due date.
  3. Every contribution obligation, such as social security, with its payment cycle.
  4. Every permit, with its expiry and the lead time needed to renew.
  5. The owner of each item, so responsibility is clear.

Two additions make the calendar genuinely useful rather than merely accurate. First, add a lead time to every entry, so a renewal that falls in March is flagged in January, when there is still time to gather documents. Second, add a column for the authority and the office involved, because a filing that sits with the Inland Revenue Department and a renewal that sits with the municipality need different documents, different visits and different correspondence. A single spreadsheet, or a shared calendar with recurring reminders, is enough. The tool matters far less than the habit.

A month-by-month rhythm

The fiscal year gives the calendar its spine. Tax registrations and returns cluster around the tax calendar: withholding deposits and VAT returns through the year, and the annual return after the fiscal year closes in mid-July. Company annual filings follow the Office of the Company Registrar's cycle. Municipal registration and licence renewals often follow the municipal year. Payroll contributions repeat every month without variation, which makes them the natural anchor for a recurring monthly routine.

A workable pattern looks like this: a short monthly review at the end of each month, covering payroll contributions, that month's returns and anything falling due in the next sixty days; a longer quarterly review covering renewals, permits and the state of the file; and an annual planning session at the start of the fiscal year that maps the whole year at once. Each review answers three questions. What fell due. What is coming, and who owns it. And is anything already late, in which case the engagement with the authority happens now rather than after the penalty notice.

A worked example

A trading company is doing well and lands a large supply contract. At the signing, the buyer asks for proof of current VAT registration and a valid import authorisation. Both are technically held, but the import authorisation expired three weeks earlier and was never renewed. The buyer pauses the contract while the company scrambles to reinstate the permit. The company lost nothing it could not fix, but it lost time, credibility and, briefly, the deal. A calendar that flagged the expiry six weeks earlier would have prevented the entire episode.

The pattern repeats across sectors. A manufacturer finds its environmental clearance renewal due in the same month as a machinery delivery, leaving no time for the site inspection. A service company discovers that a key finance staff member left without handing over the VAT filing routine, and three months of returns are late by the time anyone notices. In each case the obligation was known when it was created. What was missing was a place where every date lived together, and one person responsible for looking at it.

Keeping the calendar current

A calendar is only useful if it is reviewed. Set a regular moment, monthly or quarterly, to look ahead at the coming period, confirm nothing has lapsed, and start renewals early. When a new obligation appears, whether from a new licence or a new sector, add it immediately rather than trying to remember it later.

Keep the calendar somewhere the whole finance team can see it, and require that every completed item is ticked off with the date and the reference number of the filing or receipt. That small discipline creates an audit trail, which is what you want when a bank, a buyer or a tax officer asks to see your record. When staff change, the calendar should be part of the handover, not a private notebook that leaves with them.

Common mistakes

The recurring errors are predictable. Building the calendar once and never updating it, so a business is working from last year's deadlines. Tracking only the filings the company thinks are heavy, and ignoring the small renewals that carry the sharpest penalties. Assigning every item to one person with no back-up, so a single absence creates a gap. Watching the due date but not the lead time, which means the paperwork is gathered on the deadline rather than before it. And treating the calendar as an accounting task only, when some of the most important entries, licences, permits, registrations, sit with operations rather than finance.

A calendar that is complete, current, owned by named people and reviewed on a rhythm avoids all of these. It is the cheapest compliance infrastructure a company in Nepal can build.

Frequently asked questions

Why do I need a compliance calendar?

Because obligations fall on different authorities and dates, and missed deadlines carry penalties that are easy to avoid. A calendar maps every registration, filing, contribution and renewal to its due date so nothing depends on memory.

What should be on it?

Registrations, recurring filings, contribution obligations, permit expiries and renewals, and the owner of each item. Add the responsible authority, the lead time needed to prepare, and the reference number once each item is completed.

How often should it be reviewed?

At least monthly or quarterly, with renewals started well before their due date. A short monthly check for immediate deadlines, a quarterly look-ahead, and a full mapping session at the start of the fiscal year works well.

What happens if a filing is missed?

Penalties apply, and some activities cannot continue until the lapse is corrected. Late tax filings attract interest and fines, and a lapsed permit can suspend the activity it covers.

Is this only for large companies?

No. Small companies face the same obligations and have less margin for error, because the same penalty applies whether the company is large or small, while a small business has fewer people to catch the mistake.

Can these tasks be delegated?

Yes. Many businesses appoint a professional to build and maintain the calendar and handle the filings, while keeping one person inside the company responsible for approving and reviewing it.

Which authorities are involved?

The Inland Revenue Department for tax registrations and returns, the Social Security Fund or provident fund for contributions, the Office of the Company Registrar for annual filings, the local government for business registration, and any sector regulator for permits specific to your activity.

When does the Nepali fiscal year end?

Mid-July, in the month of Shrawan. Annual tax and company filings are usually scheduled relative to that date, which makes the start of the fiscal year a natural moment to build or reset the calendar.

What should we do if something is already late?

Engage the authority promptly rather than waiting to be asked. Filing late with an explanation and payment of the applicable penalty is almost always treated more favourably than silence, and it restores the record faster.

How much does a compliance calendar cost to maintain?

Very little. The entries can live in a shared spreadsheet or calendar with reminders. The real cost is the discipline of reviewing it, and that is a few hours a month rather than a significant expense.

How Pluto Associates can help

title: Automatic Route of FDI in Nepal: What Changed and How to Use It
content:
Since Nepal introduced the automatic route in April 2024, a large share of foreign investment applications no longer need a manual review meeting. That change has cut weeks off the process for investors who plan properly, and left others confused about which route applies to them. This guide explains the automatic route in plain terms: who qualifies, what the thresholds are, which sectors still need the manual path, and how to file without stalling.

What the automatic route actually means

The automatic route is a self-declaration pathway administered by the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer (FITT) unit at the One Stop Service Centre. When your application qualifies, the unit confirms compliance against published criteria instead of convening a committee review. Approval is typically issued within seven working days of a complete filing.

It is worth being precise about what "automatic" does not mean. It does not mean no approval. You still need an approval letter before you incorporate the company, and you still need the Nepal Rastra Bank recording before you can repatriate. What it removes is the committee step and the associated waiting time.

Who qualifies for the automatic route

Three conditions generally place an application in the automatic category:

  • The investment falls within the minimum threshold for your sector. For most sectors this is NPR 20 million. For information technology and digital services, there is no minimum.
  • The proposed business sits outside the negative list in the FITTA schedule. Retail trade below certain sizes, personal services, arms and ammunition, and real estate trading remain restricted.
  • The investment is structured as equity in a company registered in Nepal, rather than as a loan or a branch office arrangement.

If all three hold, the FITT unit processes the application under the automatic pathway. If any one fails, the manual route applies.

What still requires the manual route

Several common situations push an application into manual review regardless of amount:

  • Investment above NPR 500 million, which leaves the automatic route for the standard route at the Department of Industry; projects above NPR 6 billion go to Investment Board Nepal.
  • Acquisition of shares in an existing Nepali company rather than subscription to a new one, which requires valuation.
  • Sector-specific restrictions where the negative list permits investment only with prior conditions.
  • Technology transfer arrangements bundled with equity, where the terms need substantive review.

The practical effect is that most first-time investors setting up a new IT, consulting, services or light manufacturing company can use the automatic route, while larger industrial projects and share acquisitions should plan for the manual timeline.

The filing process step by step

The automatic route process runs as follows:

  1. Confirm sector eligibility against the FITTA negative list and the minimum threshold for your sector.
  2. Prepare the investment commitment documents: notarised certificate of incorporation, memorandum and articles of association of the foreign parent, board resolution authorising the investment, and passport or citizenship copies of individual investors.
  3. File online through imis.doind.gov.np with the FITT unit at the One Stop Service Centre.
  4. Receive the FDI approval letter, typically within seven working days of a complete submission.
  5. Incorporate the Nepali company at the Office of the Company Registrar through the CAMIS portal within three working days of approval.
  6. Register for PAN and, where applicable, VAT at the Inland Revenue Office.
  7. Register the industry with the Department of Industry.
  8. Open a corporate bank account and remit the investment through the formal banking channel.
  9. Record the investment with Nepal Rastra Bank.

Steps five through nine follow the same sequence whether you came through the automatic or manual route. The time saving happens entirely at step four.

A worked example

Consider a software company in Kathmandu. The foreign parent in Singapore commits NPR 25 million, comfortably above the general threshold and entirely outside the negative list. The parent is a private limited company with two directors.

Under the automatic route, the FITT unit reviews the filing against published criteria. If the documents are complete and the sector is clear, the approval letter issues in about a week. The Nepali subsidiary is incorporated on CAMIS within three working days, PAN and VAT registration follow in the same week, and the Singapore parent remits the capital through its bank. The NRB recording completes shortly after.

The whole sequence, from filing to a funded and registered company, typically runs four to six weeks when nothing stalls. Under the manual route with a committee review, the same sequence would commonly run eight to twelve weeks.

Common mistakes that cause delays

The most frequent cause of delay is a mismatch between the investment commitment and the remittance. If the approval letter states NPR 25 million and the first remittance is NPR 18 million, the NRB recording cannot complete until the gap is explained or the approval is amended. State the full commitment in the filing and remit in a single transfer where possible.

The second common issue is incomplete notarisation. Documents executed outside Nepal generally need notarisation in the country of origin, and for countries outside the Hague Apostille Convention, legalisation through the Nepal Embassy. Start that process before you file, not after.

The third is assuming the approval letter has no expiry. It does. Work to the stated validity period and incorporate well inside it.

What this means for your entry strategy

If you are weighing Nepal as a market, the automatic route materially changes the arithmetic. A services or IT operation with a modest capital commitment can now be approved in days rather than months, which makes a phased entry far more practical than it was. For larger industrial projects, the manual route still applies, but the surrounding steps are now more streamlined than they were even two years ago.

Either way, the sequence matters more than the speed. Filing in the right order, with complete documents, is what keeps the timeline short.

If you are planning an investment and want to confirm which route applies to your situation, our team can review your structure before you file. We handle FITT applications, company incorporation, and NRB recording as a single engagement, so nothing stalls between steps. Talk to us on WhatsApp at +977 9802356987, call +977 9802356987, or send a note through our contact page and we will reply within one working day.

Frequently asked questions

Does the automatic route apply to every sector?

No. It applies to sectors outside the FITTA negative list that also meet the minimum threshold for your activity. Retail trade, personal services, arms, ammunition and certain real estate activities remain outside it.

Is there a minimum investment for IT companies under the automatic route?

There is no minimum investment amount for information technology and digital services companies. Other sectors generally require NPR 20 million.

How long does approval take under the automatic route?

A complete filing is typically confirmed within seven working days. Incomplete filings are returned rather than processed, so document preparation matters.

Can I incorporate before receiving FDI approval?

No. The approval letter must be issued before incorporation at the Office of the Company Registrar. Incorporating first and seeking approval afterwards creates a structure that cannot be recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank.

Does the automatic route apply to share acquisitions in existing companies?

Generally no. Acquiring shares in an existing Nepali company requires valuation and typically follows the manual route.

What happens if my remittance is less than the approved amount?

The NRB recording cannot complete against a short remittance. Either remit the balance or seek an amendment to the approval before attempting to record the investment.

Is the automatic route available to investors from any country?

Yes. There is no country-of-origin restriction under the automatic route. Country-specific treaties, such as double tax avoidance agreements, may affect your tax position but not your eligibility for the route itself.

Can I use the automatic route for a branch office?

No. Branch and liaison office registrations follow their own pathways and are not covered by the automatic equity investment route.

title: Repatriating Profits from Nepal: Dividends, Capital & Tax
content:
Foreign investors who do well in Nepal eventually face a question that is asked far less often than it should be: how does the money actually leave? Repatriation is governed by a clear statutory framework under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act, but the practical steps catch people out. This guide covers what can be repatriated, the approvals involved, the tax position you need to clear first, and the documentation that makes the transfer go through cleanly.

What can be repatriated

Nepali law permits repatriation of several categories of funds once the relevant approvals and tax obligations are satisfied:

  • Dividends and profits declared by the company.
  • Proceeds from the sale of shares to another investor.
  • Amounts remaining after liquidation or winding up.
  • Approved royalty payments.
  • Technology transfer fees under an approved agreement.
  • Principal and interest on approved foreign loans.

Each category has its own approval path and its own documentation. Dividends are the most common and the most straightforward. Share sale proceeds and liquidation distributions involve more steps because they require evidence of the underlying transaction and the tax position arising from it.

Who approves what

The approval authority depends on the size of the original investment.

For approved investment of NPR 6 billion or below, the Department of Industry and Nepal Rastra Bank handle approvals jointly. Above that threshold, Investment Board Nepal and Nepal Rastra Bank take over. In practice, most foreign investors deal with the Department of Industry pathway.

The sequence is consistent. You establish that all applicable taxes have been paid, obtain the Department of Industry or Investment Board clearance, then present the package to Nepal Rastra Bank for the actual remittance. The bank will not release funds without both.

The repatriation process, step by step

  1. Confirm what is being remitted. Identify whether it is a dividend, share sale proceeds, liquidation distribution, royalty, technology fee or loan repayment.
  2. Clear the tax position. File outstanding returns, settle corporate income tax and withholding tax, and obtain the tax clearance certificate.
  3. Pass the board resolution. Document the distribution or transfer and the amount payable to the foreign shareholder.
  4. Apply to the DOI or IBN. Submit the resolution, audited accounts, tax clearance, shareholding records and evidence of the original investment.
  5. Obtain NRB approval. Present the DOI or IBN clearance and the remittance request to Nepal Rastra Bank.
  6. Complete the bank transfer. The commercial bank verifies the approvals and releases the funds abroad.

The tax position before you remit

This is where most delays occur. Nepal requires that all applicable tax liabilities be settled before repatriation proceeds. The relevant obligations typically include corporate income tax on the profit being distributed, any withholding tax on the dividend payment, and any outstanding obligations from earlier years.

If the company has not filed returns for prior periods, the Inland Revenue Office will generally require those filings before issuing the clearances the bank needs. Investors who have been away from the company for a period often discover that several years of unfiled returns need to be regularised first. That process takes time and should be planned for rather than discovered at the point of remittance.

There is also the double tax avoidance position to consider. Nepal has signed agreements with a number of countries, including India, China, Bangladesh, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Austria, Pakistan, South Korea, Norway and Qatar. If your home country has a treaty with Nepal, the withholding rate on dividends may be reduced under the treaty rather than the standard domestic rate. The treaty rate generally requires you to be a resident of the treaty country and to provide a tax residence certificate.

A worked example

A manufacturing company in Biratnagar has been operating for three years. The foreign parent holds 74 percent of the shares. In the most recent financial year the company earned distributable profit of NPR 40 million.

The company files its corporate income tax return for the year and settles the tax. The board declares a dividend in proportion to shareholding, giving the foreign parent NPR 29.6 million. Because the parent is resident in a treaty country, withholding tax on the dividend is applied at the treaty rate rather than the domestic rate, and the parent provides its tax residence certificate to support that position.

The company applies to the Department of Industry with the board resolution, the audited financial statements, the tax clearance, and the shareholding register. Once cleared, the package goes to Nepal Rastra Bank with the remittance instructions. The bank verifies the approvals and the tax position and releases the funds to the parent's account abroad.

The whole sequence, from board resolution to funds landing, typically runs three to six weeks when the tax filings are current. Where prior returns are outstanding, add the time needed to regularise them.

Documentation that gets it done

The pack that moves cleanly through both approvals usually contains:

  • Board resolution declaring the dividend or approving the transfer.
  • Audited financial statements for the relevant period.
  • Tax clearance certificate from the Inland Revenue Office.
  • Shareholding register and, where relevant, the original FDI approval letter.
  • Evidence of the original capital injection and its NRB recording.
  • For share sales, the share purchase agreement and valuation.
  • For royalty or technology transfer fees, the approved agreement and proof of the underlying payment obligation.
  • Tax residence certificate where a treaty rate is claimed.

Assembling this before you apply, rather than in response to requests, is the single biggest lever on timeline.

Common reasons transfers stall

The most frequent cause is the tax position. If returns are unfiled or assessments are open, the clearance cannot issue and the bank will not act. Resolve tax first, always.

The second is a mismatch between the approved investment amount and what was actually recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank. If the recording shows NPR 20 million but the remittance was NPR 15 million, the repatriation calculation becomes complicated. Keep the NRB record accurate and current.

The third is waiting until the funds are urgently needed. Repatriation is not instantaneous and should be treated as a process that runs alongside your financial close, not something started after the decision is made.

What this means for your investment planning

If you are evaluating Nepal as a market, the repatriation framework is a genuine strength. Profits can leave, and the route to do so is established and predictable. The obligations that come with it, particularly the tax clearance requirement, are manageable provided they are built into your compliance calendar from the first year rather than left to the point of exit.

Investors who treat tax filing, NRB recording and board documentation as ongoing hygiene rather than end-of-process chores find that repatriation takes weeks rather than months.

How Pluto Associates can help

If you are planning a repatriation and want to check your position before you begin, our team can review the tax clearance, the Department of Industry filing and the NRB package as one engagement. Talk to us on WhatsApp at +977 9802356987, call +977 9802356987, or send a note through our contact page and we will come back to you within one working day.

Frequently asked questions

How long does repatriation of dividends take in Nepal?

Where tax filings are current and documentation is complete, three to six weeks is typical. Where prior returns are outstanding, the time required to regularise them dominates the timeline.

Is there a withholding tax on dividends paid to foreign shareholders?

Yes. Domestic law applies a withholding rate to dividends paid abroad. Where a double tax avoidance agreement exists between Nepal and the investor's home country, the treaty rate may apply instead, supported by a tax residence certificate.

Can I repatriate more than the original investment amount?

Yes. Dividends from profits, share sale proceeds and liquidation distributions can all be remitted, provided the tax position is cleared.

Do I need Department of Industry approval for every remittance?

Approval is generally obtained per remittance, supported by the board resolution and tax clearance for that distribution. Standing approvals are not typical.

What if the company has unfiled tax returns from earlier years?

Those returns generally need to be filed and any tax settled before the Inland Revenue Office will issue the clearance the bank requires. This is the most common cause of delay.

Can royalty payments be repatriated?

Yes, where the royalty arrangement was approved as part of the FDI or technology transfer framework and the underlying payment obligation is documented.

Does Nepal have a double tax avoidance agreement with my country?

Nepal has agreements with India, China, Bangladesh, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Austria, Pakistan, South Korea, Norway and Qatar. If your country is not on that list, the domestic withholding rate applies.

Can repatriation be refused?

Yes, if tax obligations are unmet or documentation is incomplete. The framework permits repatriation, but it conditions it on compliance.

title: Work Permits for Foreign Employees in Nepal
content:
Foreign-invested companies in Nepal can employ foreign nationals, but the permission structure is layered and the sequence matters. A business visa alone does not authorise work, and a labour permit alone does not get someone through immigration. This guide sets out how the pieces fit together, which employees typically need which permissions, and how long each step takes.

The three permissions and how they relate

Three separate permissions commonly come into play for a foreign employee:

  • A labour permit from the Department of Labour, which confirms the position cannot reasonably be filled by a Nepali national and authorises the employment.
  • A work permit endorsement, which connects the labour permit to the immigration record.
  • A non-tourist visa from the Department of Immigration, which allows the person to remain in Nepal for the purpose of that employment.

In practice these are processed in sequence rather than independently. The labour permit comes first, the work permit follows from it, and the visa is issued or endorsed on the basis of both. Starting with the visa and working backwards is the most common mistake, and it wastes time because the visa cannot be issued without the underlying permits.

Who needs a work permit

Broadly, anyone who is not a Nepali citizen and who will perform work in Nepal for a Nepali entity needs some form of work authorisation. The categories that most often come up:

  • Directors and senior managers of a foreign-invested company.
  • Technical specialists brought in for a defined project or period.
  • Employees of a foreign parent company seconded to the Nepali subsidiary.

Investors who will be present in Nepal in a purely representative capacity, attending meetings and overseeing their investment without performing day-to-day work, may find that a business visa without a work permit is sufficient. The distinction turns on what the person will actually be doing, not on their title.

The labour market testing question

The Department of Labour expects that positions offered to foreign nationals be ones that cannot reasonably be filled locally. In practice this means the application should explain why the role requires the specific skills or experience the foreign candidate brings. For senior technical roles and for positions requiring knowledge of a proprietary system or process, this is usually straightforward to evidence. For generalist roles, it is harder.

Foreign-invested companies do receive some accommodation. The framework recognises that a company with foreign ownership may need foreign expertise, particularly in the early years, and the applications are assessed with that context in mind. That said, the application still needs to make the case rather than assume it.

The process step by step

  1. Confirm the role and the candidate's immigration status, and identify whether the position requires a labour permit.
  2. Prepare the supporting documentation: the candidate's passport, qualifications or experience evidence, the company's registration and FDI approval documents, and the job description explaining why the role requires a foreign national.
  3. Submit the labour permit application to the Department of Labour.
  4. Once the labour permit is granted, obtain the work permit endorsement.
  5. Apply for or endorse the non-tourist visa at the Department of Immigration.
  6. Where the employee will be in Nepal long term, diarise the renewal well before expiry.

Steps three to five typically take two to four weeks in total once documentation is complete. Renewals follow a similar pattern and should be started well before the current permission lapses.

A worked example

A technology company with foreign investment brings in a chief technology officer from abroad. The CTO will be resident in Kathmandu, leading a local engineering team, and will be on the company payroll.

The company prepares the labour permit application with the CTO's passport, credentials, and a role description explaining that the position requires deep knowledge of the proprietary platform. The Department of Labour reviews and grants the permit. The work permit endorsement follows, and the non-tourist visa is issued on that basis.

The CTO works in Nepal on that permission for the initial period. Renewal is diarised several months ahead so there is no gap in authorisation.

Throughout, the company keeps the labour permit, work permit and visa aligned. If any one lapses while the others remain current, the position is not properly authorised, which creates exposure for both the company and the employee.

Renewals and ongoing compliance

Work permissions in Nepal are tied to a period rather than granted indefinitely. Renewal requires demonstrating that the employment continues and that the underlying conditions still hold. Companies that diarise renewals well in advance avoid the scramble that happens when a permission expires and the employee cannot work in the interim.

It is also worth keeping the labour permit aligned with the actual role. If the employee's responsibilities change substantially, the original application rationale may no longer fit, and that is worth addressing proactively rather than leaving until renewal.

What this means if you are bringing people in

Nepal's framework for foreign employees is workable and well established. The companies that move quickly are the ones that treat the labour permit as the starting point and build the visa around it, rather than the other way around. Document preparation before submission is where the time saving happens.

If you are bringing foreign staff into a Nepali operation and want the sequence mapped before you start, our team handles labour permits, work permit endorsements and non-tourist visa applications as a single engagement. Talk to us on WhatsApp at +977 9802356987, call +977 9802356987, or send a note through our contact page and we will come back to you within one working day.

Frequently asked questions

Does a business visa allow me to work in Nepal?

No. A business visa permits presence and business activity of a representative nature, but it does not authorise employment. A labour permit and work permit endorsement are needed for that.

How long does a work permit take to obtain?

Once documentation is complete, the labour permit, work permit and visa sequence typically takes two to four weeks in total.

Can the company apply for the work permit before the employee arrives?

The labour permit application can generally be prepared and submitted in advance. The visa step typically requires the applicant to engage with immigration, and timing depends on whether they are already in Nepal.

Is there a limit on the number of foreign employees a company can have?

There is no fixed numerical cap, but each application is assessed on its own merits, including the argument that the role cannot be filled locally. A company bringing in a large number of foreign staff without a clear rationale should expect closer scrutiny.

How often do work permits need to be renewed?

Permissions are granted for a defined period and must be renewed. The appropriate period depends on the permission type and the underlying employment.

Can I transfer a work permit to a new employer?

Work permits are tied to the sponsoring employer. Changing employers generally requires a fresh application rather than a simple transfer.

What happens if a work permit expires while I am still working?

The employment is not properly authorised once the permission lapses. Renewal should be started well before expiry to avoid a gap.

Do dependants of a foreign employee need their own work permit?

Dependants accompanying a foreign employee generally hold derivative visas rather than work permits. If a dependant intends to work in Nepal, they need their own labour permit and work permit.

faqs.a: Permissions are granted for a defined period and must be renewed. The appropriate period depends on the permission type and the underlying employment.

faqs.q: Can I transfer a work permit to a new employer?
faqs.a: Work permits are tied to the sponsoring employer. Changing employers generally requires a fresh application rather than a simple transfer.

faqs.q: What happens if a work permit expires while I am still working?
faqs.a: The employment is not properly authorised once the permission lapses. Renewal should be started well before expiry to avoid a gap.

faqs.q: Do dependants of a foreign employee need their own work permit?
faqs.a: Dependants accompanying a foreign employee generally hold derivative visas rather than work permits. If a dependant intends to work in Nepal, they need their own labour permit and work permit.

title: Company Renewal and Annual Compliance in Nepal
content:
Registering a company in Nepal is the beginning of an ongoing relationship with the Office of the Company Registrar, not the end of a transaction. Every registered company has annual obligations, and missing them carries penalties that compound. This guide covers what renewals and filings are required, when they fall due, what they cost, and what happens when they are missed.

What annual compliance actually involves

A registered company in Nepal generally has four recurring obligations:

  • Annual return filing with the Office of the Company Registrar, confirming the company's status, directors, shareholders and registered particulars.
  • Audited financial statements, prepared and filed in accordance with the Companies Act.
  • Tax filings with the Inland Revenue Office, including corporate income tax returns and, where applicable, VAT returns.
  • Industry registration renewal with the Department of Industry, where the company holds an industry registration.

These are separate obligations with separate authorities. A company that is current with one but not the others is not compliant.

The annual return at OCR

The annual return is the filing that most directly affects a company's standing with the Registrar. It confirms that the company continues to exist, that its directors and shareholders are as recorded, and that its registered particulars remain accurate. It is filed through the CAMIS portal.

The filing window runs from the end of the company's fiscal year. Companies that miss the window face late fees that increase the longer the filing is outstanding. In serious cases, persistent non-filing can lead to the company being struck from the register, which is a far more serious problem to unwind than a late fee.

Audit and financial statements

Companies above certain thresholds are required to have their financial statements audited by a registered auditor. The audited statements form the basis of the tax filings and, where required, the annual return. Preparing them takes time, particularly where the company's records have not been maintained through the year.

The practical discipline here is bookkeeping rather than the audit itself. Companies that keep current records find the audit routine. Companies that defer record-keeping to year end find it expensive and stressful, and the audit frequently surfaces issues that would have been cheaper to address earlier.

Tax obligations

Corporate income tax returns are due within the statutory window after the fiscal year end. VAT-registered companies file periodic VAT returns. Withholding tax obligations arise through the year as payments are made to suppliers, employees and service providers.

Foreign-invested companies carry the additional obligation of maintaining the NRB recording of their investment, and of ensuring that any cross-border payments, whether dividends, royalties or service fees, have the approvals they need before the transfer is made.

Industry registration renewal

Companies holding an industry registration with the Department of Industry renew that registration periodically. This is separate from the OCR annual return and from the tax filings. It is commonly overlooked because it sits with a different authority on a different cycle, and because the company may not interact with the Department of Industry between renewals.

A worked example

A private limited company with foreign investment closes its fiscal year in mid-July. Within the following months it completes its audit, files the corporate income tax return, and files the annual return at OCR through CAMIS. Where the company is VAT-registered, VAT returns are filed on their own cycle through the year. Industry registration renewal falls due on its own schedule and is diarised separately.

The company's finance lead maintains a compliance calendar covering all four obligations. Each has a named owner and a date. Nothing depends on someone remembering.

Companies that operate without such a calendar tend to meet their obligations late, pay penalties they did not need to pay, and discover gaps when they apply for something else, such as a bank facility or a visa renewal, and the counterparty asks for compliance evidence.

Penalties for late filing

Late filing at the Office of the Company Registrar attracts fees that increase with the length of the delay. Late tax filings attract penalties and interest under the Income Tax Act. Persistent non-compliance can affect the company's ability to transact, obtain approvals, or renew permissions that depend on good standing.

The penalties are usually smaller than the disruption. A company that has fallen behind and needs to regularise several years of filings often finds the process more costly in professional fees and management time than the penalties themselves.

What this means for running a Nepali company

Annual compliance in Nepal is well defined and predictable. The obligations do not change year to year, the authorities are established, and the filings are routine when handled properly. The companies that get into difficulty are almost always the ones that treat compliance as something to deal with when it becomes urgent rather than as a standing part of running the business.

If your company's filings are behind, or if you want a compliance calendar set up so nothing falls through, our team handles annual returns, coordination with auditors, tax filing liaison and industry registration renewals as a standing engagement. Frequently asked questions

When is the annual return due in Nepal?

The annual return is filed with the Office of the Company Registrar after the company's fiscal year end, within the window set by the Companies Act. Late filing attracts increasing fees.

Does every company need an audit?

Companies above the applicable thresholds must have financial statements audited by a registered auditor. Smaller companies may have simpler obligations, but tax filing requirements still apply.

How often must industry registration be renewed?

Industry registration with the Department of Industry is renewed periodically on its own cycle, separate from the OCR annual return.

What happens if I miss the annual return deadline?

Late fees apply and increase with the length of the delay. Persistent non-filing can lead to the company being struck from the register.

Can I file the annual return myself or do I need a lawyer?

The filing is made through CAMIS and can be prepared in-house where records are current. Many companies use a professional to ensure accuracy and to coordinate it with the audit and tax filings.

Are VAT returns separate from the annual compliance cycle?

Yes. VAT-registered companies file periodic VAT returns on their own schedule throughout the year, independent of the annual return and corporate income tax filing.

Does a company with no activity still need to file?

Yes. A dormant company still has filing obligations. Non-filing attracts the same penalties regardless of whether the company traded during the period.

Can late filings be regularised?

Yes. Outstanding filings can be made retrospectively, with penalties and interest applied. The earlier this is addressed, the lower the cost.
