title: Types of Companies in Nepal: Choosing the Right Structure
content:
Choosing the wrong entity type in Nepal is expensive to correct later. The Companies Act 2063 offers several structures, each with different ownership rules, capital requirements, liability positions and compliance burdens. This guide sets out the main options, what distinguishes them, and how to think about which fits your situation.

The main structures available

Nepal recognises several business structures. The ones most relevant to foreign investors and growing local businesses are:

  • Private limited company.
  • Public limited company.
  • Branch office of a foreign company.
  • Liaison office of a foreign company.
  • Partnership firm and sole proprietorship, for smaller local operations.

Each has a distinct legal personality, capital requirement and compliance profile. The choice shapes everything from how many people can hold shares to whether the entity can raise capital publicly.

Private limited company

The private limited company is the most common structure in Nepal and the default choice for most foreign-invested businesses. Key features:

  • Shareholders: between one and 101.
  • Liability: limited to the unpaid amount on shares held.
  • Share transfer: restricted, generally requiring company approval.
  • Public fundraising: not permitted.

For a foreign investor taking a minority or majority stake in a new Nepali operation, the private limited company is almost always the right answer. It is well understood by regulators, banks and counterparties, and it accommodates the FDI approval and NRB recording process cleanly.

Public limited company

The public limited company differs in several respects that matter:

  • Shareholders: minimum seven.
  • Paid-up capital: a higher statutory minimum applies.
  • Share transfer: freely transferable.
  • Public fundraising: permitted, subject to Securities Board of Nepal regulation.

A public limited company is the appropriate structure where the intention is ultimately to raise capital from the public or list on the Nepal Stock Exchange. For most foreign investors entering Nepal, it is not the starting point, but it is the structure that a private limited company can convert into if the business grows that way.

Branch office

A branch office is an extension of the foreign parent company rather than a separate Nepali entity. It operates under the parent's name and the parent bears full liability for its obligations.

Branch offices are permitted in specific sectors and are typically used where the foreign company wants a presence in Nepal without incorporating a subsidiary. The compliance and reporting obligations differ from those of a subsidiary, and the liability position is less favourable because there is no ring-fence between the branch and the parent.

Liaison office

A liaison office is established for representative purposes. It cannot engage in commercial activity or generate revenue in Nepal. It exists to maintain contact, explore opportunities and coordinate, and it is funded entirely from abroad.

A liaison office is a sensible first step for a foreign company exploring the Nepali market before committing to a full investment. Once the decision is made to operate commercially, the liaison office is generally converted to a branch or, more commonly, a subsidiary is incorporated.

Sole proprietorship and partnership

For smaller local operations, a sole proprietorship or partnership remains a workable structure. A sole proprietorship has a single owner with unlimited personal liability. A partnership involves two or more partners sharing liability according to the partnership deed.

Neither structure is well suited to foreign investment. Foreign investors engaging in Nepal generally use a private limited company.

A worked example of the choice

A European technology firm wants to establish a presence in Kathmandu. It plans to hire locally, contract with Nepali clients, and eventually consider a local partner.

The liaison office is not suitable because the firm intends to trade commercially from the outset. The branch office would work but leaves the parent fully liable and complicates the tax position. The private limited company, with the European firm as the sole or majority shareholder, provides the ring-fence, the familiar structure for counterparties, and a clean path through FDI approval, incorporation and NRB recording.

The firm incorporates a private limited company. If the business grows to the point where public capital is wanted, the company can be converted to a public limited structure later.

What this means for your decision

For most foreign investors, the private limited company is the starting point, and the decision is less about which structure is theoretically optimal than about which one banks, regulators and counterparties will recognise and process efficiently. Nepal's FDI framework is built around the corporate subsidiary, and the practical friction of choosing anything else is rarely justified.

If you are weighing structures and want the trade-offs mapped against your specific plans, our team can walk you through the choice before you file. Frequently asked questions

How many shareholders can a private limited company in Nepal have?

Between one and 101 shareholders.

What is the minimum paid-up capital for a public limited company?

A higher statutory minimum applies than for a private limited company. The exact figure should be confirmed against the current Companies Act provisions.

Can a branch office do business in Nepal?

A branch office can operate in permitted sectors but carries full parent liability and has a different compliance profile from a subsidiary.

Can a liaison office earn revenue in Nepal?

No. A liaison office exists for representative purposes only and cannot generate commercial income in Nepal.

Can a private limited company convert to a public limited company later?

Yes. Conversion is available where the business reaches the point where public fundraising or listing is relevant.

Can a foreigner be the sole shareholder of a private limited company in Nepal?

Yes, in most sectors, subject to FDI approval and the applicable minimum investment threshold.

Is a sole proprietorship suitable for foreign investors?

No. Foreign investors engaging in Nepal generally use a private limited company.

What structure do banks in Nepal prefer to lend against?

Banks are most comfortable with the private limited company structure, which is well established in Nepali banking practice.

title: Company Formation Documents in Nepal: The MoA and AoA Checklist
content:
The memorandum and articles of association are the two documents that define a Nepali company. They are filed at incorporation, they govern the company thereafter, and they are the first thing a bank, regulator or counterparty asks for. This guide sets out what each document contains, what the Office of the Company Registrar expects to see, and the practical points that cause filings to be returned.

What the memorandum does

The memorandum of association is the company's charter. It defines the company externally: what it is called, what it intends to do, how much capital it has, and what the liability of its members is. The key contents are:

  • The company name, as reserved with the Registrar.
  • The registered office address in Nepal.
  • The objects clause, describing the company's intended business activities.
  • The authorised capital and the division into shares.
  • The liability clause, stating that members' liability is limited to unpaid amounts on shares.
  • The subscriber details, being the initial shareholders and their shareholdings.

The objects clause deserves particular attention. It defines what the company may lawfully do, and activities outside it create complications. For a foreign-invested company, the objects should be drafted with the FDI approval in mind, so that the approved activity and the charter activity align.

What the articles do

The articles of association govern the company internally. They set out how the company is run: the rights and duties of shareholders and directors, meeting procedures, quorum requirements, voting rights, transfer restrictions, and dividend policy.

The Registrar reviews the articles against the statutory defaults. Where a company adopts the model articles without amendment, the review is straightforward. Where bespoke provisions are included, they need to be consistent with the Companies Act. Provisions that purport to override mandatory requirements of the Act will be flagged.

Documents required alongside the MoA and AoA

The memorandum and articles do not stand alone. The incorporation filing typically includes:

  • The reserved company name confirmation.
  • The memorandum of association, signed by the subscribers.
  • The articles of association, signed by the subscribers.
  • Identification documents for each subscriber and director: citizenship for Nepali nationals, passport for foreign nationals.
  • Where a subscriber is a corporate entity, the certificate of incorporation, memorandum and articles of association of that entity, notarised and, where required, legalised.
  • Board resolution or equivalent authorisation where the subscriber is a company investing in Nepal.
  • Proof of the registered office address.
  • The FDI approval letter, where the company is foreign-invested.

For foreign documents, notarisation in the country of origin is required, and for countries outside the Hague Apostille Convention, legalisation through the Nepal Embassy. Documents in a language other than Nepali or English need certified translation.

A worked example of a complete filing

A foreign company incorporates a Nepali subsidiary. The parent company provides its certificate of incorporation, memorandum and articles of association, board resolution authorising the investment, and shareholder register, all notarised and legalised. Two directors are appointed, one Nepali and one foreign, and their identification documents are included.

The Nepali company's memorandum sets out objects consistent with the FDI approval, authorised capital matching the approved investment, and the two subscribers with their shareholdings. The articles adopt the model provisions with minimal amendment.

The package is filed through CAMIS. Because the documents are complete and internally consistent, the Registrar approves and issues the certificate of incorporation. The whole sequence, from complete filing to certificate, typically takes a matter of days.

Why filings get returned

The most common reason is inconsistency. The authorised capital in the memorandum does not match the FDI approval. The objects clause describes activity that the approval does not cover. A director named in the articles does not match the identification documents supplied. Each of these generates a query and a delay.

The second common reason is incomplete legalisation of foreign documents. A notarised document that has not been legalised where legalisation is required will not be accepted. This is worth confirming before the package is assembled rather than discovering at the point of filing.

The third is a name that has not been properly reserved. Name reservation precedes incorporation and should be completed before the documents are finalised, because the reserved name is what appears throughout the memorandum and articles.

What this means when you are preparing to file

The documents that move cleanly through the Registrar are the ones where the memorandum, the FDI approval and the identification documents tell the same story. Inconsistency between them is where time is lost, and it is almost always avoidable by preparing the package as a single coherent set rather than assembling pieces from different sources at different times.

If you are preparing an incorporation and want the document pack checked before filing, our team prepares and reviews memoranda and articles, coordinates the notarisation and legalisation of foreign documents, and files through CAMIS as a single engagement. Talk to us on WhatsApp at +977 9802356987, call +977 9802356987, or send a note through our contact page and we will come back to you within one working day.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between the memorandum and the articles?

The memorandum is the charter, defining the company externally: name, objects, capital and liability. The articles govern the company internally: governance, meetings, transfers and dividends.

Do the objects clause and the FDI approval need to match?

Yes. Activities described in the memorandum should be consistent with what the FDI approval covers. Inconsistency generates queries and delays.

Do foreign documents need to be legalised?

Documents executed outside Nepal generally need notarisation in the country of origin. For countries outside the Hague Apostille Convention, legalisation through the Nepal Embassy is also required.

How long does incorporation take once documents are complete?

A complete and consistent filing is typically processed by the Registrar within a few working days.

Can the model articles be adopted without amendment?

Yes. Adopting the model articles simplifies the review. Bespoke provisions are possible but must be consistent with the Companies Act.

Is the FDI approval letter part of the incorporation filing?

Yes, for a foreign-invested company. The approval letter is submitted alongside the memorandum, articles and identification documents.

Do documents need to be in Nepali or English?

Yes. Documents in another language need certified translation into Nepali or English before filing.

Can the registered office address be a residential property?

The registered office must be a physical address in Nepal where official correspondence can be served. Whether a specific address is acceptable depends on local requirements.

title: Double Tax Avoidance Agreements and Investing in Nepal
content:
Nepal has signed double tax avoidance agreements with a number of countries, and for foreign investors those agreements materially change the tax arithmetic of investing here. This guide explains what a DTAA does, which countries have treaties with Nepal, how the relief works in practice, and what you need to put in place to claim it.

What a DTAA actually does

A double tax avoidance agreement exists because income earned across two countries can otherwise be taxed twice: once at source in the country where it arises, and once in the investor's home country on the same income. The treaty allocates taxing rights between the two countries and sets reduced withholding rates on certain categories of payment.

For a foreign investor in Nepal, the practical effect is usually a reduced withholding rate on dividends, interest and royalties paid out of Nepal, compared with the domestic rate that would otherwise apply.

Which countries have treaties with Nepal

Nepal has signed agreements with India, Bangladesh, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Austria, Pakistan, China, South Korea, Norway and Qatar. Investors from these countries can generally access treaty benefits, subject to meeting the conditions.

Investors from countries without a treaty with Nepal are taxed under domestic law at the standard rates. That does not make investment unattractive, but it does mean the withholding position should be modelled using domestic rates rather than assuming a treaty reduction.

How the relief works in practice

Take dividends. Domestic Nepali law applies a withholding tax to dividends paid to a foreign shareholder. Where a treaty exists between Nepal and the shareholder's home country, the treaty may reduce that rate. The reduction applies automatically only in the sense that the law provides for it; the investor generally needs to establish eligibility.

The two conditions that matter most are residence and purpose. The shareholder must be a resident of the treaty country for the purposes of the agreement, and the arrangement should not exist primarily to access treaty benefits where the principal purpose is tax avoidance. In ordinary commercial investment structures neither condition is a problem, but both need to be evidenced.

What you need to claim treaty benefits

The documents that support a treaty claim typically are:

  • A tax residence certificate issued by the authorities in the investor's home country, confirming residence for the purposes of the agreement.
  • Evidence of the shareholding and the underlying investment.
  • Where the structure involves intermediaries, documentation of the ownership chain.
  • The relevant correspondence with the Nepali withholding agent or the Inland Revenue Office.

The tax residence certificate is the document most often missing. It is issued by the investor's home tax authority and should be obtained for each relevant financial year, not assumed to carry over indefinitely.

A worked example

An investor resident in a treaty country holds a stake in a Nepali company. Under domestic law, dividends paid to that investor would suffer withholding at the standard rate. Under the applicable treaty, the rate is reduced.

At the point of dividend declaration, the investor provides its tax residence certificate for the relevant year to the Nepali company. The company applies the treaty rate when computing the withholding, documents the position in its records, and reports accordingly.

Without the residence certificate, the company must apply the domestic rate. The investor can sometimes recover the excess later, but that process is slower and more uncertain than simply providing the certificate at the time of payment.

Where treaty planning matters before you invest

The choice of investing country is not always obvious. Two investors with identical operations in Nepal, investing from different jurisdictions, can end up with different after-tax outcomes on repatriated profits purely because of the treaty position.

This is worth modelling before you settle on the structure. If you have flexibility over which entity in your group makes the investment, and one of the candidate jurisdictions has a treaty with Nepal while another does not, that is a material input to the decision. It is not the only input, and it should not drive a structure that is otherwise impractical, but it is worth knowing before the structure is fixed rather than after.

It is also worth noting that treaty benefits generally require substance in the treaty country. A shell entity with no real presence may not qualify, and recent international standards on base erosion and profit shifting have made substance a more prominent consideration for tax authorities on both sides.

What this means for your investment

If you are investing from a country with a treaty, claim the benefit. It is available, it is legitimate, and failing to claim it means paying more tax than the framework requires. The discipline is in having the residence certificate and documentation ready at the time of payment rather than chasing it afterwards.

If you are investing from a country without a treaty, model the position on domestic rates and factor that into your return analysis. The investment case rarely turns on it alone, but it should not be a surprise once profits begin to flow.

If you want the treaty position reviewed against your specific structure before you invest or before your next dividend, our team can map the withholding position, the documentation required and the claim process. Frequently asked questions

What is a double tax avoidance agreement?

A treaty between two countries that allocates taxing rights and reduces withholding rates on certain cross-border payments, preventing the same income being taxed twice.

Which countries have a DTAA with Nepal?

India, Bangladesh, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Austria, Pakistan, China, South Korea, Norway and Qatar.

What document do I need to claim treaty benefits?

A tax residence certificate from your home country's tax authority for the relevant financial year is the key document, alongside evidence of the shareholding.

Does a DTAA eliminate tax entirely?

No. It allocates taxing rights and reduces withholding on certain payments. It does not exempt income from tax altogether.

Can I claim treaty benefits retroactively?

In some cases, with difficulty. The cleaner approach is to provide the residence certificate at the time of payment so the correct rate is applied from the outset.

Does my investing entity need real substance in the treaty country?

Generally yes. Treaty benefits typically require genuine residence, and structures without substance may not qualify.

Are dividends the only payment covered?

No. Treaties commonly cover dividends, interest and royalties, with different reduced rates for each.

What if my country does not have a treaty with Nepal?

Domestic withholding rates apply. The investment can still be viable, but the tax position should be modelled accordingly before you commit.

faqs.q: What if my country does not have a treaty with Nepal?
faqs.a: Domestic withholding rates apply. The investment can still be viable, but the tax position should be modelled accordingly before you commit.

title: Mergers and Acquisitions in Nepal: Process and Sector Rules
content:
Mergers and acquisitions in Nepal are governed by the Companies Act 2063 and, where market concentration is involved, the Competition Promotion and Market Control Act. The framework is established and workable, but the process has steps that catch people out, particularly where a foreign investor is acquiring an existing Nepali company rather than building one. This guide covers the mechanics, the approvals, and the practical points that determine whether a deal closes on time.

How mergers work in Nepali law

A merger under the Companies Act combines two or more companies into one, with the surviving company assuming the rights and liabilities of the merged entities. The broad sequence is:

  • The boards of the merging companies approve the merger proposal.
  • Shareholders approve the merger by the required majority.
  • Creditor notice is given, so that creditors can object if the merger prejudices them.
  • The merger is filed with the Office of the Company Registrar.
  • Assets, liabilities, contracts and permissions transfer to the surviving company.

The creditor notice step is one that parties sometimes underestimate. It creates a window during which creditors can object, and that window has to run before the filing can complete. Planning the timetable around it avoids surprises.

How acquisitions work

An acquisition, by contrast, involves one company purchasing shares or assets in another. In Nepal the more common structure for a foreign investor is a share purchase, where the buyer acquires shares in an existing Nepali company rather than buying its assets individually.

A share purchase has a particular appeal in Nepal because the company itself continues in existence, with its contracts, permissions, industry registration and tax history intact. What changes is the shareholding. That is generally simpler than an asset purchase, where each asset and permission has to be transferred individually.

The approvals that matter

Several authorities come into play depending on the transaction:

  • The Office of the Company Registrar for the merger filing or the change in shareholding.
  • The Department of Industry, where the company holds an industry registration and the change in control affects it.
  • Nepal Rastra Bank, where a foreign investor is acquiring shares in a company that has recorded foreign investment.
  • The Competition authority, where the transaction creates a level of market concentration that triggers review.

For a foreign investor acquiring shares, the NRB step is the one most often overlooked. An existing Nepali company with foreign investment has an NRB recording of that investment. When the shareholding changes, the recording needs to be updated, and where the buyer is itself foreign, the acquisition generally needs to fit within the FDI framework, including the minimum investment threshold and the sector eligibility test.

Due diligence in the Nepali context

Due diligence in Nepal follows the familiar commercial disciplines, but a few areas deserve particular attention:

  • Title to land and property, where ownership records and actual possession do not always align cleanly.
  • Tax compliance history, including whether returns have been filed consistently and whether any assessments remain open.
  • Industry registration conditions, including whether the permissions the company holds are transferable or personal to the existing shareholders.
  • Employment obligations, including whether statutory contributions have been made and whether any disputes are pending.
  • Contract change of control provisions, which may require counterparty consent on a change in ownership.

The tax history is the area where surprises most commonly emerge. A company that has not filed consistently can carry a liability that only becomes visible once the Inland Revenue Office is engaged as part of the transaction.

A worked example

A foreign investor wants to acquire a controlling stake in a Nepali manufacturing company. The company is profitable, holds an industry registration, and has no existing foreign investment.

The buyer conducts due diligence, covering title, tax, employment and contracts. Nothing disqualifying emerges, though two outstanding tax filings from earlier periods are identified and regularised before the transaction proceeds.

The parties agree terms and execute a share purchase agreement. The board and shareholders of the target pass the necessary resolutions. The change in shareholding is filed with the Office of the Company Registrar. Because the buyer is foreign, the acquisition is processed within the FDI framework: the Department of Industry is engaged, and Nepal Rastra Bank records the new foreign investment.

The industry registration is updated to reflect the new shareholding. Contracts with counterparties are reviewed for change of control provisions, and where consent is required, it is obtained.

From agreement to completion, a straightforward share acquisition of this kind typically runs three to six months, depending on the diligence findings and the speed of the approvals.

Where deals stall

The most common cause of delay is incomplete diligence. Issues found late in the process reset the timetable because they require investigation, renegotiation or restructuring. Front-loading the diligence, particularly on tax and title, compresses the overall timeline.

The second is underestimating the approval sequence. Where a foreign buyer is involved, the FDI, industry registration and NRB steps are sequential rather than parallel, and the timetable needs to reflect that.

The third is change of control provisions in material contracts. These are frequently not identified until late, and obtaining counterparty consent can take longer than the regulatory approvals.

What this means if you are transacting

M&A in Nepal is a well-trodden path. The framework is clear, the authorities are experienced with these filings, and deals close. The transactions that close on time are the ones where diligence is done thoroughly up front, the approval sequence is mapped before signing, and the tax history is understood before the price is fixed.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a merger and an acquisition in Nepal?

A merger combines two companies into one surviving entity. An acquisition involves one company purchasing shares or assets in another, with both continuing to exist separately.

Does a merger need creditor notice?

Yes. Creditors must be given notice and have the opportunity to object before the merger filing can complete.

Can a foreign investor acquire shares in an existing Nepali company?

Yes, subject to FDI eligibility, the minimum investment threshold, and the necessary approvals including the Nepal Rastra Bank recording.

Is competition review required?

Where the transaction creates a level of market concentration that triggers the Competition Promotion and Market Control Act, review may be required. Most transactions do not reach that threshold.

How long does a share acquisition take?

A straightforward acquisition typically runs three to six months from agreement to completion, depending on diligence findings and approval speed.

Do I need new FDI approval when buying shares in a company with no existing foreign investment?

Generally yes. The acquisition by a foreign buyer brings the company within the FDI framework, and the associated approvals apply.

Are change of control provisions a common issue?

Yes. Material contracts frequently contain provisions requiring counterparty consent on a change in ownership, and these are often identified late in the process.

Can industry registration be transferred to a new owner?

The registration is updated to reflect the new shareholding. The process involves the Department of Industry and should be planned as part of the completion steps.

excerpt: A practical guide to obtaining NRN Visa and Business Visa in Nepal for non-resident Nepalis, foreign investors, and businesspersons.
content:
Overview

Nepal offers NRN (Non-Resident Nepali) related privileges and business/entry visas for eligible foreigners and NRNs. The exact process is handled by Nepal Immigration and, for investment-related matters, coordinated with relevant authorities.

NRN Visa

NRN Visa may be available to eligible Non-Resident Nepalis as per prevailing NRN rules. Applicants typically need to establish NRN identity/status, submit required forms, and meet eligibility criteria.

Business Visa

Foreign nationals coming to Nepal for business purposes (investment discussions, company setup, meetings) can apply for business visa through Nepalese missions abroad or immigration as applicable. For those engaged in business activities in Nepal, appropriate visa category/renewals apply.

Key Steps (General)

  1. Determine eligibility (NRN certificate/status or business purpose).
  2. Prepare documents (passport, photos, supporting letters, investment/registration documents if applicable).
  3. Apply at Nepalese Embassy/Consulate or Immigration Office as per category.
  4. Pay prescribed fees and comply with interview/verification if required.
  5. Receive visa/endorsement and ensure compliance with visa conditions.

Practical Notes

  • Visa rules change periodically � confirm current requirements at the time of application.
  • For investment-linked visas, coordination with Department of Industry/Nepal Rastra Bank may be needed.
  • Overstay/visa violations carry penalties.

This article provides general information; for specific cases consult qualified legal counsel.

content:
Overview

Establishing a Montessori/pre-school in Nepal involves company/firm registration (if operating as institution), securing local approvals, meeting premises requirements, and complying with education-related regulations.

Typical Process

  1. Structure: Decide legal form (private company, partnership, or as appropriate).
  2. Registration: Register at Office of the Company Registrar (if company) or relevant authority.
  3. Premises: Secure suitable location with necessary approvals (municipality/building occupancy).
  4. Local/Municipal: Obtain business registration/license from local government as per Local Government Operation Act.
  5. Education Coordination: Check current requirements with concerned education offices/local authorities for pre-schools/Montessori.
  6. Tax/Other: PAN/VAT as applicable, staff compliance.

Key Considerations

  • Premises safety, space norms, sanitation.
  • Teacher qualifications may be expected per local norms.
  • Regulations evolve; verify latest requirements at time of establishment.

General guide only � confirm current requirements with authorities.

excerpt: Comprehensive overview of establishing a hospital/healthcare facility in Nepal including registrations, licenses, and regulatory approvals.
content:
Overview

Setting up a hospital in Nepal is highly regulated. It involves entity registration, land/premises, health facility registration/license, medical council/departmental clearances, fire safety, and other approvals depending on size/services.

Key Steps

  1. Legal Entity: Register company/organization as appropriate.
  2. Site & Infrastructure: Land, building plan approval, fire safety, environmental as applicable.
  3. Health Facility Registration: Apply for hospital/health institution registration/license with the relevant health authority.
  4. Human Resources: Ensure qualified medical personnel as per applicable rules.
  5. Other Approvals: Local government business license, PAN/VAT, pharmacy/drug related if applicable.
  6. Ongoing Compliance: Renewals, reporting, standards compliance.

Practical Notes

  • Requirements depend on bed capacity, specialty services, and ownership (public/private).
  • Foreign investment in healthcare may have sector-specific considerations.
  • Always verify current rules with the Ministry of Health/concerned authorities.

General informational guide � consult qualified legal/technical advisors.

content:
Overview

NGOs in Nepal are typically registered under the Association Registration Act (or as applicable). Registration is done at the District Administration Office (DAO) or as per prevailing rules.

Process

  1. Formation: Form a general assembly/founding members with clear objectives.
  2. Draft Documents: Prepare constitution/bylaws, objectives, structure.
  3. Registration: Apply at DAO with required documents and fees.
  4. Post-Registration: PAN, bank account, and comply with reporting obligations.

Key Requirements

  • Minimum founding members as per rules.
  • Clear non-profit objectives.
  • Registered office in Nepal.

Ongoing Compliance

  • Annual/general meetings, reports as required.
  • Maintain records and comply with tax/exemption provisions if applicable.

Verify current legal requirements at the time of registration.

content:
Overview

INGOs seeking to operate in Nepal require appropriate approval/affiliation from the concerned government authority (commonly Social Welfare Council as per prevailing framework) in addition to other registrations.

Key Steps

  1. Review: Confirm mandate and activities are permissible.
  2. Documentation: Prepare project agreements, constitution, country registration, and proposed activities.
  3. Application: Apply for affiliation/approval through the designated authority with required documents.
  4. Review & Approval: Authority reviews and may grant approval with terms/conditions.
  5. Post-Approval: Comply with reporting, project agreements, and renewals as required.

Important Considerations

  • Activities must align with approved objectives and development priorities.
  • Project-based agreements are common.
  • Strict compliance with reporting obligations.

excerpt: How to register a travel or trekking agency in Nepal: capital, bank guarantee, licence fees, documents, process, FITTA restrictions and compliance.
content:
Quick Answer

To register a travel or trekking agency in Nepal, you generally need to: decide agency type, choose legal structure, register business, meet capital and bank-guarantee requirements, apply for tourism licence, complete tax/local registrations, obtain route permits as needed, and maintain ongoing compliance.

1. Minimum Capital Requirements

Agency typeMinimum capital (published Rules)
Travel agency registered as a firmNPR 5 lakh
Travel agency registered as a companyNPR 10 lakh
Trekking agency registered as a firmNPR 3 lakh
Trekking agency registered as a companyNPR 6 lakh

2. Bank Guarantee Requirements

Agency typeBank guarantee (published Rules)
Travel agencyNPR 3 lakh
Trekking agencyNPR 2 lakh

3. Licence Fees, Validity and Renewal

RequirementFigure (published Rules)
Initial licence feeNPR 15,000
Renewal feeNPR 10,000
Licence validityFive years

Note: Figures are from the published Travel and Trekking Agencies Rules, 2062; confirm current consolidated Rules and Department of Tourism fee schedule before applying.

4. Foreign Investment (FITTA)

Foreign investment in tourism-related travel agencies, tourism guides, trekking and mountaineering guides, and homestays/rural tourism is restricted under the Negative List of FITTA, 2075. Obtain legal advice before accepting foreign shares/control.

5. Step-by-Step Process

  1. Define activities (travel/trekking/both)
  2. Choose legal structure (firm/company)
  3. Register business (OCR as applicable)
  4. Arrange capital and bank guarantee
  5. Apply for tourism licence to Department of Tourism
  6. Complete tax registrations (PAN/VAT as applicable)
  7. Obtain route permits if needed before operating

6. Key Documents (typical)

  • Firm/company registration certificate
  • MOA/AOA (for company)
  • Citizenship/identity of owners/partners/shareholders
  • Proposed name/address details
  • Ownership/shareholding details
  • Capital details
  • Bank guarantee documentation
  • Prescribed forms/declarations

7. Ongoing Compliance

  • Renew licence every 5 years and maintain bank guarantee
  • Tax/compliance obligations
  • Worker/insurance/reporting requirements as per Rules
  • Obtain destination permits for restricted routes

FAQs

What is the minimum capital for a travel agency in Nepal?

NPR 5 lakh (firm) / NPR 10 lakh (company) as per published Rules � confirm current requirement.

Can a foreigner own a travel/trekking agency?

Generally restricted under FITTA Negative List for these categories � verify proposed structure.

Which office handles licensing?

Department of Tourism (confirm current route/forms).

General information only � consult qualified Nepali counsel for your specific case.
